News.title: How ‘Mindhunter’ who claimed to have quizzed world’s worst killers was fantasist PC from Kettering exposed by The Sun
News.content:
KILLER CON How ‘Mindhunter’ who claimed to have quizzed world’s worst killers was fantasist PC from Kettering exposed by The Sun

AS a criminal profiler dubbed Britain’s Mindhunter, Paul Harrison had his audience entranced with chilling tales of the world’s most notorious serial killers.

A packed theatre sat spellbound as he recounted his ­meetings with Jeffrey Dahmer, Ted Bundy and John Wayne Gacy in a bid to work out what made them tick — and all at the request of the FBI.



The only problem was, none of it was true.

Harrison, also a true crime author, made an estimated £100,000 from sell-out shows like the one I attended at the Tyne Theatre in Newcastle.



But that event would prove to be the beginning of his end after I set about investigating his fantastical claims to have quizzed 70 of the world’s worst killers.

When The Sun published an exposé in 2019 — revealing that in reality Harrison had been a beat bobby in Kettering, Northants — he apologised to fans and vanished from public view.



But his incredible story is now being retold in an absorbing ­podcast called The Mindhunter.

Narrated by journalist Francisco Garcia, the six-part Audible Original show, out today, lays bare the full extent of Harrison’s deception.

As well as his criminal profiling claims, he also said he had been at gangster Reggie Kray’s death bed, had worked as a close personal protection officer for the King of Jordan and was the inspiration for numerous fictional television detectives.

He also reckons he worked as a firearms officer escorting nuclear convoys and as an undercover officer who had infiltrated a football hooligan gang.



In an earlier and even more bizarre chapter of his life, he even faked his own death amid a legal battle, claiming to have died on an archaeological dig in Egypt.

The case has striking parallels to that of Professor Jason Arday, the academic who last week quit Cambridge University over a string of dodgy claims about his achievements.

Fantasist Harrison targeted the world of true crime rather than academia but, just like Arday, his sparkling CV went unchallenged for years.



Following his supposed death in Egypt, he re-emerged a few years later, claiming to be one of the world’s foremost experts on criminal psychology.

Harrison alleged that he first worked with the FBI in 1982 when agents invited him to its Quantico academy after he wrote to them out of the blue about his interest in profiling.

He said he was given access to America’s most infamous killers on an almost daily basis and worked on and off with the FBI for a decade.

As well as Dahmer, Bundy and Gacy, he said he had met Charles Manson and Amityville Horror murderer Ronald DeFeo.

Harrison told his audiences: “Ted Bundy walked in like Liam Gallagher. He had a look of contempt on his face. He slowly walked behind me and stopped right behind me.



“Every part of my body was telling me to look round as you’ve got Ted Bundy behind you. I sensed him move forward, I felt his body heat on me. Then he bent down.

“He sniffed me and I thought this is going to be horrific, but he said, ‘I can smell your cologne’.”

In his book Mind Games, Harrison boasted that Bundy told him he was the “guy who gets inside our heads”.

He said he worked with the FBI’s pioneering Behavioural Science Unit which features in the film Silence Of The Lambs and the Netflix series Mindhunter, leading to his nickname of Britain’s Mindhunter.



Harrison’s growing profile meant he landed a regular slot on the CBS Reality channel as a criminal expert and was able to splash out on a ­Jaguar, which he drove to his shows.

He also claimed that Peter Sutcliffe invited him to Broadmoor so they could discuss writing his life story — but that they failed to hit it off.

Harrison said in an interview: “He said to me, ‘Why are you so cold towards me? You seem completely indifferent to me. I’m scared of you’.

“I wanted to tell him what I thought. I said to him, ‘Good. I don’t like you’.”



Harrison also claimed that notorious London gangster Reggie Kray wanted him to write his life story, and that they became such close pals he invited him to visit him on his deathbed in 2000.

But his barely believable claims — and his lucrative career — fell apart when The Sun began investigating.

It is not easy to prove someone did not do something they claimed they did, especially when it was decades ago in the pre-internet age.

I knew that the only way we could publicly accuse Harrison of being a fantasist was to methodically unpick every one of his claims.

I had a contact who had links to the Krays’ inner circle who was able to check for me whether he had indeed been a friend of Reggie’s.



Former Krays henchman Freddie Foreman responded with the message: “Reggie Kray was not a friend of Paul Harrison. He wouldn’t entertain the police in his company and he certainly wasn’t at Reggie’s final days.”

Another contact was close to the Yorkshire Ripper and was able to ask Sutcliffe whether he had ever invited Harrison to Broadmoor.

His response, in a letter passed to The Sun before his death in 2020, was even more cutting, calling Harrison a “charlatan, a con man and a wazzock”.



He added: “He never corresponded with me, nor did he ever visit me.”

Crucially, I needed to check ­Harrison’s claims that he had worked for the FBI.

The agency’s press office would not help with staffing matters so I tracked down former agent Mark Safarik, who did work in the Behavioural Science Unit for 12 years.

He told me: “I have never heard of Paul Harrison. He is making all this up.”

Not only that, Mark reached out to a number of other former agents, seven of whom confirmed they had never heard of Harrison.



The most bizarre chapter of Harrison’s life came in 2010 when he sued Carlisle United over the copyright of some photos the club had used. As well as being a Leeds fan, Harrison is a Carlisle supporter and has written a number of books about the club.

But he had a falling-out with them over the snaps and took the club to court in a case which would have left him with a hefty legal bill had he lost. It was lined up to be heard at Romford County Court in London but the court then received a letter to say Harrison was dead.

Fellow Carlisle fan Neil Nixon heard the news and wrote an obituary in a fanzine, but was then stunned to discover Harrison was still alive.

Neil said: “He sent me an email to tell me he’d been through some really difficult stuff. I was left thoroughly bemused.”

Harrison has been married four times, with his third marriage to Mandy Doyle falling apart after we published our investigation.



Mandy said: “When he started the serial killer talks he got bigger and bigger. It was amazing and the money he made was ridiculous. He would come home with wads of cash.

“I think he made around £100,000, easily, but his books were all fiction.

“I did the research on the killers for him. He never met any of them.” When he was exposed, Harrison posted on Facebook to say: “I’ve let everyone down, I’m sorry.”

He has never responded to The Sun’s requests for comment and did not respond this time either.

But he did send an email to the podcast team answering some of the claims against him.



However, he did not respond to the claims that he was never a criminal profiler, had never spoken to Peter Sutcliffe and was not present in Reggie Kray’s final days.

In relation to the stories told in his show, he said: “I won’t discuss in depth the shows. I was always told they were good entertainment.

“The producers knew and were told they were for entertainment purposes.”

He denied writing the Facebook message apologising to fans, blaming it on his social media team. He did not deny an email was sent to people saying he had died, but did deny that he sent it.

He maintains that he did work as a protection officer for the King of Jordan, as a nuclear cop and as an undercover cop and that he had been the inspiration for TV detectives.



He described the claims that he made up his meetings with notorious serial killers as “false allegations” and said they would be dealt with in his own podcast in the near future.

Until then, fans of true crime — and all the other areas Harrison has written books about — can tune in to The Mindhunter to decide for themselves whether his incredible life is fact or fiction.

News.title: Labour MP accused of raiding historic cafe’s fridges during sombre D-Day trip after fellow backbencher missed ferry
News.content:
WORLD WAR BRIE Labour MP accused of raiding historic cafe’s fridges during sombre D-Day trip after fellow backbencher missed ferry

A LABOUR MP has been accused of raiding a historic cafe’s fridge on a sombre trip to Normandy to mark the anniversary of D-Day.

Amanda Martin is said to have barged into the kitchen and started helping herself to food at the Café Gondrée, the first place liberated by the Allies during the landings in 1944.



The visit last June caused further embarrassment when fellow backbencher Samantha Niblett reportedly missed the ferry over to France, then clashed with the organisers.

Both of them were later ticked off by Commons Speaker Sir Lindsay Hoyle.



A source told The Sun: “It was quite embarassing, really.”

Both MPs are understood to believe the episodes are “misunderstandings” and insist they did not misbehave.

They are also understood to deny being reprimanded by Sir Lindsay and instead said they discussed the “misunderstandings”.

The Speaker’s Office declined to comment.

A Labour spokesperson said: “Both MPs were honoured to visit France with the Armed Forces Parliamentary Scheme, which provides valuable insight into military life and the brave work our servicemen and women do to keep Britain safe.”

News.title: Gormless jobsworth who dreamt up ‘vertical drinking’ ban needs to sit down & shut up – life wouldn’t be same without it
News.content:
MY name is Dominic and I hereby confess to having been a vertical drinker for the past 40 years.

Probably 43, if I’m honest. I used to swig a little port from the family’s drinks cabinet on occasion, although my father began locking it not long after.



Of course, sometimes the vertical ­drinking has left me horizontal, but that is just a rite of passage through which we all must travel.

So I spluttered into my Stella this week when reading that the body which ­controls the naughty corner of devilry that is Soho — namely Westminster ­Council — is inexplicably continuing with its determination to force drinkers to sit down and sup up.

Their draught, apologies draft, plans outline a mission to reduce alleged anti-social behaviour and excess drinking, which they believe can be caused by those partial to a little erectile consumption.



Poppycock. Hogwash. Horseshit. Balderdash and associated exclamations — for this is an artic truck load of ­absolute bollockery.

In the 1940s, the forever-prescient George Orwell wrote that the pub was “one of the basic institutions of English life”, which “carries on despite the harassing tactics of non- conformist local authorities”.

I’ll drink to that.

The gormless grinch who conceived such misguided regulatory twaddle has probably never been invited down the boozer for some raucous ­merriment after work because nobody likes them.

This is where the magic happens. Stress relieved. Jokes conceived and relentless piss-taking received. No, their Friday nights are probably spent listening to The Lighthouse Family and watching reruns of Richard Wilson On The Road on the ITV player while sipping a lukewarm cup of camomile. Alone.



Perhaps a few hours scrolling through the Plane Finder app and rearranging book shelves in alphabetical order before dreaming up further jobsworth gibberish to justify their non-job and then undoubtedly early to bed.

My life as an old-school vertical drinker has helped me form some of my most enduring friendships, assisted my career and improved my sex life, even ­leading me to marriage.

Cheers indeed.

For my wife and I’s eyes met while sampling a sherbet perpendicularly — and not long after we were tippling together in a rather more horizontal position.

I have been offered many jobs too while enjoying a spot of casual VD-ing.



Some of the best business deals, talent signings, newspaper headlines, silly ­feature ideas and columns have been agreed and composed during this sacred act of upright imbibement, an essential cog in British society and bloody good for one’s mental health too.

I’ve done drinking vertically, diagonally, sideways, curled up. Thinking drinking. Sometimes sad drinking.

But, like many things in life, I’ve always preferred doing it standing up.

I’ve got up and guzzled eye-to-eye with several Prime Ministers, an heir to the throne and a queen, Liam from Oasis, Rod The Mod, the Chancellor of The Exchequer, a couple of Home Secretaries, Zoe Ball, Pierce Brosnan, Damon Albarn, Chris Evans, Tina Turner and Christopher Biggins, among others.

Soho, the most creative square mile on Earth, was built on outdoor drinking and it is why gazillions flock to its hedonistic streets from around the globe.



Many fine hostelries will be forced to close if such legislative buffoonery is allowed to pass. Imagine all the extra charges that will be added to our table-serviced rounds too — and who wants to be forced to sit down when you’ve been stuck at an office computer all day?

Drinking breaks down barriers and inspires creativity, particularly when face-to-face while clutching a jar and indulging in a spot of vertical bantering, overhearing conversations nearby, and butting in while befriending strangers and watching footie. We call it F.U.N.

Let us call last orders on this non- sensical twaddle. Sit down and shut up ­Westminster Council.

Get your meddling hands off one of our finest traditions, a delight to Dickens, ­celebrated by Shakespeare and adored by Orwell, all pub-lovers who lit up ­literature and sold the British dream across the planet.

It is time to stand up for vertical drinking.



THAMES WATER A DRIP – OFF

SO, let me get this straight. Thousands of homes and businesses were left without water after a huge Thames Water main burst in East London this week, leaving many to queue in blistering heat for supplies.

Another exploded close to my home a few days ago, leading to a major route being closed, causing traffic hell.

Britain’s biggest water company is drowning in debt of £18.5billion.

Last year it was handed a record fine of £122.7million by the regulator, who said it had “let down its customers and failed to protect the environment”.



In other words, they’ve pumped your street’s turds into a chalk stream at a local beauty spot.

In the past year, Thames Water boss Chris Weston saw his pay increase 14 per cent to £1.63million. Bonuses are supposedly barred after government intervention.

But now we learn that Britain’s worst-run company paid its new finance chief a £1million signing-on fee last month. Chairman Sir Adrian Montague described the payment as a “necessary incentive”. Tosh. It is a devious way around the bonus ban.

Thames Water, which supplies 16million people across London and the Thames Valley, recently warned it only has enough cash to last until the end of the year, putting pressure on the new Government to decide what to do with it.

I’m with Burnham on this one. Our water companies are conspiring against us, rather than working for us. Thames Water certainly should be taken under public ownership.



They’ve been taking the piss for too long. And the excrement. And then pumping it straight into our rivers and seas.

An abhorrent dereliction of public duty and one which scars this country and must not be allowed to happen again.

BRITAIN may feel broken, immigration is out of control, our prisons full and high streets collapsing, but bananas are now growing on trees in tropical Dorset. So, as far as I’m concerned, all is right with the world.

So, as far as I’m concerned, all is right with the world.

J-LO AND BEHOLD…I GUESS SHE CAN BE A DIVA



JENNIFER LOPEZ is obsessed with the colour white and is one of the world’s biggest divas, according to some goon who worked on Top Of The Pops decades ago.

I interviewed the singer-turned-actress 20 years back in Philadelphia and actually found her witty and down-to- earth – nothing like her Jenny From The Block persona. She was even better looking in the flesh and wasn’t wearing anything pale.

But newly single Jen has brushed off the criticism and owned it, posing for a snap in her pants and bra, both white of course, looking rather like a diva.

So –for journalistic reasons, you’ll understand – I am obliged to reprint it here.

IF Amazon boss Jeff Bezos is successful in acquiring 30 per cent of Liverpool FC, does this mean delivery of the Premier League title will be guaranteed the next day before 10am – the trophy lobbed over Anfield’s Shankly Gates along with a message saying nobody was in?



BEASTIE THEFTS BETTER

IN the late 80s, we had the family’s Volkswagen Golf badge nicked after Mike D of the Beastie Boys wore one around his neck in a video as a fashion statement.

The culprit was never found but the sight of logo-less VW grilles was common in Thatcher’s Britain.

Now, the badge theft trend is here again, but with very different motives. Apparently, the logos now contain radar sensors required for driver-assistance features and can be flogged for hundreds of pounds online after being snaffled in a matter of seconds.

Crooks are using drones to locate VWs and, in an organised spree, 70 were stolen in just four days across South East London.



Life was so much simpler in the 1980s, when we stole in the name of fashion, not profit.

BRILLIANT Lucy Davis from The Office, who captivated millions of us with her portrayal of Dawn, has revealed a devastating diagnosis of incurable breast cancer.

Lucy, 53, is the daughter of comic Jasper Carrott and has vowed to fight her terminal illness with ­humour. The animal lover also says she is looking forward to being reunited with her terrier Gracie, who passed away in 2024, and is “at peace” in her life.

To handle such a heartbreaking moment with such grace is worthy of all our admiration. The nation is with you, Lucy.

THE size of that uber-dinghy carrying 230 migrants on their cruise across the Channel . . .



At this rate, the ­smugglers are gonna need an even bigger boat for their next stampede.

Intelligence sources tell me this craft, above, is being readied for the next voyage to our ­promised land.

That’ll be some ­odyssey but, be sure of this: The crossing won’t last anywhere near as long as the film.

News.title: Stunning moment solar eclipse peaks in UK as moon covers nearly all the sun leaving Brits in awe at cosmic show
News.content:
THIS is the stunning moment the solar eclipse peaked in the UK with the moon covering nearly all of the sun.

Millions of Brits across the country were left in awe as they caught a glimpse of the best solar eclipse in almost three decades.



And footage showed the moment the unique moment occurred for lucky viewers who turned their eyes skywards tonight.

The moon was seen slowly moving across the sun this evening as the rare phenomenon reached its peak.



In a few minutes, only a sliver of the brightly shining sun was left visible thanks to the cosmic show.

Brits could not hold back their excitement as they were caught on camera watching the rare phenomenon unfold before their eyes.



In other footage captured tonight, crowds cheered as a once-in-a-generation eclipse reached its peak in the UK.

Viewers were seen holding their phones aloft as temperatures dropped slightly with darkness falling across the country.



As much as 95 per cent of the sun was obscured by the moon for certain parts of the country as the eclipse peaked.

Many had gathered at viewpoints, including beaches and parks, across the nation as the incredible celestial event got underway.

The UK reached the totality of the eclipse at 7.10pm.

News organisations were able to use specialist cameras to film it and keep the momentous occasion on record.

Between 90 and 96 per cent of the sun was covered as the sky darkened across Britain.



This scale of eclipse coverage will not be reached in the UK again until 2081.

It comes after some Brits even took holidays to Spain and Greenland in order to see the total solar eclipse – the first of it’s kind since 1999.

Parts of Spain have now experienced a total solar eclipse for the first time since 1905.



Meanwhile, football fans in Austria are watching the Solar eclipse with special glasses ahead of the UEFA Super Cup 2026 match between Paris Saint-Germain and Aston Villa.

In Iceland, the Sun was completely covered by the moon – known as totality.

Brits had scrambled to get their hands on protective solar glasses as looking directly at the eclipse risks serious eye damage.



Many used who couldn’t get their hands on protective glasses used colanders to watch the shadows of the eclipse.

Huge queues were seen outside the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, South East London, as desperate viewers tried to get a pair.

Another stunning spectacle is set to take over skies soon after the magic of the total eclipse.

Between midnight and 5.30am on Thursday morning, Brits can enjoy “one of the most dramatic things to see in the night sky”.

A dramatic meteor shower will peak overnight tonight, shortly after the UK experiences its deepest eclipse since 1999.



The Perseid meteor shower occurs annually between July and August, however, tonight’s display is set to be one of the most impressive yet as it coincides with a new moon, meaning the sky will be darker than usual.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Described by Royal Museums Greenwich as “one of the most dramatic things to see in the night sky”, the meteor shower has been active since July 17 and will continue until August 24.

The number of meteors increases every night throughout this time-frame, peaking during the early hours of Thursday, August 13.

News.title: Lindsay Clancy’s lawsuit against doctors hits roadblock after they make under-the-radar move during her murder trial
News.content:
LINDSAY Clancy’s psychiatrist – who faced a brutal grilling on the stand during her murder trial – is fighting back against a civil lawsuit filed by the mom who killed her three children.

Dr. Jennifer Tufts, who treated Clancy for severe mental health issues before she strangled her kids, is demanding a medical malpractice tribunal to decide whether the negligence case against her stacks up.



The move would see a panel including medical and legal experts scrutinize Tufts’ treatment of Clancy and decide whether there is evidence she failed her patient in the months before the horrific killings.

Documents obtained by The U.S. Sun reveal the legal move was made in Norfolk Superior Court in Massachusetts as Clancy’s blockbuster criminal trial plays out around 40 miles away in Plymouth.



Clancy filed the medical malpractice lawsuit in January 2026, accusing Tufts and other healthcare professionals and organizations involved in her care of failing to properly recognize and treat her deteriorating psychiatric condition before the killings.

Tufts began treating Clancy in September 2022 and saw her 14 times over nearly five months, with her final appointment taking place on January 23, 2023 – the day before the violence.

She never met the mom in person and all of their appointments were conducted virtually.

Clancy is accused of strangling Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan with exercise bands and leaving them in the basement of the family’s Duxbury home.

She then jumped from a second-story window in a failed suicide attempt that left her paralyzed.

The horrific scene was discovered by her husband at the time, Patrick, who had been out running errands.



Clancy’s defense argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors maintain she planned the murders and committed them in cold blood.

Tufts has since emerged as a key figure in the case that has gripped the nation, with her treatment of Clancy coming under intense scrutiny during the trial.

But while attention has been focused on the dramatic scenes unfolding in the courtroom, the psychiatrist has quietly been fighting a parallel legal battle behind the scenes.

If Tufts’ request is granted, the tribunal would bring in experts to look at her treatment of Clancy and decide whether there is enough evidence to back up Clancy’s claims.

Tufts insists there isn’t – and is hitting back hard at the psychiatrist Clancy has brought in to make her case.



Dr. Whaley claims Tufts should have spotted signs that Clancy may have been suffering from bipolar disorder with psychotic features before the killings.

But Tufts’ lawyers argue there were no clear warning signs at the time, pointing out that Clancy repeatedly denied wanting to kill herself or anyone else and said she was not experiencing hallucinations.

They accuse Whaley of looking back at her behavior through the lens of what later happened to the children, dismissing his conclusions as “speculation and retrospective analysis.”



Whaley has also criticized the medication Clancy was given, claiming she should have been treated with a mood stabilizer or antipsychotic.

Tufts’ lawyers hit back that she did prescribe lamotrigine, which is used as a mood stabilizer, and say overlooking that key detail leaves his opinion “fatally flawed.”

The filing comes after defense attorney Kevin Reddington spent hours grilling Tufts at Clancy’s murder trial over many of the same issues now being fought over in civil court.

Tufts had an impressive academic background but was still early in her career as a psychiatrist when Clancy landed in her care.

She studied psychology at Cornell University, went to medical school at the University of Vermont and completed her psychiatry residency at Boston Medical Center.



But she had only finished her residency in July 2022 and was just starting out in private practice when she began treating Clancy – something Reddington seized on during his blistering cross-examination.

He grilled Tufts over her experience with serious postpartum conditions and at one point likened her approach to that of a box-checking “robot.”

Reddington also hammered home that Tufts never once met Clancy face-to-face.



He questioned why she had not obtained complete records from her other doctors and highlighted that the mom had called a suicide hotline twice – something Tufts admitted she did not know.

Reddington then picked apart her prescribing decisions, including increasing Clancy’s Amitriptyline shortly before the killings, suggesting the change had “pushed her over the edge.”

Tufts fired back, “I don’t think so.”

And in another striking exchange, she told the court, “I do not believe that I’ve been negligent.”

The psychiatrist is one of 11 defendants – seven individual medical or mental health professionals and four healthcare organizations – named in Clancy’s civil lawsuit.



Her ex-husband Patrick, who has also taken the stand during her criminal trial, separately filed a wrongful death lawsuit in January on behalf of himself and the estates of their three children.

His case names four defendants – Tufts, nurse practitioner Rebecca Jollotta, Aster Mental Health and South Shore Health System – all of whom also face claims in Lindsay’s case.

Patrick alleges those responsible for Lindsay’s care failed the family through allegedly uncoordinated prescribing and failures to respond appropriately as her mental health deteriorated.

Tufts has also asked a judge to dismiss Patrick’s case, leaving her fighting civil claims from both sides of the shattered Clancy family as the murder trial continues to unfold.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Her requests in both civil cases remain pending.



If you or someone you know is affected by any of the issues raised in this story, call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988, chat on 988lifeline.org, or text Crisis Text Line at 741741.

News.title: Parents publicly called out by cops for behavior when child went missing on beach – & they still ignored police warnings
News.content:
A CAREGIVER has been publicly blasted by rescuers after a child vanished on a busy beach in an incident officials branded “very preventable.”

Even after the youngster was found safe, emergency crews said they watched the adult immediately turn their attention straight back to their phone.



The alarming incident unfolded Monday at Mother’s Beach in Kennebunk, Maine, where the child had wandered away from the area where their caregiver was staying.

A search was launched before the youngster was eventually located safely and reunited with the adult.



But Kennebunk Fire-Rescue said what personnel witnessed next prompted them to step in.

“After the child was safely reunited with the caregiver, our personnel observed the caregiver immediately return their attention to their phone,” the department said.

Officials then gave the caregiver a “stern warning” about what had happened and their responsibility to watch the child.

The department did not identify the adult or reveal their relationship to the youngster.

It also did not say how long the child had been missing or how far they had traveled.

But officials said the youngster had reached “a completely different beach area” before being found.



The scare prompted the department to issue an unusually blunt public message to parents and caregivers.

“A Reminder to Parents and Caregivers: Phones Down. Eyes Up,” it wrote on Facebook.

Officials warned that keeping watch near the ocean requires constant attention rather than relying on lifeguards to notice when a child wanders off.

“When you are at the beach, pool, lake, or anywhere near the water with a child, put the phone down and keep your eyes up,” the department said.

“Active supervision means maintaining constant awareness of where your child is and what they are doing.”



Fire officials also hit out at the extra burden missing-child searches can place on Kennebunk’s Ocean Guards.

“Our guards are there to protect everyone using our beaches—they are not babysitters and cannot replace parental or caregiver supervision,” the department said.

The guards must normally scan the water for distressed swimmers, monitor changing conditions and respond to medical and life-threatening emergencies.

A search for an inadequately supervised child can pull their attention and resources away from those jobs, officials warned.

The department also stressed that drowning emergencies can happen quickly and may not involve the screaming or splashing many people expect.



It urged adults to stay alert even when lifeguards are on duty, saying their presence does not shift responsibility away from a child’s caregiver.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Phones down. Eyes up. Know where your children are at all times,” the department said.

“A few seconds of distraction near the water can have lifelong consequences.”

News.title: Fears over ‘Jaws-like’ shark attacks along US coast after social media trend draws predators closer to shore
News.content:
A SOCIAL media trend has local officials worried about an increase in shark encounters in the shallow waters in one US state.

The concerns come after a video went viral of a group of people seen pulling an eight-foot-long bull shark onto the beach.



Social media users are using bait to lure sharks close to shore to take part in land-based shark fishing, and it has a local New Jersey mayor concerned.

“It’s not illegal to fish here. It’s not illegal to fish for shark, but it is bringing in predators, they’re looking for food and there’s a lot of swimmers here,” Bay Head Mayor Bill Curtis told CBS News.



Curtis said he is alarmed by videos showing people attracting the predators to shore just to take photos with them.

The mayor is concerned that the bait used to reel in the sharks is bringing them dangerously close to the beach where there could be unsuspecting swimmers.



“Putting food in the water there for the fish to go after is just luring them closer to shore,” he said.

Some shark fishers paddle out to 15-foot-deep waters to drop bait, and then pull in sharks from reels on the beach.

A group of anglers called the East Coast Shredderz have reeled in several sharks in July and August, including bull and tiger sharks.

The group reels in the beasts before taking a few photos and releasing it back into the water.



With all of the social media attention, East Coast Shredderz put out a statement about the importance of responsible shark fishing.

“We do NOT chum the water,” the statement began.

“We should be using common sense and choosing responsible times to fish — preferably when lifeguards are off duty and people are no longer swimming.

“If you’re on a crowded beach and people are in the water, don’t drop baits in the middle of swimmers just because you want to fish.”



East Coast Shredderz also talked about the need to respect the sharks.

“Don’t unnecessarily drag sandtiger sharks or other sharks far out of the wash just for a picture or video.

“Keep the fish in the water as much as possible, handle them properly, and get them released safely and quickly.”

The group advised that those new to shark fishing go with an experienced group, use proper gear and equipment “and know what you’re doing before putting a shark in that situation.”



Captain John Schaible took a CBS News crew out into the area where shark fishers might drop bait, and said he doesn’t think what the shark fishing groups are doing is dangerous.

“They are just having fun,” he said. “They’re not killing them. They’re maybe taking a couple pictures with them and letting them go.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Everybody can coexist, just be a little careful with what you are doing,” Curtis told CBS.

“Common sense and consideration for everybody.”

News.title: Double killer and rapist given whole life sentence
News.content:
A serial sex attacker who had a "morbid fascination" with sex has been jailed for the rest of his life after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later. Earlier that year, he raped a third woman in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC sentenced Levy to a whole life order, meaning he will never be released.

The sentence comes after police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) apologised over a series of disastrous decisions that left him free to roam the streets.

When Levy carried out the attacks, he was on bail and being monitored by the Met.

The police watchdog is currently examining how he was managed over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

Following Wednesday's sentencing, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the handling of Levy's case was a "whole system failing".

News.title: Burnham urges shops not to sell disposable BBQs over wildfire risks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has urged shops to stop selling disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister said he was urging "all retailers big and small" to adhere to voluntary guidance to suspend sales during extreme heat.

He added that in the "longer term" the government would look at potentially banning the single-use grills during summer months.

It comes after a potential ban was discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures.

A number of large retailers and supermarkets have voluntarily stopped selling the devices under a framework, external agreed in 2023 between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

This says that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.

Earlier, Burnham told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

After the Cobra meeting, Burnham said: "We would say to retailers do not put disposable barbecues on sale at this moment in time."

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

News.title: Students wait for A-level, T-level and BTec results
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive A-level, T-level and BTec results on Thursday morning.

Another record number of students are expected to find out they have secured a place at their first choice of university.

The cost of going to university has been in the spotlight this year, with mounting pressure on the government to reform student loan repayments and a renewed focus on technical education under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

But the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents more than 140 vice-chancellors, urged students to not "let politicians make your decision for you".

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer.

Around 250,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications are also expected to be released to students in England, including BTec National, Cambridge Technical, Cambridge Advanced National and T-level results.

AS-levels, which will count towards students' final A-level results next summer in Wales and Northern Ireland, will also be released.

This year, the pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board.

And last year, the proportion of students getting top A-level results reached a record high, with 28.3% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland marked at A* or A.

News.title: Trump says White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post
News.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of the month, President Donald Trump has announced.

Leavitt, whom the president called one of his "most trusted aides", will depart from her role to spend time with her young children and family - "a decision I totally understand and respect", Trump wrote in a social media post.

"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," he added.

Leavitt, 28, took the job as White House Press Secretary last year - becoming the youngest person to ever have the role. It was not immediately clear who will replace her.

Leavitt welcomed her second child, a baby girl, with husband Nicholas Riccio in May. She also has a two-year-old son. She returned to work from maternity leave last month.

She wrote on X following the president's announcement that her job has been "the honor and adventure of a lifetime".

"Being a mother and welcoming a new baby while working in one of the most demanding jobs in the world has been the most rewarding yet challenging season of my life, to say the least," she wrote.

"The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary - and that is why I have ultimately made the bittersweet decision to depart the White House and embark on a new chapter in my life," she continued.

Before her tenure at the White House as press secretary, she had a long career working with Trump, first as an assistant press secretary and speech writer during his first term in office.

She later went on to become a top aide to New York Republican congresswoman Elise Stefanik as communications director.

In 2022, Leavitt unsuccessfully ran for Congress in New Hampshire, emerging victorious from a contested Republican primary, but ultimately losing to Democrat Chris Pappas.

She later became a spokesperson for Maga Inc - a pro-Trump fundraising group - before joining his 2024 electoral campaign as national press secretary.

News.title: Jasper Carrott says family is 'so proud' of Lucy Davis after cancer diagnosis
News.content:
Actor and comedian Jasper Carrott has spoken about his pride and love for daughter Lucy Davis after she announced she has incurable breast cancer.

The actress, best known for playing receptionist Dawn Tinsley in BBC sitcom The Office, has received an outpouring of support since she revealed her diagnosis on Tuesday.

Carrott, who was one of the most familiar faces on British television over several decades, told BBC News: "This is a very difficult time for the whole family and we have been supporting her in every way possible since her diagnosis.

"We are so grateful for all the support we have had over this trying time and we are very hopeful for her future being what she wants it to be."

He added: "We are so proud of our daughter and love her so much. The way she has conducted herself through many traumatic health issues is a lesson to us all.

"We would request privacy for the coming months, but thanks once again for the love and concern shown by so many people."

Carrott, whose real name is Robert Davis, became a household name in the 1970s thanks to his stand-up comedy and novelty songs.

He has presented programmes such as Canned Carrott, Golden Balls and Carrott's Commercial Breakdown, and acted in comedy series such as The Detectives.

News.title: Ministers push ahead with housing asylum seekers on ex-military sites
News.content:
Home Office minister Anna Turley has said the government is sticking with plans to accommodate asylum-seekers on former military bases despite protests from local residents.

She told the BBC the government's priority was to ensure asylum-seekers were looked after in a "secure" and "appropriate" place.

That included disused Ministry of Defence properties because they had on-site facilities and were "more contained," she added.

But campaigners in areas earmarked for asylum centres have said small communities with limited infrastructure would not be able to cope with large numbers of people.

There have been protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a site near the village.

Mike Nixon, the vice-chairman of Piddington Parish Council, said there was a "huge amount of concern and worry" among residents and that an asylum centre would have a "dramatic effect" on the way they lived their lives.

The proposal has prompted Piddington to hold a symbolic independence referendum, asking its 400 or so residents if they want to remain part of the UK.

Nixon said: "We're still very frustrated. Andy Burnham did say that he's willing to listen, but we've had no formal contact. No consultation, nothing from the Home Office.

"We felt that the only way of making our views felt was to say 'well if we're not going to be listened to, what's the point of being a part of the country?'"

The government has promised to end the use of hotels for asylum seekers, announcing on Wednesday that a further 13 across England had been closed.

It plans to use former military sites instead with two already up and running - RAF Wethersfield in Essex, and Crowborough Training Camp in East Sussex.

In June, it announced proposals to open three more, including the site near Piddington.

The two other planned sites are a former RAF base in Barnham in Suffolk where there were protests last week and RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire where the area's Labour mayor said it was "simply the wrong place".

Defending the proposals on BBC Breakfast, Turley said the public wanted the government to end the use of hotels, pointing to how an "iconic" hotel in Blackpool, the Metropole, was no longer being used to accommodate asylum-seekers.

She said it sent "an important message" that the government wanted the hotel to be part of Blackpool's future.

"The priority is to ensure we look after asylum seekers in a secure place that is more appropriate and we limit the impact on communities."

Asked what she meant by secure, she said: "Examples we are looking at is former military bases and we have two up and running and possibly another three.

"They have have facilities on site and are more contained and it limits the impact on on communities.

"We are looking at other sites such as former industrial sites, student accommodation - accommodation that is more more appropriate than hotels."

News.title: River Danube's low water levels reveal remains of WWII soldiers and motorcycle
News.content:
The bodies of two World War Two German soldiers have been found in Budapest's Danube river, due to record-low water levels after an intense drought.

Found alongside their remains were the identification tags of the two soldiers, a largely intact German army Wehrmacht motorcycle, a wedding ring and a Kuban shield - a combat badge of the Wehrmacht, the German War Graves Commission said.

The remarkable finds have sparked hope that some families could finally discover the fates of their ancestors, more than 80 years on from the war.

"Now begins a puzzle, in which we will try to determine the identity of the two dead," Arne Schrader, of the German War Graves Commission, told German newspaper Bild.

The wreck in the Danube was reportedly discovered on 2 August, when a passersby reported part of the motorcycle protruding from the rocks on the riverbank in downtown Budapest.

The team also found anti-tank mines, leading to the temporary closure of the riverbank as a bomb disposal unit was deployed.

Some of the items found in the river, notably the identification tags and motorcycle, are remarkably well-preserved due to the mixture of harbour sludge and oil found on the river bed, the German War Graves Commission said.

The commission is a German non-profit organisation that searches, recovers and buries the war dead on behalf of the German government.

The motorcycle is thought to be a DKW NZ 350-1 model, the organisation said, which was produced specifically for wartime use from 1944.

The commission added that of the two tags found, one belonged to a Wehrmacht soldier, and the other to a member of the Waffen-SS, which was declared a criminal organisation responsible for war crimes at the Nuremberg Trials.

News.title: Ann Widdecombe's loved ones gather for her funeral
News.content:
Police officers and sniffer dogs were in the grounds of the abbey ahead of the service, which lasted about 90 minutes.

The private requiem mass included a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, Abbot of Buckfast.

He said: "In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this Abbey Church which Ann called her safe haven."

A statement from the Abbey Church earlier said Widdecombe would be "missed and fondly remembered" and "many in our worshipping community knew her as a kind and warm character".

"Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics," it said.

It added: "Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant."

The order of service also included tributes paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe's nephew, and Sir Christian Sweeting, a close friend.

A public memorial for Widdecombe is due to be held later this year.

News.title: New Forest wildfire continues as temperatures rise
News.content:
Firefighters on the fourth day of battling a wildfire in the New Forest are facing "challenging" weather conditions with temperatures set to rise again

The blaze began on Sunday 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31, with 23 drivers abandoning their vehicles as the fire took hold.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews had implemented fire breaks and had a 'good hold' of the perimeter of the fire, while changing wind conditions were proving challenging.

National Highways said repairs to the A31 were not expected to be begin until Friday 14 August at the earliest.

News.title: Green councillor charged with assaults
News.content:
A Birmingham Green Party city councillor has been charged with attacking a member of the public, three police officers and a member of police staff.

Siobhan Harper-Nunes, 66, was arrested on suspicion of assault after police were called to the junction of Monument Road and Hagley Road in the city, at about 17:00 BST on Thursday.

Harper-Nunes, of Monument Road, was charged on Friday.

West Midlands Police said that she was arrested again at Monument Road on Wednesday morning on suspicion of harassment.

She remained in custody while inquiries continued, police said.

Harper-Nunes will appear at Birmingham Magistrates' Court on 10 September on the assault charges, the force said.

The councillor was elected in May to represent the Ladywood ward for the city council.

She previously stood as the Green Party's candidate for West Midlands mayor in the 2024 election.

The Birmingham Green Party has been approached for comment.

News.title: Estonia rejects proposals to take prisoners from UK jails
News.content:
The Estonian government has rejected the idea of taking prisoners from the UK to help ease the overcrowding crisis in British jails.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta told the BBC Estonia would not rent jail cells to other countries while it was housing criminals from Sweden in its half-empty Tartu prison under a deal signed last week.

The Conservatives and Reform UK have both suggested renting cells in foreign prisons, including in Estonia, to free up space and prevent the early releases of some offenders in England and Wales.

The Labour government also explored the idea in 2024 but talks with Estonia came to nothing.

Pakosta said Estonia had received no proposals to rent its prison space from the UK, adding that if one was to be made "our answer would be unequivocal - in Margaret Thatcher's famous words: No. No. No."

She added: "Such a proposal would not merely be mistaken, misguided or unacceptable; it would deserve to be rejected outright."

Thatcher memorably repeated "no" three times in 1990 speech, as she fiercely rejected calls for deeper political and economic integration of the European Community, which later evolved into the European Union.

In 2024, the Labour government, when Sir Keir Starmer was prime minister, held talks with Estonia to discuss the Baltic state's policy to house some prisoners from abroad.

Pakosta previously told the BBC she had met then-UK Justice Secretary Shabana Mahmood in Lithuania.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham's government is planning to release thousands of prisoners early this October, as it scrambles to free up space in jails almost at 100% capacity.

On Monday, Downing Street did not rule out renting space in foreign prisons, when asked by reporters if the government was considering doing so.

A No 10 spokesperson said the government was focused on "creating that extra capacity within the system domestically".

"In terms of renting prison places abroad, it's just not a quick fix," the spokesperson added.

"It will require primary legislation underpinned by a complex international agreement which would take several years to agree."

A government source told the BBC that renting foreign prison space would not help with the short-term crisis in jails.

Burnham has ordered the justice secretary to come up with a plan to create more space in jails by September.

He said the plan would be based on removing more foreign national offenders from prisons, releasing some offenders on indefinite sentences, and using space in women's jails for male inmates.

News.title: Victim of fatal Clapham shooting named
News.content:
A man who was shot dead in south-west London has been named by police as Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa.

Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor pub.

The 25-year-old, who worked as a bus driver, was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.

A 22-year-old man was later arrested on suspicion of murder after attending hospital with a gunshot wound on Tuesday. He remains in hospital under police guard.

Det Ch Insp Claire Guiver said her thoughts were with the victim's family as they "come to terms with this tragic incident".

News.title: I share concerns over Arday appointment, says Cambridge University head
News.content:
The vice-chancellor of the University of Cambridge has said she understands the concerns raised by the appointment of Jason Arday and shares them too.

In a letter to staff, Prof Deborah Prentice acknowledged the "anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case".

The university head also announced Cambridge's investigation would be independent and carried out by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge and will begin "as soon as possible".

Arday resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education last week amid allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements.

The 41-year-old - who became Cambridge's youngest ever black professor in 2023 - denies any plagiarism and said the recent furore had led to "an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack".

In a letter to university staff, Prof Deborah Prentice said: "I fully understand the concerns being raised across the University and well beyond it, regarding Jason Arday's appointment and I share them...

"We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago.

"That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge."

The findings of the investigation, previously announced on Friday, will inform a review into the process for the appointment of senior academic roles, the university has said.

Prentice added "our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements, and the contributions they make" and said the case "should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge".

Cambridge had previously said allegations of plagiarism regarding Arday's thesis and some journal publications had been investigated by Liverpool John Moores University (LMJU) and the journals in question.

LJMU - which awarded his PhD in 2015 - had investigated the allegations that were made last year, and found he did not commit plagiarism.

In an interview with the Times, Arday defended himself by arguing that he had not received adequate supervision during his PhD given his autism and "learning disabilities".

The University of Cambridge said it had advised people to contact the relevant institution or pass on complaints.

But after Cambridge announced its own investigation, some academics pushed for the inquiry to be independent, questioning whether the university could adequately investigate its own processes.

It is not yet clear how the independent investigation will work or who will lead it. The university said it will look at the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education in 2022 and his time in Cambridge since his appointment.

Arday worked as a PE teacher before earning his doctorate at LMJU and going on to become an associate professor at Durham University and professor of sociology of education at the University of Glasgow.

Glasgow has also announced a review into Arday's previous academic post.

When he resigned from his post, Arday said he was not a "liar" and that his resignation "should not be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me."

News.title: Windermere signs to warn of algae poisoning risk
News.content:
Dozens of signs warning people about the dangers of algae poisoning are to be placed around England's largest lake.

About 40 notice boards alerting visitors to blue-green algae blooms, which can produce toxins that make humans ill and be fatal to pets, will be installed at Windermere, in the Lake District.

Blooms occur naturally but are more frequent during warm, dry weather and are exacerbated by nutrients from phosphate in pollutants such as sewage.

Funded by the Environment Agency (EA), a further 40 signs will be placed at other locations across Cumbria.

The Love Windermere Partnership, which includes organisations such as the EA, Lake District National Park Authority and United Utilities, said it was installing the permanent signs in response to requests for "clearer and more consistent public information".

As well as explaining what blue-green algae looks like, the notices will provide guidance on where to find current information about blooms and how to report suspected sightings using the Bloomin' Algae app, external.

The microscopic organisms can look like blue-green paint, scum or greenish-brown discolouration.

News.title: Burnham warned Iran war could hit UK growth next year
News.content:
Andy Burnham has been warned that the UK economy could barely grow next year if disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues until the end of 2026.

Treasury sources have confirmed that internal modelling presented to the new prime minister and chancellor suggests UK GDP growth could be as low as 0.3% in 2027, as first reported by Bloomberg.

Government officials say they routinely plan for all possible scenarios.

The UK economy saw a strong start to the year, but growth then faltered with the conflict in the Middle East affecting some businesses. The Iran war has pushed up oil and fuel prices, and also disrupted supply chains.

On Thursday, official figures will show how much the economy grew between April and June of this year.

Economists are expecting growth of 0.4% for the three months.

Burnham and Chancellor John Healey were presented with a reasonable worst-case scenario of the Strait of Hormuz remaining effectively closed for the next five months, and no permanent US-Iran peace deal until the new year.

The Treasury modelling for that scenario was that the UK economy would grow by 0.9% over 2026 - slightly under the 1.1% forecast by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March.

The prospect was much dimmer for next year, with just 0.3% growth projected - much lower than the OBR's 1.6% forecast for 2027.

Under the modelling, inflation would peak at 4.3% in the first three months of next year. It currently stands at 2.6%, just above the Bank of England's 2% target.

The prime minister and chancellor will face pressure to use the upcoming Budget on 28 October to ease the financial burden on households and businesses.

Since taking office three weeks ago, Burnham has announced policies including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to "subscription traps".

But this week he told the BBC's Wake up to Money the announcements, aimed at tackling the cost of living, are not enough on their own, hinting at further support.

He has asked Healey to look at what more the government can do on the cost of living in the Budget, with the chancellor saying it will be his "main focus".

But Healey has said he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â which will limit how much the government has to spend.

Burnham has said his government will stick to the party's 2024 manifesto pledges not to increase people's income tax, VAT or National Insurance contributions.

He also promised to follow the fiscal rules imposed by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, which include a pledge to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenues by the end of the decade.

News.title: Man bled to death after being bitten by American XL Bully, court hears
News.content:
A man died from extreme blood loss after suffering "catastrophic injuries" when he was bitten on the leg by an American XL bully in his daughter-in-law's garden, a court has heard.

Keven Jones, 62, from Chester, who was in poor health, taking methadone and blood thinning medication, was staying at Chanel Fong's house at the time of the incident.

The incident took place before XL Bullies were added to the banned dog list in October 2023.

Fong, 33, denies being the owner of the dog, which the prosecution said was dangerously out of control at the time, and also denies an alternative charge of being the person in charge of a dog at the time of the attack.

Opening the case at Caernarfon Crown Court, prosecutor Mark Connor said it was a "sad and tragic case for everyone concerned" and told the jury they would be shown some "graphic images" of Jones' injuries during the trial.

He said it was not a case of whether the XL Bully, named Cookie, was a banned breed, but rather that the dog had been "dangerously out of control" and whether Fong was legally responsible for it, either as its owner or the person responsible for it at the time.

The court was told the dog was owned by Fong and her partner, Joshua Jones, the son of the victim, but that he was not present at the time of the attack.

Connor added that, in her police interview, Fong said on paper Cookie belonged to her partner.

He went on to describe how there were a number of dogs at the property on Holt Road in Wrexham, including Cookie and another XL Bully called Fire, who were in the back garden at the time.

Cookie's mother, an XL Bully called Rogue, was inside the property and was "in season" meaning she had been kept separate from the other dogs in the house.

News.title: Staying in a traditional hanok revealed a refreshingly slow side to Seoul
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

“Shh!” A tour guide raises her index finger to her lips, signalling for my group and I to keep it down. We are in the Bukchon Hanok Village in central Seoul, next to the famous first palace of the Joseon Dynasty, Gyeongbokgung. Hordes of tourists, charmed by the area’s low-rise, wing-tipped houses and hilly streets are wielding selfie sticks. Many are clad in hanbok (traditional dress) from nearby rental shops.

Wearing the hoop-skirted dresses or flowing wraparound jackets is a popular sightseeing activity, but this isn’t technically a tourist attraction – the neighbourhood is residential; a labyrinth of around 900 tightly-packed hanoks (traditional houses).

My guide was not simply a spoilsport either; the nearly 6.4 million tourists who descend on the area annually has led local authorities to deploy uniformed rangers to manage the overtourism. There are signs imploring people to “talk quietly please”, and curfews too.

The area is just as novel to most locals as it is to visitors. Only around 4,500 hanoks remain in the city, mostly scattered across pockets in the central Jongno-gu area. The majority of the nearly 9.6 million locals reside in high-rise apartment blocks, or apateu, which shot up apace after the 1960s – to the sacrifice of historical and traditional buildings; many of which were already destroyed during the Korean War and the Japanese occupation.

Museums like the Namsangol Hanok Village offer the chance to see painstakingly restored single-storey hanoks, made from all natural materials: wood, clay, stone and paper; and laid out as they would have been used during the Joseon Dynasty.

However, there is a way to get a much more intimate glimpse into life in a hanok – by staying in one.

open image in gallery Old meets new: Namsangol Hanok Village and the Seoul Tower in the background ( Getty/iStock )



On my final night in the city I had chosen to book one of the remodelled and restored hanoks located in Anguk near the Palace. Following a stay in a towering hotel with bustling corridors and sweeping views of the skyline, a private hanok offered the chance to sample a slower pace of life in the city.

My taxi driver had dropped me off beside an alley, signalling I’d arrived with a shrug. I couldn’t see another soul in the vicinity. I wandered down an alley, toward the pin drop on my maps app, until I reached an imposing wooden entrance gate, and heaved my 19kg of luggage over the threshold to find two smaller locked doors.

Once I’d successfully discerned which was mine (named “Stay Sunshine”), I tapped in my entry code, and ducked through the gate into a neat Taoist-inspired garden (designed as miniature, idealised versions of nature), before lowering my head again to go through the front door.

I discovered a cavernous, minimalist space. The kitchen-diner was equipped with all the useful items I could – and would never – have thought of. In a basket there was a steamer and indoor shoes. A tea set was waiting on the dining table. The bedroom even had an adjoining walk-in closet.

open image in gallery The miniature garden in a rental hanok in Seoul ( Butler Lee )



My hanok’s layout and style had been specifically designed for 21st-century living, though a few days earlier at the Namsangol Hanok Village, my Inside Asia guide Meggie Yu had explained how the the homes used to look, laid out to reflect Confucian social order, based on gender, age and status (no prizes for guessing whose quarters were largest). In all the kitchens, huge gamasots (cast-iron cooking pots) were the centre-piece.

I was taken by the ornate folding screens hand-painted with vibrant motifs, which would have reflected the occupant's wishes or ideals – mandarin ducks for marital harmony, and mountains for protection, for example.

The homes were positioned according to baesanimsu – a principle to ensure harmony with nature, meaning "mountain in the back, water in the front". And South Korea’s history of ingenuity is demonstrated perfectly in how they were adapted for the seasons, with ondol (underfloor heating) for harsh winters and wooden-floored maru halls for summer cooling.

My home for the night had plenty of mod-cons, from central heating to a Toto heated toilet, and a projector. Though it nodded to the past with a mattress close to the floor (previously a way to maximise that ondol heat), the low front door (to minimise how much cold air could seep in) and a traditional square soaking tub for jok-yok (ritualised baths or foot soaks).

Slowly, the numbers of people living in hanoks is rising. Meggie explained how more locals are now yearning for the way of living they offer versus the prevalent high-rise homes. “Korean people are enthusiastically returning to traditional styles and aesthetics, with an enhanced passion for wellbeing, as well as the younger generation's turn towards ‘slow living’. They are reinventing traditional buildings to suit the modern era.”

As well as the efforts to protect the community and homes of Bukchon, the government has been introducing more measures to help preserve hanoks across the city in recent years. Owners have been eligible for grants and low interest loans to restore them since 2002, and recently, the strict definitions (including the need to abide by baesanimsu) have been loosened in more hanok hotspots to allow people to carry out renovations, and to build them anew.

open image in gallery The bedroom of Hayley's modernised hanok stay ( Butler Lee )

It’s also common for Seoul residents to take “healing trips” to hanoks in the countryside in order to “relax and enjoy the quiet and clean air”, Meggie explained. I could see why.

After spending my evening in the neon glow of Seongsu – arguably the coolest neighbourhood of the moment, packed with fashion and beauty lovers attending its graphic pop-up shops and arty installations – I returned to my little residence and was struck by how peaceful the nearby streets were, lined with hanok tea houses and cafes.

To wind down, I soaked my feet in the bath, made tea and fired up the projector while cocooned in bed to watch Beef, the Netflix show set between Southern California and Seoul. I fought off sleep as long as I could, in denial that I was leaving the city in the morning.

The hanok was the homiest place I stayed in the city. I had lapped up the gleaming and edgy sides of Seoul – its spas, shops and late-night scene – but my final night was an opportunity to slow down, feel grounded and peek into its past. The perfect send-off.

Hayley travelled as a guest of Inside Asia



How to do it

Inside Asia can arrange hanok stays as part of a cultural adventure to South Korea.

Stay Sunshine is managed by Butler Lee who have around 50 hanoks in central Seoul.

How to get there

Virgin Atlantic operates direct daily flights from London Heathrow to Incheon International Airport in Seoul, starting at £889 economy. Flight time is around 15 hours.

News.title: Nick Reiner laid in wait before killing his parents, new indictment alleges
News.content:
The latest headlines from our reporters across the US sent straight to your inbox each weekday Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Your briefing on the latest headlines from across the US Email * SIGN UP I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

Nick Reiner has been indicted on murder charges in the deaths of his parents, actor-director Rob Reiner and Michele Singer Reiner, and he faces a new allegation that he was lying in wait before attacking them.

A grand jury indictment unsealed Wednesday replaces the case filed against 32-year-old Nick Reiner on December 16. His 78-year-old father and 70-year-old mother were found dead around 3:30 p.m. on December 14 at the couple’s home on Chadbourne Avenue, between Sunset and San Vicente boulevards.

The charges include a special circumstance allegation of multiple murders as well as the lying in wait allegation, though the indictment did not say how or why Reiner was lying in wait. Prosecutors also allege that Reiner personally used a knife in the commission of the crimes.

Reiner pleaded not guilty in court on Wednesday. He is scheduled to return on September 15 for a pretrial hearing.

open image in gallery Nick Reiner was arrested by Los Angeles police in the Exposition Park area near USC less than six hours after his parents' bodies were discovered ( Kevin Winter/Getty Images )

Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters outside court earlier this year that his office will be "looking at all aggravating and mitigating circumstances" and that Nick Reiner's attorney has been invited to present written and oral arguments before a decision is made on whether to seek the death penalty.

"It will be subject to not only a rigorous analysis, but many of the most experienced individuals in the D.A.'s Office with death penalty experience will be helping me evaluate that information," Hochman said.

Nick Reiner had been awaiting a hearing to determine whether there was enough evidence to require him to stand trial, but the grand jury indictment allows the case to proceed to trial more quickly.

The L.A. County Office of Medical Examiner classified the couple's deaths as homicides, with both dying from "multiple sharp force injuries."

The death certificates note they were killed "with knife, by another."

Nick Reiner was arrested by Los Angeles police in the Exposition Park area near USC less than six hours after his parents' bodies were discovered. He remains behind bars without bail.

Los Angeles Police Department Chief Jim McDonnell declined soon afterward to provide any details on what led to Nick Reiner being identified as the suspect.

open image in gallery Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters outside court earlier this year that his office will be ‘looking at all aggravating and mitigating circumstances’ ( Mario Tama/Getty Images )

In a statement released the day of their brother's initial court appearance, Nick Reiner's older brother, Jake, and younger sister, Romy, said, "Words cannot even begin to describe the unimaginable pain we are experiencing every moment of the day. The horrific and devastating loss of our parents, Rob and Michele Reiner, is something that no one should ever experience. They weren't just our parents; they were our best friends.

"We are grateful for the outpouring of condolences, kindness, and support we have received not only from family and friends but people from all walks of life," the two said. "We now ask for respect and privacy, for speculation to be tempered with compassion and humanity, and for our parents to be remembered for the incredible lives they lived and the love they gave."

Rob Reiner was best known for his iconic role as Archie Bunker's liberal son-in-law Michael "Meathead" Stivic on the classic sitcom All in the Family -- a role for which he won two Primetime Emmy Awards and directed films including Stand By Me, The Princess Bride, A Few Good Men, Misery, This Is Spinal Tap and When Harry Met Sally.

According to multiple reports, the couple's 28-year-old daughter discovered her father's body. One report suggested that a massage therapist had shown up at the couple's home for a pre-scheduled appointment but got no answer at the door and contacted their daughter, who went inside the home and found Rob Reiner slain. She contacted authorities, who subsequently found Michele Reiner's body in the house.

open image in gallery It was reported in December that Nick Reiner had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and was taking medications that made him ‘erratic and dangerous’ ( Michael Buckner/Getty Images )

Rob and Michele Reiner, along with Nick, attended talk-show host Conan O'Brien's Christmas party the night before, and sources said Rob Reiner and his son got into a heated argument over his son's odd behavior at the event. Rob and Michele Reiner wound up leaving the event, but it was unclear when Nick Reiner left. TMZ reported that Nick Reiner checked into a Santa Monica hotel around 4 a.m. the next day, and that blood was later found in the room.

It was reported in December that Nick Reiner had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and was taking medications that made him "erratic and dangerous."

Citing two sources with knowledge of the situation, TMZ reported that he had been under the care of a psychiatrist for mental illness, but that his behavior had grown more alarming in recent weeks.

Nick Reiner has been open about his struggles with drug abuse over the years, even working with his father to produce a 2015 semi-autobiographical movie titled "Being Charlie," based on Nick's drug-addiction issues and the family's struggles to cope.

In media interviews and podcast appearances, he previously described being in and out of rehab programs throughout his teen years, and spending time homeless in various states, including Texas, New Jersey and Maine. He also described an instance when he was high on cocaine for multiple days and trashed his parents' guest house.

Rob Reiner -- who was married for 10 years to actress/director Penny Marshall before they divorced in 1981 -- married Michele Singer in 1989 after meeting her while he was directing When Harry Met Sally. Reiner often told the story about how his romance with Singer led him to change the ending to the movie -- with the characters played by Billy Crystal and Meg Ryan reuniting rather than going their separate ways.

Rob Reiner was a vocal Democratic Party activist, helping to spearhead efforts to legalize same-sex marriage in California and to pass a 1998 initiative that created the First 5 California childhood-development services program, funded by a tobacco tax
