World.title: Building a Legacy: Abiodun’s urban transformation through housing, By Kayode Akinmade
World.content:
Drive along the Siun-Sagamu Expressway today and it is easy to miss how recently the landscape around Kobape was little more than open bush. Today, standing prominently on that corridor is Prince Court Estate — a thriving residential community of completed and occupied homes, with its own electricity supply, shopping mall, health centre, ATM gallery and security post.

It is more than an estate. It is a statement of what housing policy can become when it is conceived not merely as the provision of shelter, but as an instrument of economic development, urban renewal and wealth creation.

That is perhaps the most important story behind the housing transformation taking place quietly across Ogun State under Governor Dapo Abiodun.

When the first phase of Prince Court Estate took shape at Kobape, few would have imagined that it would become the anchor of a rapidly developing residential corridor. The estate has since expanded through four phases, while the surrounding area has recorded significant growth in residential and commercial activity.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The model has subsequently been replicated across the state. From Idi-Aba in Abeokuta to Sagamu, Itanrin in Ijebu-Ode, Ilaro and the Gateway Aviation Village at Iperu, the Abiodun administration has deliberately spread housing development across Ogun’s three senatorial districts.

The objective is clear: to ensure that the benefits of Ogun’s rapid economic expansion are reflected not only in factories, roads and commercial investments, but also in the quality and availability of homes for the people who live and work in the state.

Housing as economic policy

The significance of the programme lies in its architecture. The Abiodun administration has approached housing as both a social responsibility and an economic asset. Its portfolio cuts across affordable housing for ordinary families, premium housing for middle- and high-income earners, public-private partnerships, urban regeneration and the redevelopment of underutilised government assets.

The first phase of the Kemta, Idi-Aba scheme, comprising 150 two- and three-bedroom homes, sold out rapidly. That response was an early indication of the enormous pent-up demand for decent and affordable housing in Ogun.

At Kobape, some of the early Prince Court homes were sold to civil servants and members of the public for between about N4.95 million and N5 million. According to figures provided by the state’s housing authorities, similar properties are now worth substantially more on the open market.

That transformation is significant. It means the government’s intervention did not simply put roofs over people’s heads. For many early beneficiaries, it created an appreciating asset and opened a pathway to household wealth.

In a country where housing remains one of the biggest barriers to economic security for working families, that is a powerful dimension of public policy.

From estates to communities

The most striking feature of the Ogun model is that the government has not treated housing as the construction of isolated blocks of buildings.

Prince Court illustrates the philosophy. Electricity, healthcare, security, banking and commercial facilities have been integrated into the development, creating a community rather than merely an estate. That approach matters because modern housing policy is ultimately about the quality of life around the house.

A home without reliable infrastructure, access roads, security, healthcare, commerce and other essential services can quickly become another form of urban vulnerability. But when housing is integrated with these services, it becomes the foundation for a functional community.

This is where the Ogun intervention acquires a broader development significance. Housing generates demand for roads, electricity, water, retail, transportation, security and other services. Construction itself creates jobs across a long chain of activities involving artisans, engineers, architects, surveyors, suppliers, manufacturers, estate managers and financial institutions.

Every new estate therefore has an economic footprint that extends well beyond the walls of the individual houses.

Unlocking forgotten public assets

The administration’s housing philosophy is perhaps even more evident in its urban regeneration projects at Ibara in Abeokuta and Igbeba in Ijebu-Ode.

For decades, more than 200 civil servants’ quarters constructed over 50 years ago had deteriorated and become largely unusable across approximately 25 hectares of valuable government land.

The Abiodun administration chose not to allow those assets to continue decaying.

Instead, it moved to replace obsolete structures with modern buildings, producing more than 250 smart buildings across the two locations. The policy significance is substantial

Government land in prime urban locations is a finite public asset. When buildings on such land become obsolete and unusable, the state faces a choice: continue spending scarce resources maintaining failing structures or redevelop the land in a way that creates new value. Ogun chose the latter.

The result is not simply new housing. It is the conversion of underutilised public land into productive urban assets, while simultaneously modernising the physical character of some of the state’s most important government layouts. That is urban regeneration with a balance sheet.

A programme still gathering momentum

Far from winding down, the programme is expanding as the Abiodun administration enters the final stretch of its tenure.

The Ogun State Executive Council has approved another package of projects comprising 450 two-bedroom semi-detached bungalows with supporting infrastructure, 28 official quarters for members of the Ogun State House of Assembly, 28 sellable duplexes at the Ibara Government Reservation Area Scheme II and the reconstruction of the Ogun State Governor’s Lodge in Asokoro, Abuja.

Taken together, the approvals reveal the breadth of the administration’s housing and urban-development strategy.

The 450 bungalows will expand the supply of affordable housing. The Assembly quarters will provide modern accommodation for legislators and preserve institutional assets. The 28 Ibara GRA duplexes will unlock further value from a prime government location, while the reconstruction of the Governor’s Lodge will preserve an important state asset and provide a modern institutional facility.

The projects also reflect a broader government policy of replacing obsolete public infrastructure with modern, functional and durable facilities capable of serving the needs of a growing state.

That policy is particularly relevant to public housing and government quarters inherited from previous decades. Where structures have become severely degraded and rehabilitation is no longer economically sensible, redevelopment offers an opportunity to create more valuable, efficient and sustainable assets.

The new housing projects, meanwhile, extend the administration’s affordable-housing intervention while stimulating activity across the construction value chain.

From contractors and engineers to artisans, manufacturers, suppliers and service providers, housing construction generates employment and creates demand across multiple sectors of the economy.

The Ibara GRA Scheme II duplexes add another dimension: the strategic use of prime public land to generate modern residential assets, attract private investment and strengthen the value of the state’s property portfolio.

In that sense, the latest approvals are not isolated construction projects. They are part of a deliberate policy of combining housing delivery with urban regeneration, institutional development and asset optimisation.

The numbers behind the ambition

The scale of the intervention is reflected in the numbers. At a briefing in January on the 2026 housing roadmap, the Commissioner for Housing, Jamiu Akande Omoniyi, disclosed that Ogun planned to deliver no fewer than 3,000 additional housing units in 2026, backed by more than N100 billion allocated to the housing sector. The plan forms part of the administration’s broader ambition to deliver 10,000 housing units by 2027. (Punch Newspapers)

The commissioner had also said that more than 4,000 affordable housing units were delivered between 2019 and 2023, with additional units subsequently taking the reported delivery figure above 5,000.

The numbers are important not simply because they represent houses. They represent the scale of public intervention required to respond to a rapidly growing state whose strategic location next to Lagos continues to drive population growth, industrialisation and investment. Ogun’s housing challenge is therefore inseparable from its economic success.

As more factories, businesses and people move into the state, demand for housing will increase. A government that fails to anticipate that demand risks allowing economic growth to produce housing shortages, informal settlements and uncontrolled urban expansion. The Abiodun administration’s response has been to get ahead of that curve.

Housing the workforce of a growing economy

There is also a strategic economic dimension to affordable housing. Ogun has positioned itself as one of Nigeria’s leading investment destinations, with major industrial clusters and expanding commercial activity. But investors do not operate in isolation. Workers need homes. Families need schools and healthcare. Businesses need functioning communities around them.

Housing is therefore part of the infrastructure of investment. By expanding residential communities around major growth corridors, government is helping to create the conditions for a more balanced relationship between where people work and where they live.

That has implications for productivity, commuting, family welfare and the long-term sustainability of urban growth. It is why the state’s housing programme should not be viewed as a collection of government estates scattered across Ogun. It is part of the broader infrastructure supporting the state’s economic transformation.

The legacy taking shape

Perhaps the clearest evidence of the programme’s significance is the way individual projects have begun to alter their surrounding environments. Kobape is a case in point

What began as a housing project has become part of a broader residential and commercial ecosystem. The same principle is now being applied in other parts of the state, while the regeneration of Ibara and Igbeba demonstrates that the administration is also looking inward — renewing old government assets rather than endlessly expanding into new land. This is the policy legacy taking shape.

Governor Abiodun’s housing programme has evolved from providing houses to creating communities; from constructing buildings to unlocking land value; from meeting immediate shelter needs to supporting economic growth; and from developing new estates to regenerating ageing urban centres.

The ambition to reach 10,000 housing units is therefore more than a numerical target. It represents an attempt to institutionalise a housing culture in which government, private developers and residents all participate in expanding the state’s housing stock.

And the programme is not being designed merely as a legacy of photographs and commissioning ceremonies. The administration has repeatedly affirmed its determination to complete the projects it has initiated before the end of its tenure.

That distinction matters. A legacy is not defined by what a government announces. It is defined by what remains standing, occupied, functional and valuable after the government has left.

Across Kobape, Kemta, Idi-Aba, Sagamu, Ijebu-Ode, Ilaro, Iperu and the regeneration sites at Ibara and Igbeba, the evidence is increasingly visible.

The quiet transformation of Ogun’s housing sector is, in reality, part of a much larger story — one in which housing has been repositioned from a welfare item on a government balance sheet to an engine of urban renewal, economic participation, asset creation and social stability.

That may ultimately be one of the most enduring dimensions of the Dapo Abiodun legacy.

*Mr Akinmade is the Special Adviser to the Ogun State Governor on Media and Strategic Communication

World.title: ANALYSIS: #OsunDecides2026: How governorship election will be won and lost
World.content:
Residents of Osun State will go to the polls on Saturday to elect their governor for the next four years. The off-cycle election appears to be shaping up as one of the most competitive political contests in Nigeria since the 2023 general elections.

A total of 15 candidates have been cleared by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). However, the APGA candidate, Adesina Adeyemi-Doro, announced he was withdrawing from the race to support the APC candidate. He is, however, still expected to be on the ballot.

The three major contenders are Governor Ademola Adeleke of the Accord Party, who is seeking a second term in office; a former Commissioner for Finance, Bola Oyebamiji, of the All Progressives Congress (APC); and Najeem Salaam, a former speaker of the state House of Assembly, who is running on the ticket of the African Democratic Congress (ADC).

The others are Olanrewaju Farinloye (AA); Esan Olajide (AAC); Adeagbo Opawoye (ADP); Adewale Adebayo (APM); Clement Adesuyi (APP); Masilo Adeleke (BP); Taofeek Adeleke (NNPP); Saliu Oyelami (PRP); Ogunsakin Olalekan (YPP); and Adefemi Adesuyi (ZLP).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The PDP, Mr Adeleke’s former party, which ruled the state under former Governor Olagunsoye Oyinlola and on which platform Mr Adeleke was elected in 2022, is not fielding any candidate due to a leadership crisis at the national level. The governor dumped the party for Accord last December.

Issues shaping the poll

The race is intriguing, first, because Mr Adeleke’s party does not control the state’s local government structure, which is particularly important. After all, local governments are often regarded as the grassroots foundation of Nigerian politics. The leadership of the 30 local government areas in the state remain in dispute, although many people believe that they are currently controlled by the APC, Mr Oyebamiji’s party, which has chairpersons in all the councils.

After Mr Adeleke won the 2022 governorship election, the then outgoing governor, Gboyega Oyetola, conducted the local government elections, with his party, the APC, sweeping the poll. When the former assumed office, he dissolved the councils and held new elections, all of which were won by his own party, the PDP.

The local government dispute subsequently became the subject of a prolonged legal battle. After the courts declared the removal of the elected APC council chairpersons as illegal, and the Court of Appeal restrained the state government from removing them, the federal government withheld allocations to the councils. The Supreme Court later dismissed a suit filed by the state government over the withheld council allocations. The apex court ruled that only the local governments had the legal standing to bring such actions.

The judgments effectively restored the APC chairpersons to office, although the state government still refused to recognise them. The state government also argues that even if the council chairpersons were returned, their tenures have lapsed and they should not remain in office. The councils’ situation may impact Saturday’s polls.

Another factor that makes the race particularly interesting is that the faction of the transport union currently controlling motor parks across the state has sympathy for the APC. Politicians use the union members as enforcers during elections. Aside from that, some members of the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW) will be responsible for moving election materials from Registration Area Centres (RACs) to polling units and, subsequently, to collation centres on election day.

The faction forcefully took control of the motor parks about two weeks ago, with the support of the national leadership of the transport union, displacing the faction recognised by the state government.

These two developments have altered the political calculations in Osun State ahead of the off-cycle poll. In previous elections, control of the local government structure was a critical factor. Successive governors have typically sought to deploy local government machinery during election periods.

With the APC controlling the local government structures and the NURTW faction playing a role in moving election materials on election day, Mr Adeleke’s party faces an unusual challenge.

Despite being the incumbent party, the Accord Party appears overwhelmed at the grassroots and is now forced to navigate an electoral environment in which key structures traditionally controlled by the party in power are largely outside its control.

Battle of the West

Another unusual feature of the election is that the three leading candidates are all from the Osun West Senatorial District. Mr Adeleke is from Ede, Mr Oyebamiji is from Ikire in Irewole Local Government Area, while Mr Salaam hails from Ejigbo.

The district has historically been a battleground in Osun governorship elections. It comprises 10 local government areas, namely Aiyedaade, Aiyedire, Ede North, Ede South, Egbedore, Ejigbo, Irewole, Isokan, Iwo and Ola-Oluwa, and has a substantial voting population.

The 2022 election illustrates its importance. Mr Adeleke won Osun West with 144,558 votes, representing 53.49 per cent of the valid votes cast in the district, while Mr Oyetola polled 116,860 votes, or 43.24 per cent. Mr Adeleke’s particularly strong performances in his home councils, Ede North and Ede South, contributed significantly to his advantage in the district.

The western district has not, however, been a permanent stronghold of any single party. In the 2014 election, Mr Aregbesola won several councils in Osun West, including Ede North, Ede South, Irewole, Egbedore, Iwo and Ejigbo, even though some councils in the district were won by his main challenger, Iyiola Omisore. Mr Aregbesola eventually won 22 of the state’s 30 local government areas and secured re-election.

The 2018 election further demonstrated how closely fought elections in the district and the state could be. Mr Adeleke initially emerged with a 353-vote advantage over Mr Oyetola statewide, scoring 254,698 votes against Mr Oyetola’s 254,345. Following the supplementary election, however, Mr Oyetola overtook Mr Adeleke and won by just 482 votes.

The presence of three major candidates from Osun West, therefore, creates a different electoral calculation. Rather than the district serving primarily as a two-way battleground, votes that might previously have consolidated behind one of the major candidates will now be divided among three candidates.

Who’s feeling the heat?

Although Mr Adeleke enters the race with the strongest advantage of incumbency, including greater visibility through capital projects and welfare initiatives, the reality is that he does not control some of the state structures that could have strengthened his chances of winning. These include the security apparatus, as well as the local government and transport union structures.

The governor had planned to mobilise personnel of Amotekun, the state-owned security outfit, to monitor the election in collaboration with the police, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) and other security agencies. The police have rejected that move and banned Amotekun and other such paramilitary outfits from election duty. The police have also deployed 15,000 officers for the election.

Mr Adeleke’s campaign organisation, popularly known as the Imole Campaign Council, has repeatedly accused the police in Osun State of intimidating and harassing its supporters. The police have denied the allegations.

Bamidele Sallam, a federal lawmaker and chairman of the media and publicity sub-committee of the campaign council, said more than 60 leaders and members of the governor’s party are currently in police detention.

The campaign spokesperson, Pelumi Olajengbesi, also alleged that the governor’s supporters were arrested without justification and transferred to the Force Headquarters in Abuja. On 3 August, the campaign council petitioned the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), seeking the unconditional release of its supporters, who it said had been arrested and detained by the police.

The allegations escalated recently when the police raided the Osogbo residence of the Secretary to the State Government (SSG), Teslim Igbalaye, and arrested him alongside five others over alleged vote-buying.

The police said they recovered N4.8 million in cash, a Dynabook laptop, a photocopying machine, a printer, two voter cards and a voters’ register covering Wards 1 to 15 in Osogbo Local Government Area.

Mr Igbalaye was later released after the state government and the state House of Assembly intervened.

Amid the allegations and counter-allegations, some residents believe the police are being influenced by individuals within the Presidency to frustrate Mr Adeleke’s administration. However, no independent evidence is presented in these accounts to substantiate the allegation of presidential interference.

Isaika Osuntogun, a commercial driver in Osogbo, said many of his passengers believed the APC was using federal power to wrest control of Osun State from the opposition.

“The APC is using federal power to victimise Ademola. They want to deploy every means to hijack the state from the opposition. Ademola has really tried for us in Osun compared to what the APC left. That is what many people are saying,” he said.

Fatimah Irewole, a secondary school teacher in the Ife area of the state, shared the same sentiment. “The pressure is too much on Governor Ademola Adeleke. I don’t like how the Presidency has been victimising him. This is democracy; every candidate should test their popularity not through victimising.”

Mr Adeleke’s strengths

Mr Adeleke has significant visibility in capital projects, particularly road infrastructure, across the state’s three senatorial districts. In agriculture and food security, his administration has expanded support for rural farming by providing agricultural inputs and encouraging farmers to increase production.

The administration has also maintained a relatively cordial relationship with civil servants by ensuring timely salary payments, improving career progression, and regularly paying outstanding pension arrears.

Civil servants constitute arguably Mr Adeleke’s strongest support base ahead of the election. Although there is no single official, publicly available figure for the number of civil servants in Osun State, government payroll estimates and state data generally put the active workforce and other public-sector employees at approximately 35,000. The governor may benefit from a bloc vote from the workers.

Mr Adeleke also retains strong support in Ede, his hometown, and across significant parts of the Osun West political bloc. His administration’s populist, accessible and media-friendly style continues to resonate with many voters, particularly young people and civil servants, who prefer it to the technocratic style associated with previous APC administrations.

The governor’s dancing at public events resonates with the people, though the elite sees him as unserious.

Another factor that could benefit Mr Adeleke is the fragmentation of opposition votes. If the ADC succeeds in its perceived spoiler role by taking votes from the APC, Mr Adeleke could emerge victorious without securing an overwhelming majority.

Despite these drawbacks, the governor, who recently defected from the PDP to Accord because of the leadership crisis in the former, says he will win.

“Forget about me losing this election, I am confident I will win,” he told Arise TV in an interview.

In another interview, he said, “I’m so confident I’m going to win. If I could defeat an incumbent and now that I’m the governor, within two years, it’s unprecedented what we have achieved. I’m so confident that nobody can beat us there.”

APC’s strengths and weaknesses

Mr Oyebamiji, popularly known as AMBO, resigned as the managing director and chief executive officer of the National Inland Waterways Authority to pursue his governorship ambition.

His candidacy benefits from several factors. First is the federal advantage associated with the APC at the national level. Osun is believed to be the ancestral home of President Bola Tinubu. Consequently, there appears to be desperation on the part of the Presidency and the APC to win the state at all costs to avoid humiliating the president.

Second is the campaign structure built over the years by the APC and Mr Oyetola, under whom Mr Oyebamiji served as Commissioner for Finance during his single term as governor. Third is his access to influential business and political networks within Osun State.

However, Mr Oyebamiji’s biggest challenge may ironically come from Osogbo, the state capital, because of his link with the minister.

Some political actors in Osogbo believe that while he was governor, Mr Oyetola, who is President Tinubu’s cousin, failed to identify with the state capital. One frequently referenced example is the controversy surrounding the proposed siting of an army barracks in Osogbo. There were reports that the project could have been relocated to Iragbiji, Mr Oyetola’s hometown, before Osogbo leaders intervened and insisted that it remained in the state capital.

The episode has contributed to lingering suspicions among some political stakeholders that Mr Oyetola was averse to developing the state capital.

There are also deeper cultural and emotional grievances against the Oyetola political tendency. Critics accuse him of maintaining a distant political style, unlike former governor Rauf Aregbesola, who cultivated strong grassroots loyalty through regular interactions with traders, artisans, drummers and informal community groups. Accounts of Mr Oyetola’s perceived reluctance to give money generously during public engagements have also continued to shape his image at the grassroots.

The APC is also still dealing with the unresolved fallout between Mr Oyetola and Mr Aregbesola. Some supporters believe the two should have reconciled much earlier, given the influence and respect Mr Aregbesola continues to command among ordinary party loyalists.

Mr Oyebamiji, meanwhile, will need to demonstrate that his Ikire roots and the APC’s political structure can translate into votes across the wider district rather than only in his immediate base.

The former commissioner says he will win convincingly without rigging, as alleged by Mr Adeleke.

“Adeleke is already reading defeat on the wall. We have been to all the local governments, and we have entered into agreement with the people on inclusive government, and I am sure if the election holds today, I will win,” he said.

Mr Oyebamiji added, “Governor Adeleke is confused; that is why he is shouting about rigging. We are not like them in 2022 when they rigged the APC out through internal sabotage. This time, he should know that the people of Osun are the ones who will vote for APC and send him packing on August 15.

“My administration will put an end to lack of seriousness in government. We will make every kobo we invest in the development of Osun worth it and transform the lives of the people.”

The Aregbesola factor, Salaam’s gain

Mr Aregbesola remains one of the most influential political figures in Osun. He served two terms as governor and later served as Minister of Interior under the APC before defecting to the ADC, where he was appointed National Secretary of the faction led by former Senate President David Mark.

His supporters dominate several local political networks, especially among the youth and ward mobilisers.

If these loyalists fully align with the ADC, both Messrs Adeleke and Oyebamiji could lose significant votes in core progressive strongholds.

Still, Mr Oyebamiji’s camp retains support from important Osogbo stakeholders such as Olatunde Badmus, popularly known as Baba Twins, whose philanthropic reputation and influence among traditional rulers and federal appointees remain politically significant.

Mr Salaam, a former speaker of the state House of Assembly, may not enter the race as the outright favourite, but his candidacy remains unpredictable.

The ADC’s greatest strength lies in protest votes and anti-establishment sentiment. Many voters frustrated with both the Adeleke dynasty and the APC establishment may see Mr Salaam as a compromise candidate.

His strongest advantage is likely to come from the Aregbesola political machine. Such support would instantly transform the party from a fringe platform into a formidable statewide structure.

However, Mr Salaam, a doctoral degree holder, said some may vote for him because of the former governor, while others will not.

“I’m not Aregbesola’s man. Just because I know that people are myopic in their thinking, people think I do not know my worth. I can stand on my own, and I have been here since grassroots – local government, House of Assembly, speaker, I am not a dullard.

“I am proud to be with him, and I am not regretting it. With my level of exposure, I have a clear objective of what I want to do with my 10-point agenda. Some will vote for me because of Aregbesola. Some will not. People know me. They know my quality. On my own, I will be a man of myself,” he said.

The ADC may also benefit from younger voters, politically displaced APC members, and sections of Osogbo elites searching for a fresh political arrangement.

However, Mr Salaam faces serious obstacles. The ADC lacks the electoral infrastructure of the APC and the Adeleke political network. Its funding capacity may also be comparatively weaker. In addition, many voters may still perceive the election as essentially a contest between Mr Adeleke and the APC, while strategic voting could hurt the ADC if opposition voters fear splitting anti-incumbent votes.

Who has the best chance?

At the moment, Mr Adeleke appears to have a slight advantage. His incumbency, combined with the fragmentation of the opposition, remains a significant electoral asset. His populist image and strong statewide name recognition also give him an edge.

The governor could also benefit from tactical support in Osogbo. Osogbo and Olorunda Local Government Areas, both in Osun Central Senatorial District, have historically recorded some of the highest vote counts in the state, reflecting their large urban populations, concentration of civil servants, and significance as the state capital.

Osogbo and Olorunda could also prove crucial to the 2026 contest. The two local government areas have historically been important electoral strongholds for the APC, particularly during the Aregbesola administration.

In the 2014 governorship election, Mr Aregbesola polled 39,983 votes in Osogbo against Mr Omisore’s 11,513, while in Olorunda, he scored 26,551 votes against 8,483 for Mr Omisore. The two councils, therefore, gave the APC a combined margin of more than 46,000 votes.

Osogbo was also Mr Aregbesola’s highest-voting local government area in that election, underscoring the electoral importance of the state capital.

However, the historical pattern is not entirely fixed. The 2022 election showed that Mr Adeleke could make significant inroads into areas previously regarded as APC strongholds. This makes Osogbo and Olorunda particularly important in the current contest, as the APC seeks to reclaim its traditional advantage while the incumbent tries to consolidate the gains made in 2022.

For Mr Oyebamiji, a strong performance in the two councils could provide the APC with the kind of urban vote margin it has historically relied on. For Mr Adeleke, maintaining or improving on his 2022 performance there could compensate for any weakness elsewhere. With the election expected to be closely fought, even relatively modest changes in the voting pattern of Osogbo and Olorunda could have consequences for the statewide result.

Nevertheless, the APC could underperform in Osun Central if grievances against Mr Oyetola persist. Mr Oyebamiji’s chances will, therefore, depend largely on his ability to reconcile internal divisions within the party, rebuild its emotional connection with grassroots voters and prevent significant vote leakage to the ADC.

World.title: The 1945 general strike in the womb of history, By Ahmed Aminu-Ramatu Yusuf
World.content:
By 9 August, the strike became so severe that the residents of Beau telegraphed high ranking colonial officials in Lagos and Enugu, that the: “Labour situation Victoria division seriously deteriorating. Intimidation against loyal workers and assaults on Europeans increasing. Probable that more Police will be required and request 80 be ordered stand by in case of need.”

The first General Strike in the country was suspended on 6 August, 1945; that was eighty-one years ago. The suspension was by the African Civil Service Technical Workers’ Union (ACSTWU).

The strike lasted 45 days in the Lagos area; at least 53 days in the Northern and Southern regions; and 74 days in the “British” Cameroons.

Yet, the strike had been presented, first, as a Lagos affair; second, a Southern region affair; and third, as a strike by Southerners. So how general was the 1945 General Strike?

The strike was, without doubt, a Lagos affair. But why should it not be, when Lagos was the capital city of Nigeria, the seat of the national government, the economic nerve of the nation, the heartbeat of trade unionism in the country, the headquarters of nationalist politics, and the soul of a highly politicised and restless civil society?

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The strike was so successful in Lagos that even non-unionised workers in the public and private sectors joined it. Non-strikers were booed by Lagosians. Even army personnel, called to carry out skeletal services, were reported to be “reluctant to work owing to the jeers and insults of crowds.”

Large sections of the civil populace saw the strike as theirs. They gave credit facilities to the strikers, while daily paid workers were fed for free. In the Western provinces, the situation was not radically different from that of Lagos.

The General Strike began in the Eastern provinces at 0.00 hours on the 21st and 22nd of June, 1945. Enugu, the capital of the Eastern Province, was “principally affected” as all, with the exception of clerical workers, “came out” for the strike.

In Aba, the strike action was confined to the railways, while in the Onitsha Division, the Railway and P&TD workers fully observed it. In the former, there was, “widespread bewilderment that Government did not accede to the strikers’ demands in full or in part. Government being the source of all money should not have found it difficult to make a little more and save the general public the not inconsiderable inconvenience of ceasing its postal orders and drawing on its Savings accounts. After all a little more money to the workers would mean better prices for the farmers and who would deny the farmer a few more pence?”

In Port Harcourt, the Railway, Marine, Public Works, and Post & Telegraphs workers, with the exception of a few supervisory officers, joined the strike. The commercial workers of Dempster’s coal and wharf labourers also downed tools. The Township Conservancy labourers “struck for days, during which the work was done by prisoners.”

In Kaduna, nurses and printers joined and were reluctant to call off the strike, despite directives from their national unions in Lagos. While the printers repudiated their apex union for not actively participating “on grounds that it is contrary to orders of the Federation,” the nurses completely doubted the authenticity of the “telegram instructions” that they suspend the strike for humanitarian reasons.

So popular was the strike, and so widespread was societal support for the strikers that the Resident of Onitsha Province, Captain DPJ O’Connor, wrote: “There can be little doubt that the strike weapon will make its appearance periodically henceforth and… it is none the less proper to record here… that in all future “General Strike” there will be an increasingly Black versus White, racial atmosphere.”

In Yola, the Resident reported that the strike was “being conducted in an extremely friendly way and there is not the least likelihood of any trouble.”

In Plateau province, the strikers were reported to “have been well-behaved.”

The situation was not different in Zaria, where it was reported that the atmosphere was “one of cheerful resignation” and that there was “no violence, no any picketing and few threats.” There, the strike leaders kept warning strikers not to tamper with or destroy any government property, and that “anybody caught damaging anything will be responsible for his action.”

In Kaduna, nurses and printers joined and were reluctant to call off the strike, despite directives from their national unions in Lagos. While the printers repudiated their apex union for not actively participating “on grounds that it is contrary to orders of the Federation,” the nurses completely doubted the authenticity of the “telegram instructions” that they suspend the strike for humanitarian reasons.

In no other region did the traditional aristocrats so readily cooperate with the colonial authorities to break the strike than in the Northern provinces, for fear that the “apparent success of the agitators may draw further recruits to their ranks from disgruntled elements in the North.”

The Magajin Gari (District Head) of Jos expressed serious concern about what the “continued defiance of Government [will have] upon the minds of the general public, especially the Northern elements, and the increasing damage of confidence which is occurring.” He added that: “every day longer that the strike lasts is increasing the deep underlying bitterness, is hardening public opinion against all Europeans, and is creating a situation which will be more and more difficult to clear up afterwards. In a place like this the tendency is for the strikers to show increasing defiance and insolence, for the authority of the [strike] leaders to grow, for the Hausa corner boys to take up attitude of the strikers and to laugh at the Government.”

Even when the strike was suspended by the trade union movement, the strike leaders in Niger, Zaria and Plateau provinces, delayed to call off the strike because of their suspicion that the various telegrams and airmail letters were false and part of the government’s tricks to break the strike.

By 13 August, the strike had engulfed the entire plantations in the “British” Cameroons, with the exception of UAC Plantations in Bwinga, near Tiko. Four major reasons accounted for the delay in the “British” Cameroonian workers’ joining of the General Strike…. First, Cameroonian workers were not unionised and did not have any trade union experience. Secondly, they were largely agricultural workers, with little or no literacy, and were based in rural areas.

In the “British” Cameroon, plantation workers first joined the General Strike on 11 July, when about 1,500 rubber tappers in Kumba Province “struck without warning.” By 7 August, some 1,450 plantation workers in Moliwe, another 1,100 workers in Bota; and 700 workers in Likomba; among others, struck, bringing virtually “all transportation to a standstill.”

By 9 August, the strike became so severe that the residents of Beau telegraphed high ranking colonial officials in Lagos and Enugu, that the: “Labour situation Victoria division seriously deteriorating. Intimidation against loyal workers and assaults on Europeans increasing. Probable that more Police will be required and request 80 be ordered stand by in case of need.”

By 13 August, the strike had engulfed the entire plantations in the “British” Cameroons, with the exception of UAC Plantations in Bwinga, near Tiko. Four major reasons accounted for the delay in the “British” Cameroonian workers’ joining of the General Strike.

First, Cameroonian workers were not unionised and did not have any trade union experience. Secondly, they were largely agricultural workers, with little or no literacy, and were based in rural areas.

Thirdly, the “British” Cameroon, though divided into the Northern and Eastern provinces, were largely treated as an autonomous region, and it was the most inadequately administered in terms of labour and other matters.

Fourthly, the communication network was virtually non-existent. There were no railways connecting Nigeria and the British Cameroons, while the road network was equally non-existent. These restricted contacts between workers of both sides.

The General Strike continued on an “on” and “off” basis in the Cameroons up to September 1945. Whereas in Nigeria it had been suspended since 4th August 1945.

The 1945 General Strike was the first nation-wide action by Nigerians. It gave them a sense of national unity and consciousness.

Ahmed Aminu-Ramatu Yusuf worked as deputy director, Cabinet Affairs Office, The Presidency, and retired as General Manager (Administration), Nigerian Meteorological Agency, (NiMet). Email: [email protected]

World.title: CBN removes FX, government securities restrictions on discount window access
World.content:
The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) has removed restrictions on banks’ access to its Standing Lending Facility (SLF) arising from participation in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and primary auctions of government securities.

The apex bank disclosed the changes in a circular signed by CBN’s Acting Director, Financial Markets Department, Okey Umeano, on Wednesday.

The review followed an assessment of developments and existing market practices in the foreign exchange, money, and fixed-income markets, as well as the frameworks governing access to the SLF, Tenored Repo Operations, and participation in Open Market Operations (OMO).

The apex bank said the existing restriction on institutions accessing the Discount Window from participating in OMO auctions on the same day would, however, remain in force.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Restrictions on access to the Discount Window arising from participation in the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) are hereby removed,” CBN said.

It also stated that restrictions linked to participation in primary auctions of government securities had been removed.

The regulator also announced the lifting of the suspension of Tenored Repo Operations, saying the move would provide greater flexibility for liquidity management.

“The suspension of Tenored Repo Operations is hereby lifted. Accordingly, the CBN may conduct repo operations across approved tenors ranging from 4 to 90 days to support effective liquidity management, improve money market functioning and enhance monetary policy implementation,” CBN stated.

OMO participation framework

CBN further revised its OMO participation framework to allow a broader range of investors to participate in both primary and secondary OMO markets through Deposit Money Banks (DMBs).

It said eligible investors would include individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions, while DMBs would continue to submit bids and settle transactions on behalf of their customers.

“OMO participation (primary and secondary markets) shall be open to all eligible investors through Deposit Money Banks (DMBs). Eligible investors include individuals, corporates and non-bank financial institutions.

“DMBs shall continue to submit bids and settle transactions on behalf of their customers,” CBN said.

The apex bank added that the volume, tenor, and frequency of OMO issuances would continue to be determined by prevailing liquidity conditions and monetary policy objectives.

OMO auctions, CBN said, would also continue to use the existing single-bid auction format.

The new provisions take immediate effect, with CBN directing all banks, authorised dealers and other market participants to ensure strict compliance.

“All banks, authorised dealers and market participants are required to ensure strict compliance,” the apex bank said.

World.title: Malawi make history, reach first-ever WAFCON final after beating Algeria 3-1
World.content:
Malawi have reached their first-ever Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) final after defeating Algeria 3-1 in a thrilling semi-final in Rabat on Wednesday.

The Scorchers secured the historic victory at the Olympic Stadium in Morocco, continuing their remarkable run in their debut appearance at the continental tournament.

The match was a high-intensity contest, with both sides reduced to 10 players after receiving red cards during the first half.

The first dismissal came early in the game, before Algeria were also shown a red card roughly 20 minutes later as the physical battle intensified.

Despite playing with a reduced number of players, Malawi maintained their composure and eventually pulled away from their North African opponents to secure a 3-1 victory.

The result marks another landmark achievement for Malawi, who had already secured qualification for their first-ever FIFA Women’s World Cup after reaching the semi-finals.

CAF had noted ahead of the match that neither Malawi nor Algeria had previously reached a WAFCON final, meaning the winner would make history by becoming the seventh different nation to reach the final since the competition adopted its current format in 1998.

Malawi had reached the last four after defeating Ghana 2-1 in the quarter-finals, a result that also secured their place at the 2027 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

Their victory over Algeria now takes their extraordinary debut campaign one step further, with the Scorchers set to contest their first continental final.

World.title: How LASU’s Aerospace Engineering graduate, Adebanjo Oluolamide, achieved 4.97 CGPA
World.content:
By Enitan Abdulatwab

For Adebanjo Oluolamide, graduating from Lagos State University, LASU with a 4.97 CGPA was the culmination of years of academic discipline, research and relentless focus.

The Aerospace Engineering graduate emerged as the overall best graduating student for the 2025/2026 academic session, earning First Class Honours and the highest graduating score recorded by the university for the session.

4.97 / 5.00 CGPA. 🎓

Overall Best Graduating Student, Lagos State University (2025/2026).

Out of 8,653 graduates across all faculties, God did it! First Class Honours in Aerospace Engineering.

Full journey thread dropping soon.@LASUOfficial #LASUConvocation #Valedictorian pic.twitter.com/u69VpIp9fo — Samuel Oluolamide Adebanjo (@SamuelAdebanj19) August 12, 2026

Oluolamide celebrated the achievement on X, attributing the feat to God’s grace while reflecting on the effort that went into his undergraduate journey.

“4.97 / 5.00 CGPA. First Class Honours in Aerospace Engineering at Lagos State University. Official Senate Approval.

“All glory to God for His grace, wisdom, and strength every step of the way. What God cannot do does not exist!”

His success extended beyond his academic results, with the graduate also actively involved in research and other extracurricular activities during his time at LASU.

On August 9, Oluolamide disclosed that he had been named Scholar of the Year at the AESA-LASU Dinner, making it his second time receiving the award during his undergraduate studies.

Reflecting on the achievement, he said the recognition was a fitting end to years of hard work.

“Winning my 2nd Scholar of the Year title during my undergrad is the best way to close a chapter. Late nights, heavy research, and relentless focus paid off.”

His interest in research also earned him recognition beyond the university. In July, Oluolamide revealed that two of his research papers had been accepted for presentation at the Society of Petroleum Engineers’ NAICE 2026 conference in Lagos.

He had subsequently appealed for financial assistance to attend the conference and present his research, stating that he needed ₦200,000 to support his participation.

Oluolamide is among thousands of students expected to receive their degrees as LASU holds its combined 29th and 30th convocation ceremonies from August 14 to 23.
