World.title: Irakli Kobakhidze: “‘Deep state’ is trying to artificially fuel Russophobia in Georgia”
World.content:
“Radical anti-Russian sentiment in the country is being artificially fuelled and is part of a new campaign against Georgia,” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He said attempts to intensify Russophobia in Georgia were part of a plan carried out by agents of the “deep state”.

Kobakhidze recalled that the Georgian government had repeatedly said that, after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, the so-called “global war party” had tried to draw Georgia into the conflict and open a “second front” in the country.

The prime minister said this “window of opportunity” created an “existential threat” to Georgia and its population. He said calls for Georgia to join international sanctions against Russia soon followed. According to the government, complying with those demands would have had serious consequences for the country’s economy.

“Because the Georgian government refused to comply with these demands, pursued a sovereign policy and acted in the interests of the state, our country became a target for the European bureaucracy and Western leaders working in tandem with informal oligarchic forces,” Kobakhidze said.

He also addressed the sanctions imposed by Western countries on the Georgian government. According to Kobakhidze, pressure mechanisms, including sanctions, were already being used when the previous US administration under Joe Biden was in power.

Kobakhidze said the sanctions had targeted senior Georgian government officials, ruling party honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, judges, senior police officers and others.

He said the West had also used Georgia’s EU membership prospects as a tool to pressure the government.

“They failed to break the ruling party, which enjoys the support of the Georgian people, so now they are trying to use their agents to drag Georgia into a new provocation,” he added.

Kobakhidze said a “new stage of the attack” on Georgia, its people and its sovereignty had begun:

“This is a qualitatively new stage of the attack on Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s sovereignty, unfolding simultaneously on several fronts.”

Background

Several days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy letter addressing the issue of “Russophobia”.

In the letter, Kobakhidze discussed the links between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic political situation and the opposition’s position. He said the “global war party” benefited from the ongoing conflict in Ukraine because it wanted to “fuel Russophobia at the highest level among its agents around the world, including in Georgia”.

Kobakhidze accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current tough stance towards Moscow as “Russophobia”.

The letter reignited political disputes over the events of the 2008 war. This time, however, the debate focused not only on the circumstances that led to the war and Russia’s responsibility. The prime minister shifted the focus from Russia’s actions to the position of his Georgian opponents.

Georgian PM on “Russophobia”

World.title: Ilham Aliyev’s AzTV interview during Nakhchivan visit: industrial park, energy projects and Zangezur Corridor
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

On 11 August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. It was Aliyev’s 17th visit to Nakhchivan since he became president.

During the visit, officials held foundation-laying ceremonies and opened several facilities. Aliyev also visited historical sites and presented battle flags to military units.

The visit ended with an interview with Azerbaijan Television (AzTV), in which Aliyev outlined his plans for Nakhchivan’s development.

The interview focused on the autonomous republic’s economic and social development, energy security and transport infrastructure. Aliyev also discussed Nakhchivan’s place in Azerbaijan’s broader strategy, particularly its future development in conjunction with Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, territories that came under Baku’s control after the Second Karabakh War.

Key events during the visit

During the visit to Nakhchivan, President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva inspected work at the Shams-1 and Garbi Ufug solar power plants, which have a combined capacity of 50 MW.

One of the key events was the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park. It will be Azerbaijan’s second-largest industrial park by area, after the Sumgayit Industrial Park. A 300 MW thermal power plant is also planned for the site.

Nakhchivan’s total generating capacity currently stands at around 200 MW. Once the new plant comes online, this will increase by roughly half.

The visit programme also included:

the opening of the Nakhchivan Regional DOST Centre;

the presentation of new electric buses and an inspection of railway infrastructure reconstruction works;

the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan hotel complex, which is expected to be completed by around 2028;

the laying of the foundation stone for a social housing complex;

an inspection of restoration work at the Momine Khatun Mausoleum and the unveiling of a monument to architect Ajami Nakhchivani;

the presentation of Nakhchivan’s General Development Plan through 2044, which envisages expanding the city and increasing its population;

the presentation of battle flags to new commando units of the Separate Combined Arms Army.

Key points from the AzTV interview

Aliyev described his visit to Nakhchivan as a “sign of the autonomous republic’s comprehensive development”. He said every visit should produce concrete results. He highlighted strengthening defence capabilities, energy security, job creation, preserving historical and cultural heritage, and developing transport links as key priorities.

Defence and governance

Aliyev said Nakhchivan’s geographical position – particularly its lack of a direct land connection with mainland Azerbaijan – requires special attention to the region’s defence. He highlighted the creation of the Separate Combined Arms Army and new commando units as key steps.

According to the president, “Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces carry weight in the region”. He also said Nakhchivan had introduced a system of special presidential representatives, similar to the model used in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur. Aliyev said the benefits of this system of governance were already becoming apparent.

Energy

Nakhchivan has been fully supplied with gas for around 15 years, Aliyev said, thanks to a gas swap agreement with Iran.

The president also placed particular emphasis on the region’s solar energy potential. He said Nakhchivan was Azerbaijan’s most favourable region for solar power generation. More than 600 hectares of land have already been allocated for the development of this sector. The potential is estimated at at least 500 MW and could reach 1 GW in the future.

Aliyev also highlighted the growing role of the private sector. Projects to build solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 MW are already under way.

The president described electricity exports as a strategic priority. Iran and Turkey are currently the main destinations, but Azerbaijan ultimately hopes to export electricity from Nakhchivan to the European market as well.

Zangezur Corridor – TRIPP

Aliyev said that “the creation of the Zangezur Corridor was our initiative”, recalling that connecting mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, an integral part of the country, had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

He said he had insisted that a provision on the corridor be included in the trilateral statement signed by Azerbaijan, Russia and Armenia on 10 November 2020. Aliyev claims the Armenian side did not want to agree to this, but had no other alternative because continuing the war was not in its interests.

Noting that there had been no practical progress on the issue for five years, Aliyev said a solution emerged after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025, when the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) was launched.

Speaking about the current state of the work, the president said the Horadiz-Aghband highway was almost complete, with only minor technical issues remaining. He said construction of the railway was also progressing rapidly.

Aliyev added that a project for power transmission lines linking mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenia had already been prepared, and locations for the pylons had been identified.

Aliyev predicted that these projects would eventually turn Nakhchivan into one of the region’s key transport and energy hubs.

A unified development concept

The president stressed that Nakhchivan, Eastern Zangezur and Karabakh should develop under a unified concept. He said the geographical proximity of the three regions requires a common approach to their development.

Aliyev noted that master plans for cities in the territories that came under Azerbaijan’s control after the Second Karabakh War had already been approved. He also said he had ordered the preparation of a similar document for Nakhchivan. The “Nakhchivan City Development Master Plan through 2044” was presented to the president during the current visit.

Speaking about the region’s tourism potential, Aliyev said Nakhchivan had significant opportunities thanks to its rich historical heritage, scenic landscapes and clean air. At the same time, he acknowledged that the hotel infrastructure remained underdeveloped and that the existing hotels were generally of a low standard, hindering the growth of tourism.

He said that to address the problem, construction had begun on a new five-star hotel complex in the city centre. The project is expected to be completed around 2028.

Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

World.title: Child seats, rear-seat seat belts and alcohol interlocks: changes to Georgia’s traffic rules

Georgia plans to tighten road safety rules under the National Road Safety Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the government on 5 August 2026. The strategy includes changes in several areas.

At this stage, the measures remain proposals, and some will require further legislative amendments before they can take effect.

World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Breaking: Trump spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt to leave White House
World.content:
Donald Trump's top White House spokesperson, Karoline Leavitt, is leaving the role.

Ms Leavitt, who recently returned from maternity leave, said she had decided to quit the position to focus on being a mother.

"Since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve," Ms Leavitt wrote on X.

Mr Trump said Ms Leavitt would continue to be one of his "top outside advisors".

World.title: Men charged after alleged sex assault at train station as others go unreported
World.content:
The woman on the platform is scrolling on her phone to pass the time as she waits for the train to arrive.

Warning: This story contains details of alleged sexual assault and harassment

It's broad daylight but that doesn't stop the two unknown men the 28-year-old alleges approached and sexually assaulted her.

Exact details of what Josie Bosker alleges to have occurred on that December day are the subject of two ongoing court cases, which means we're prohibited from publishing them.

Ms Bosker was waiting for a train at Alderley Station in Brisbane's north when she was allegedly sexually assaulted. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

What she can do is describe the shock of being allegedly assaulted by two strangers about 4pm on a hot summer's day.

And to recount how a day she'd been looking forward to – a Christmas party in Brisbane's CBD – soured.

Ms Bosker says she feels less safe on public transport following the alleged incident. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

"I was pretty nervous, not going to lie," Ms Bosker remembers feeling as the two men allegedly approached her. "It was bright, it was sunny so I wasn't super worried that it would escalate too much further. "But I definitely felt very uncomfortable, quite violated and was just hoping that the train would arrive soon so I could jump on."

Adding to her feelings of vulnerability, she said no one else attempted to intervene.

That was despite her efforts to sidle closer to another group of people nearby and to try catch another man's attention.

The charges against the two strangers are now before the court. (ABC News: Christopher Gillette)

Charges laid

Sexual assault support lines: Lifeline (24-hour crisis line): 131 114

Full Stop Australia: 1800 385 578

Bravehearts: counselling and support for survivors of child sexual abuse: 1800 272 831

Child Wise: counselling provider: 1800 991 099

Queensland police have confirmed a 23-year-old and a 40-year-old man have each been charged with sexual assault whilst in company.

The 23-year-old's case has been committed to the District Court, but no date has yet been set for when he will appear.

The 40-year-old's matter remains in Brisbane's Magistrates Court.

Both men are currently out on bail.

The 28-year-old wasn't initially going to report it. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

The decision to report the alleged assault was not straightforward for Ms Bosker.

It was not the first time she had dealt with uncomfortable behaviour on public transport – things like men sitting too close or making suggestive comments.

"I think all women have had at least some experiences with sexual harassment and stuff on public transport," she said.

Have you had a similar experience? Contact Lottie Twyford on Twyford.Lottie@abc.net.au

"It was probably the scariest.

"You sort of just learn to brush it off a lot of the time or ... try not to make the situation worse by being aggressive."

She says the process of reporting it was straightforward and she felt supported by police. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

It was her husband's response which changed Ms Bosker's mind.

"He was really upset and was like 'yeah, that's not okay' and that's what led me to report it," she explained.

Research shows many incidents of sexual violence on public transport go unreported. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Experts believe much goes unreported

Experts believe many incidents of sexual assault and harassment on public transport go unreported.

Monash University's Dr Nicole Kalms has dedicated much of her career to exploring women's experiences in public spaces, and how to make them safer.

She was part of a team commissioned by the Victorian government to investigate harassment of women and girls on public transport following the rape and murder of Aiia Maasarwe in 2019.

The 21-year-old was killed while on her way home, just after getting off a tram.

Monash University's Dr Nicole Kalms has extensively researched the experience of women and girls on public transport. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Her research across five continents has shown public transport is one of the most likely places sexual violence occurs.

That ranges from both verbal harassment, to physical assault, to digital harassment, such as people watching pornography on their device or victims being shown pornographic material while on public transport.

Experts say there's a variety of reasons why public transport can be unsafe. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

There is no one clear reason for why public transport is unsafe, but Dr Kalms highlighted several factors at play.

She explained crowded spaces can give perpetrators "plausible deniability" in terms of groping and sexually harassing women and girls.

"On the other side of that, though, is that the spaces are often quite isolated when they're not incredibly busy," she said.

"That also creates an environment of incredible risk and vulnerability for women and girls."

'He zoomed in on my breasts'

Brisbane student Abi Englart says sexual harassment on public transport is a common occurrence for her, and something the majority of her friends have experienced too. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

As an almost daily public transport user, Abi Englart said she regularly feels uncomfortable due to men's behaviour.

The 21-year-old said that can range from someone sitting too close, staring or making rude comments.

But a recent occasion, when her partner caught a man flipping his tablet around and filming her, has made her even more wary.

"He zoomed in on my breasts," she said.

"I felt pretty vulnerable, really uncomfortable [and] the next time I went on a bus I felt a lot of anxiety."

Ms Englart says she's changed her behaviour since being filmed on the bus. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

She did not file a police report, instead saying she changed her own behaviour in response.

"So, I usually like to wear headphones. Now I always keep one part off so I can hear what's happening. "I try and position my body to the centre so I have a better field of vision. "I don't wear my glasses super often, but I've been wearing [them] more often so I can see what's happening ... stuff like that."

Both Queensland Rail and Translink, which manages the state's buses, trains and ferries, say safety for passengers and staff is their highest priority and they work with police to target antisocial behaviour.

Incidents reported to Translink through their online form are followed up with police or other authorities involved where appropriate.

There is CCTV cameras at train stations across Queensland and specialist police can be deployed across the network. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

But there is a lack of statistics on the prevalence of sexual violence on public transport.

Police in Queensland say they do not collate offence data in that level of detail. Some services around the country, including New South Wales and Victoria, do through their statistics agencies.

In New South Wales, for example, there were 2,389 incidents reported to police last financial year, compared with 2,316 in the previous year.

Ten years ago, there were 1,971.

Adding to the lack of data; a national survey which measured perceptions of safety when travelling alone on public transport (along with a variety of other measures about attitudes towards the police) has been discontinued.

Police Minister Dan Purdie said in a statement the government is committed to giving police the resources they need to make the state safer.

A spokesperson for Queensland Rail said there are fewer than four police-recorded customer assaults per million passenger journeys but "any incident is one too many".

Specific police officers also patrol the state's rail network, and a police unit was deployed across the network almost 200 times last financial year.

Loading...

Just last month, a man was charged by Queensland police accused of – on two separate occasions – approaching teenage girls at a major train station in Brisbane, before allegedly travelling with them via train and assaulting them.

Police are investigating whether there could be additional alleged victims.

Experts say isolated spaces like underpasses and empty stations can be unsafe for women and girls. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

Dr Kalms would like to see not only more statistics about where sexual violence is occurring, but for it to be made easier for victim-survivors to make a report and to know that report will be taken seriously.

She said understanding the breadth of the issue is important, as is giving women options when it comes to reporting.

"That is certainly a way for us to understand the situation [and] potentially where there are particular hotspots and to start to enact some kind of change within the public transport environment."

Experts would like more data and to make it easier for women to report sexual violence on public transport. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi)

In a statement, the Queensland Police Service said it was committed to ensuring the community was safe and felt safe.

"All reports of suspicious behaviour are assessed and investigated based on the information available to police," a spokesperson said.

World.title: Farage faces man in a bin, 'Loonies' and an Australian in bizarre by-election
World.content:
All eyes in the UK are on the seaside electorate of Clacton, where one of the strangest by-elections in recent British history is about to begin.

Brexit architect Nigel Farage is facing an "intergalactic space warrior", an Australian software engineer and 31 other unusual candidates after Britain's major parties decided to sit this one out.

As the leader of the anti-immigration Reform UK party, Farage is seeking to return to parliament after quitting his seat in July, amid scrutiny of his personal finances.

But his main rival is Count Binface — a comedian in a bin-shaped helmet who is promising cheaper bus fares, 99-pence ice creams, the construction of at least one affordable home, and even a referendum on whether Pluto should be a planet again.

Comedian Jonathan David Harvey is legally standing for election under the name Count Binface. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

A recent poll suggests the 5,900-year-old space warrior could win as much as 20 per cent of the vote, enough to put a sizeable dent in Farage's share.

"Never underestimate the power of the bin," the Count has warned the ABC.

So who exactly is standing against the far-right Farage, and what would happen if, against all odds, British democracy elected a man in a bin instead?

Here's what you need to know ahead of the election.

When is the Clacton by-election?

Clacton voters will go to the polls on Thursday, August 13.

Polling stations will be open from 7am to 10pm, local time. That is 4pm Thursday to 7am Friday, AEST.

The winner will become the MP for the Essex seaside electorate of Clacton, which includes Clacton-on-Sea, Frinton-on-Sea and Walton-on-the-Naze.

The electorate of Clacton is named after the seaside town of Clacton-on-Sea, in south-east England. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

What triggered it?

Nigel Farage triggered the by-election himself, when he quit as the MP for Clacton on July 7.

His dramatic resignation followed a parliamentary investigation into his finances, including an undeclared gift worth 5 million pounds ($9.31 million) from a cryptocurrency billionaire.

Under House of Commons rules, the probe has been paused during the by-election but will automatically resume if Farage is re-elected to parliament.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage drinks a beer in Clacton-on-Sea. (ABC News: Andrew Greaves)

Farage has denied wrongdoing, and framed his decision to recontest the seat as a chance for voters to decide whether they still support him.

He has cast the contest as a battle between "the people" and the establishment, saying constituents "should be the judges of my actions".

But Britain's major parties have decided not to play along.

Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats and the Greens have all declined to field candidates, describing the contest as a "political stunt".

That has left a conspicuous gap on the ballot paper, which has since been filled by a parade of conventional independents, fringe party candidates and outright political satirists.

The ballot paper is … how long?

With a record-breaking 34 candidates on the ballot paper, the list is about 90 centimetres long.

The previous record for a UK parliamentary election was 26 candidates, set at the 2008 Haltemprice and Howden by-election.

A mock-up of the unusually long Clacton by-election ballot paper. (Supplied: Tendring District Council)

Who is standing in the election?

There is, of course, Nigel Farage, standing for Reform UK as the only mainstream party candidate in the race.

He took the seat in 2024 with 46 per cent of the vote, and the majority of Reform voters in the seat say they will back him again, according to a recent Survation poll for Mandate Research.

Awareness of the controversy that triggered the by-election is high, but Clacton voters are divided over whether Farage did anything wrong.

According to the Survation poll, 35 per cent say Farage acted within the rules, while 25 per cent say he acted wrongfully. Eight per cent say both or neither, while 32 per cent don't know.

Then there is Count Binface, standing for the Count Binface Party. He's a political persona that has already gone up against former Conservative prime ministers Boris Johnson, Rishi Sunak and Theresa May.

Behind the bin helmet is comedian Jonathan David Harvey, who is legally standing for election under the Count Binface name.

And this time, Binface is offering Clacton voters a surprisingly extensive platform.

A recent poll shows Count Binface could take 20 per cent of the vote. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

His manifesto promises to cap bus fares at 1.99 pounds and the price of 99 Flake ice creams at 99 pence, regenerate Walton Pier and build "at least one" affordable home.

He also wants oil and gas companies to pay for solar panels for everyone, a referendum on whether Pluto should regain its planet status, and for MPs who resign in the middle of a parliamentary term to be barred from contesting the resulting by-election.

Plus, in another pointed reference to the circumstances that triggered this election, one pledge states: "I will not accept 5 million-pound gifts from crypto billionaires (on Earth)."

Three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party are standing. (Supplied: Official Monster Raving Loony Party)

Then there are the 32 other candidates, who range from conventional independents to fringe parties and outright political satirists.

Among them are three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, namely Howling Laud Hope, Baron Von Thunderclap and Nick the Incredible Flying Brick.

The satirical group, which also stood candidates in the Makerfield by-election in June, is running on a series of deliberately nonsensical policies.

It pledges to "replace all red tape with Sellotape", give every voter the chance to be prime minister for 15 minutes during their lifetime, and "ban any by-election that has been created purely for political self-interest".

There is also former actor and right-wing Reclaim Party leader Laurence Fox, independents Attieh Fard, Andy Erlam and Nick Pelas, and Melbourne-born candidate Daniel Pocock.

Melbourne-born Daniel Pocock is a software engineer. (Supplied: Daniel Pocock)

According to his website, Pocock is a software engineer who moved to Europe after graduating and worked for companies like Barclays Capital, Thomson Reuters, and UBS.

"Should people make a tactical vote for a man with a bin on his head or a strategic vote for the great-grandson of an ANZAC hero?" he writes on his website.

Pocock says he was motivated to nominate himself for Clacton by the prospect of "novelty candidates".

"If the Essex Lion was to appear on the ballot paper, I suspect it would have an equally good chance of winning. I have yet to see a single report about the real, day-to-day issues facing residents of the district," he said.

" In a parody of this situation, I have chosen the codename Pocock-on-Sea for the operation to unleash an Australian upon London's Establishment. "

Some of the other candidates have names that sound like they were generated by a particularly chaotic political-name generator, including Woke Trump Carrzee and Joseph 77.

Polling shows Nigel Farage remains the clear favourite to win the by-election. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

But despite the crowded field, the election is widely considered to be a two-horse race between Farage and Count Binface.

The Survation poll of 502 Clacton adults put Farage well ahead at 73 per cent of the vote, but gave Count Binface an unexpectedly strong 20 per cent.

The space warrior has lost every election he has contested, with the most votes he has ever received being 308.

When the ABC recently asked Farage whether he was confident he could beat Count Binface, he laughed and said: "I should hope so."

What if Binface actually wins?

If Count Binface achieves the seemingly impossible, he would actually become an MP.

There is no novelty-candidate exemption in Britain's electoral system: if he wins the most votes, the man behind the bin helmet becomes the member for Clacton.

There is, however, one small problem.

Binface's costume is unlikely to pass parliament's dress rules.

Nigel Farage's big gamble Nigel Farage is facing intensifying scrutiny over his finances and millions of dollars' worth of donations. Here's how he got here.

MPs are expected to wear business-like attire, and parliamentary guidance says members should not, in principle, have their faces covered when speaking or voting.

So the sight of an intergalactic warrior in a dustbin helmet taking his seat in the House of Commons is probably not on the cards.

He would have to enter parliament as the comedian Jonathan Harvey — at least if he wants to follow the rules.

Still, if he did win, the costume might be the least remarkable part of the story.

Farage would lose the seat he deliberately vacated in the hope of securing a fresh mandate, while Count Binface would go from political satirist to elected legislator.

That would make this very strange by-election even stranger.

World.title: Grandparents filling child care gaps as cost-of-living pressures rise
World.content:
A year after her daughter Coco was born, Hayley Boyle went back to work.

With cost-of-living pressures on the rise, she and her husband, Chris, needed both their wages to make ends meet.

Hayley Boyle (right) with her family. (ABC Gold Coast: Charmayne Allison)

But they soon faced a dilemma: the more they worked, the more expensive Coco's childcare needs became.

"You can't financially not go back to work," Ms Boyle said.

" You're damned if you do and you're damned if you don't. "

The Boyles could not afford to place Coco in family day care five days a week, and they struggled to pick her up in the afternoons because of their inflexible workplaces at the time.

So they turned to their respective mothers for help to fill the childcare gaps.

"We're lucky we're a family that all get on and it works well," Coco's grandma Julia Boyle said.

"And it's just building that closeness and that relationship with [Coco] that is just priceless."

Myra Hamilton says grandparents often fill child care gaps. (Supplied)

Grandparents filling child care gaps

A white paper published this year by insurance provider Australian Seniors, which surveyed more than 4,000 grandparents, found 52 per cent provided regular childcare.

Of those surveyed, 14 per cent said they cared for their grandkids five or more days a week.

"What we do know from demographic trends is there are more families where both parents are working full-time," University of Sydney sociologist Myra Hamilton said.

" That's where grandparents are really stepping in. "

Georgie Dent says parents are facing significant financial pressures. (ABC News: Adriane Reardon)

A 'catch 22' for parents

Georgie Dent, chief executive at The Parenthood, said over the past five years, the cost of education and care had skyrocketed faster than inflation.

However, she said the more parents worked, the less of a childcare subsidy they received, leaving them with an "impossible catch 22".

"For a lot of parents, they feel broke if they do work, they feel broke if they don't work," she said.

Dr Hamilton said as parents increasingly turned to their parents for help, escalating pressures were disproportionately impacting women.

"Essentially, what it means is that the child care moves from mothers to grandmothers," she said.

Patricia Sparrow says it's crucial grandparents have honest conversations around child care. (ABC News: Simon Tucci)

'Tipping point' for childcare hours

Dr Hamilton said while child care had significant benefits for grandparents' health, mood and physical fitness, it could come with a cost.

Her research showed there was a "tipping point" when grandparents provided more than 13 hours of child care a week.

"That's where we started to see more negative impacts on grandparents' work, economic security [and] physical health," she said.

Council on the Ageing Australia chief executive Patricia Sparrow said it was crucial grandparents had honest conversations with their families around child care.

"If those boundaries aren't set clearly, people can have different expectations, and it can get difficult," she said.

Grandparents are helping to fill childcare gaps. (ABC Gold Coast: Charmayne Allison)

'Very mixed policy messages'

Some parents have called for childcare subsidies to be made available for grandparents, but Dr Hamilton was sceptical.

"It risks sending a message that it's not the government's responsibility to fill the gaps in our current system," she said.

She said while there had been increased investment in child care in recent years, it was still "inaccessible to many".

Workplaces also need to be more flexible, and the paid parental leave scheme must be extended further and made more accessible for fathers, she said.

"There's still a lot of strong gender norms that make it difficult for fathers to use parental-leave policies, even if they're available," she said.

In the meantime, she said grandparents were receiving "very mixed policy messages".

"On the one hand, we see a really big focus on boosting mothers' workforce participation, and we also see a kind of persistence of barriers to accessing formal child care," she said.

World.title: Thomas Embling Hospital staff battling burnout, drug abuse and violence
World.content:
Victoria's only mental healthcare provider for the criminal justice system is inefficient with government funding and struggles with a junior workforce that is burning out, according to a leaked report.

Thomas Embling Hospital, a secure facility in Melbourne's inner north, treats patients found not guilty of serious violent crimes because of mental illness. Other patients are transferred from prisons when they need temporary care for an acute issue.

Extra beds will open up in September following the delayed expansion of the Fairfield facility, needed to meet worsening demand and a key recommendation of the Royal Commission into the mental health system.

But the facility run by specialist provider Forensicare — which also treats people within prisons and those transitioning into the community — is already battling staff turnover, violence, and drug abuse onsite.

A $515.7 million expansion of the Fairfield hospital will be completed in September, adding 82 new beds. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Insiders have described a dysfunctional workplace.

Forensicare in February commissioned an independent review to identify the root causes of "workforce dissatisfaction, operational inefficiency, and sustainability risk".

The confidential report, handed down in June, confirmed the medical workforce was enduring "significant workload pressure".

"Sustained pressure erodes morale," the report said.

Review finds inefficient use of hospital funding

The review found the workforce was "disproportionately junior". "Supervision safeguards" were needed for international medical graduates, it said, who were sometimes placed in "senior roles prior to full college endorsement" as required from the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (RANZCP).

The ABC requested a copy of the report using freedom of information (FOI) laws but never received a response, prompting a complaint to the state's Information Commissioner.

The ABC separately obtained a leaked copy of the review, finalised in June by Queensland's Director of Forensic Mental Health, Ed Heffernan, and the Queensland Director at the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist, Bobbie Clugston.

The reviewers found Forensicare receives "comparable", even "favourable", government funding for medical staff as other states.

But this funding is not used efficiently.

"This finding points to a systems and utilisation problem rather than a resourcing deficit: where budgeted [equivalent full time staff] is not efficiently utilised, it will inevitably be experienced as insufficient."

The report did not examine how many of the funded positions were actually filled, and whether they were filled with appropriately trained staff.

The report found issues with staffing despite adequate funding of the facility. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

The secure hospital was last year stripped of accreditation to host seven trainee positions because they faced violence and did not get adequate supervision.

Two positions were returned in February, the RANZCP confirmed, but Forensicare has not yet applied to have accreditation for the remaining five reinstated. Registrars were also allowed to rejoin the on-call roster in January.

"The RANZCP continues to work closely and constructively with Forensicare senior executives to monitor the training environment for local college-accredited and international medical graduate trainees," Victorian chair and Associate Professor Simon Strafrace said.

The review also found the workforce was fragmented, and overly dependent on part-time arrangements that created pay disparities.

The fragmented system further meant workers have unclear roles that added to workforce pressure and administrative burdens, the review said.

"If left unaddressed, these conditions will constrain Forensicare's ability to attract and keep the calibre of workforce the service requires," the report said.

Staff battle bureaucracy and administrative burdens

The reviewers heard that patients last year made 13,000 requests for leave, such as day release, from Thomas Embling Hospital. "While necessary and important for patient recovery", this placed "significant administrative burden on the medical workforce".

One source — speaking anonymously to protect their employment — argued this could result in leave being approved or denied inappropriately. Several patients have absconded from leave.

These decisions can impact public safety as well as a patient's rehabilitation and recovery, as does decisions on whether or not to discharge someone to live in the community, or to treat with seclusion and restraints (which is being phased out).

The Supreme Court has been tracking the case of a woman, known only as CC, secluded at the hospital for 11 years. The court last year heard she lived in almost total isolation, except for when her wrists and ankles are shackled around staff.

A seclusion room at Thomas Embling Hospital. (ABC RN: Emma Nobel)

Sources in the sector described an overly bureaucratic organisation that sidelines highly skilled medical professionals. Forensicare needed to rebuild trust, the review said.

The operator's medical advisory committee is supposed to report to the executive leadership, but the report said their expertise was "underutilised and undervalued".

Dr Tobias Mackinnon, the Executive Director of Clinical Services at Forensicare, who commissioned the review, outraged consultants in the system in January by privately accusing them of attempting to form a "cartel" and reduce their hours. The email, obtained by the ABC, was mistakenly sent to consultants themselves.

The report made clear the workforce was a "highly skilled and dedicated group of clinicians operating in a complex and demanding specialty", and the reviewers were confident Forensicare could implement the recommendations and deliver meaningful improvements.

It noted that the service was dealing with a growing prison population because of bail reform. Forensicare has also expanded and managed law reform from the royal commission, while battling the effects of COVID-19 and going through internal leadership changes. Workforce challenges have been felt across the broader health sector.

Forensicare in February issued a call-out for psychiatrists needed to fill short stints "ASAP" in prisons, Thomas Embling Hospital and in community settings.

Forensicare commits to recommendations

The operator welcomed the findings in a statement and committed to implementing the recommendations.

"The review found we have a highly skilled and dedicated medical workforce and are well resourced relative to similar services, while identifying opportunities to strengthen governance, leadership, role clarity and accountability," a Forensicare spokeswoman said.

"While the review confirms that Forensicare is comparatively well resourced, continued investment in our workforce, systems and operating structures will be essential to meet increasing demand and support future growth."

The review backed the skills of the hospital's workforce, and noted the service was under increased demand due to external factors. (ABC RN: Emma Nobel)

A government spokeswoman said Forensicare was putting the recommendations into action.

"Forensicare commissioned the review to help manage and strengthen their workforce — it found the service is well resourced compared to similar services around the country," she said.

The expanded hospital will open in phases from September to relieve demand, which sometimes means high-risk patients are languishing in prisons without appropriate care while they wait for a bed at Thomas Embling.

Associate Professor Strafrace, the Victorian chair of the RANZCP, said the safety and wellbeing of trainees was a critical priority.

"We want Thomas Embling to succeed as Victoria's specialist forensic mental health service and as an excellent training environment," he said.

Forensicare, in response to questions for this story last week, said an administrative error meant the FOI request was never processed. Forensicare did not explain why the FOI unit had also missed the ABC's repeated requests for an update.

World.title: 'Same businesses every single week': Hospitality app users raise concerns
World.content:
The Fair Work Ombudsman will scrutinise hospitality marketplace Supp, after a worker raised concerns it was misclassifying people who use the platform to find shifts.

Supp is branded as a "recruitment app that's made for the rush", and since 2017, it has been operating as a central hub for bars, pubs and cafes to advertise work.

Individuals can sign up to the platform and apply for shifts posted by businesses, with a description of the work and the hourly rate.

SUPP was created in 2017 and acts as a hospitality marketplace for businesses and workers. (ABC News: Adelaide Miller)

The Supp website refers to workers as "independent contractors" and says it is workers' responsibility to divide their payments to "meet their relevant taxation and superannuation obligations".

Rather than hospitality businesses paying workers through an ordinary payroll system, the Supp platform handles payment on their behalf.

Employment lawyer Fay Calderone told the ABC she is concerned this arrangement could be leaving workers without their correct entitlements, including to superannuation.

"One of the key legal risks in this area is assuming that contractual labels will be determinative," Ms Calderone, a partner at Hall and Wilcox, said.

" The mere fact that a worker holds an ABN or is described as an independent contractor does not determine their legal status. "

Employment lawyer and partner at Hall and Wilcox Fay Calderone says calling someone a contractor doesn't necessarily mean this is correct. (ABC News: Abubakr Sajid)

The Fair Work Ombudsman spokesperson said it will make inquiries into Supp: "We are unable to comment on those further."

"We encourage any workers with concerns to contact us directly for assistance," the spokesperson said.

"The FWO also has an online anonymous report tool, including options to report in languages other than English."

Concerns about sham contracting in the gig economy, where employers say workers are independent contractors not employees, have been raised for years, with companies battling claims in court.

Supp rejects 'sham contracting'

The Supp website states that it has links to at least 15,000 venues, and more than 200,000 workers, across Melbourne, Sydney, Los Angeles and New York City.

One Melbourne-based hospitality worker has been using the Supp platform for more than three years. He requested anonymity as he still uses Supp for work.

Unpaid super crisis More than 80 per cent of unpaid superannuation goes unrecovered — and the agency in charge rarely penalises employers who do not pay it.

He believes the type of work he has been hired to do reflects that of an employee, rather than a contractor.

"They'll be asking me to do whatever, [for example], you'll be behind the bar serving people," he said.

"They'll let you know if it's going to be mainly customer service or if you'll be in this area or that section."

Ms Calderone said there was a number of factors to take into account when determining if someone was a genuine contractor, rather than an employee.

"The question is not whether a worker enjoys some flexibility, but whether the arrangement as a whole reflects a genuinely independent business relationship [and] a number of factors are commonly examined," she said.

"Including the degree of control exercised over the worker, whether the worker can genuinely operate an independent business, whether they can delegate work to others and whether they bear any real commercial risk."

How payday super could protect workers Melbourne bakery workers are likely to be thousands of dollars out-of-pocket in unpaid super entitlements. Could a new law have protected them?

In a statement to the ABC, Supp's chief executive Jordan Murray said: "We reject any suggestion that Supp deliberately misrepresents working relationships or facilitates sham contracting".

"Supp was built to address two longstanding problems in hospitality: venues filling short-term gaps through informal networks like Facebook groups, often with very little transparency or protection around the transaction, and workers wanting greater visibility, choice and access to both additional income and permanent opportunities.

" Supp was designed to bring those transactions into the open with visible rates, digital payments, minimum rate protections, two-way reviews and a portable work history. "

'I started to get a little more concerned'

In July 2022, the monthly minimum income threshold for compulsory superannuation was removed, meaning any employee over the age of 18 was now eligible for entitlements regardless of earnings.

Supp's chief executive told the ABC that it was not Supp's responsibility to pay superannuation.

"Supp is not the engaging business or employer in any engagement, and businesses using the platform are responsible for complying with their legal obligations to the people they engage," Mr Murray said in a statement.

Daniel McBurnie says he has never been paid superannuation from his shifts through the SUPP platform. (Supplied: Daniel McBurnie)

Daniel McBurnie, who has been using the Supp platform since 2021, said chasing up unpaid superannuation contributions through individual businesses would not be worth his time.

"I've done a one-off shift at many venues and that one-off shift probably I've accumulated maybe just short of $20 super," he said.

"So for a one-off claim to go back and go through the process of disputing things and waiting for responses and then escalating it if you're not happy ... I go, well, why would I do this to myself?"

He is worried thousands of workers using the platform are missing out on building their retirement savings.

A third of young workers are exploited Jarod Graham says he is owed $10,000 of unpaid super from his former boss. He's not the only one.

"As the app got more popular, and as it seems like more businesses were starting to use it, I started to get a little more concerned," he said.

While he initially used the app to pick up last minute shifts, he started to notice more regular shifts offered.

" I started seeing the same businesses every single week, every time I opened the app. "

The Supp app shows some businesses have used the platform to fill thousands of shifts.

Even contractors may be entitled to super

Even workers legitimately engaged as contractors may still be entitled, in some circumstances, to superannuation contributions paid by businesses, Ms Calderone said.

"That is an area that is often misunderstood by both businesses and workers," she said.

"Even where a worker is properly characterised as an independent contractor for employment law purposes, superannuation obligations may still arise where the contract is wholly or principally for the worker's labour."

Watch The Business, Mondays to Thursdays 8:44pm on ABC News Channel, after the Late News on ABC TV, and anytime on ABC iview.

World.title: Six months into the job, Taylor is taking a detour
World.content:
Today marks six months since Sussan Ley was dumped by her colleagues.

She's been on an unusual journey of discovery since then.

After being defeated by Angus Taylor for the Liberal leadership and quitting parliament, Ley fulfilled a long-time dream of riding on Greyhound buses down the length of inland USA. She found a bleak interior and plenty of misery.

"Chains. Parking lots. Cheap builds. No trees. No spaces to gather," Ley wrote in the Australian Financial Review. "It was the underlying weariness. Everyone works hard. That part is true. But working hard is no longer enough."

Reflecting on the experience, Ley told 7:30's Sarah Ferguson of her great discovery: the extent of disconnection.

"This feeling of disconnection I found by the end of the trip really quite interesting, quite fascinating".

The former opposition leader took a Greyhound bus trip through Route 83. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

A problem of disillusion and disconnection

Ley wasn't deliberately sending a message to anyone in particular but it served as a powerful reminder. Political leaders need to stay focused on what really matters. The disconnected aren't interested in political games.

The dramatic shift in support away from the major parties in Australia this year points to a similar problem of disillusion and disconnection.

Much of this shift happened on Ley's watch. She carries at least part of the blame for weary voters walking away from the Liberal Party.

Ley was often criticised, including by her own colleagues, for whipping up issues that just didn't connect.

Issues like the prime minister's choice of T-shirt, Penny Wong's capacity to shed tears in public, or whether Kevin Rudd should be recalled as ambassador for upsetting Donald Trump.

Too much hyperventilating over the wrong issues. Not enough focus on the substantive concerns of disconnected voters.

Which brings us to the melons.

Taylor shifts direction

In his first speech as Liberal leader, six months ago today, Taylor vowed a "change or die" reset. Cost of living, immigration and Australian values would be his focus. In large part, he's so far stuck to those priorities.

This week, however, with the return of parliament after the five-week winter break, Taylor shifted direction.

He's gone after the prime minister's ill-fated and now infamous decision to appear on the satirical Bush Deep podcast where Anthony Albanese talked about the "melons" given to him by his Japanese counterpart.

Angus Taylor has gone after the prime minister's ill-fated and now infamous decision to appear on the satirical Bush Deep podcast. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The opposition leader has not been half-hearted in his pursuit. Repeatedly demanding Albanese apologise in Question Time, trying to move a motion in parliament to condemn the prime minister, accusing him of damaging relations with Japan.

The Coalition has even asked the Australian Federal Police to investigate who leaked a confidential note from Tokyo suggesting the Japanese government believed there was no "ill intention" behind the comments.

It's been a full court press from the opposition. And the government has been unable to shut it down, despite the efforts of various ministers from Tanya Plibersek to Katy Gallagher to defend the prime minister.

Having already issued an apology for his comments on the podcast about Kylie Minogue, Albanese has so far refused to offer another. He rejects any interpretation he was engaging in lewd jokes about Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

The melon 'joke' drama spreads to Japan For a month the Japanese government has studiously remained quiet on Anthony Albanese's melons "joke". But the media frenzy in Australia has forced it to respond.

Japan, for its part, is trying not to stoke the issue further.

"We have been informed by the Australian side that Prime Minister Albanese did not make the comments in the way that has been reported," Ambassador to Australia Kazuhiro Suzuki told the ABC.

Barnaby Joyce, himself familiar with the odd embarrassment or two, reckons there's no doubt what most people will make of it all.

"Turn the volume down and watch him [on the podcast]. You have a man in a T-shirt, with an empty bottle of bourbon in front of him, gesticulating with his arms and anybody would say 'I think I know what you're talking about there, mate'," said the One Nation MP. "Imagine if for instance I had done that. It would be a riot."

Loading

Bipartisanship behind closed doors

Behind the scenes, Taylor and Albanese have been engaged in a rare level of cooperation this week.

They've been holding a series of personal meetings aimed at reaching bipartisan deals on gambling ads, forcing tech giants to pay for journalism, and reining in the NDIS. Both leaders have a pragmatic interest in squaring these issues away.

But in public, Taylor is using the melon saga to mount an all-out assault on Albanese's character. "He's full of hubris. There's no humility when he makes a mistake," the opposition leader told 2GB.

Choosing to pursue this may prove to be the right strategy. It's the sort of thing that can cut through and damage the prime ministerial image. Labor was devastatingly effective in going after Scott Morrison's character whenever they had the chance.

There is a risk for the Coalition, however, that weary, disconnected voters might not feel this is really the main game. They might feel there are bigger problems affecting their lives that deserve such attention.

Either way, Taylor is marking six months in the job this week with a slight detour from the plan he laid out at the start.

David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

World.title: 'Lawnmower' patterns of Chinese research vessel raising suspicions in Pacific
World.content:
In the final days of May, a Chinese research vessel ventured 74 kilometres into Palau's waters and reportedly spent 14 hours moving slowly through the island nation's maritime zone.

With a bow built to push through a metre of Arctic sea ice, the 89-metre icebreaker, Ji Di, might have looked out of place in the warm waters of the North Pacific.

The Ji Di was designed to push through polar sea ice. (U.S. Coast Guard Courtesy Photo)

Exactly what it was doing remains unclear to Palau's President Surangel Whipps Jr.

"Their research vessels come into our EEZ (Exclusive Economic Zone) uninvited and do whatever they want," he said.

" What are they looking for, and what is the ultimate intention? "

Launched in 2024, the Ji Di was designed to carry out environmental monitoring and surveying to respond to climate change, according to Chinese state media.

Its fleet of unmanned drones and underwater vehicles can map the sea floor and collect data on everything from undersea minerals, ocean currents and marine ecosystems.

But security experts fear the vessel, and dozens of others like it, might also be gathering intelligence for a military purpose — one that could aid Beijing in the event of a future conflict over Taiwan.

The Ji Di travelled roughly 74 kilometres into Palau's EEZ between May 30 and 31. (Micronesia Security Monitor)

Hidden agenda

The Ji Di's incursion was not an isolated incident for Palau.

Similar incidents were reported in 2018, 2024 and 2025, while in 2023, a Chinese vessel allegedly operated near Palau's fibre optic cable.

The most recent incursion, according to Mr Whipps, came in July, a day after China launched a ballistic missile from a submarine that flew over multiple Pacific islands.

The ABC was unable to independently confirm the incursion.

"They're surveying over the top of our fibre optic cable and they have gear in the water, so for us it's a security concern," Mr Whipps said.

Surangel Whipps Jr said Chinese research vessels have become a security concern for his country. (Supplied)

Sixteen Chinese research vessels have been deployed into the north Pacific this year, according to the Pacific Centre of Island Security — a think tank that tracks vessels and geopolitical activity in the region.

Jennifer Parker, an adjunct professor of defence and security at the University of Western Australia, said while some vessels would be used for "pure science", the scale and location of China's activities also suggested they could be gathering intelligence to conduct submarine and anti-submarine warfare against the United States.

China reminds world of growing military power This latest military test demonstrates China's growing willingness to use its military strength to send a warning to the Pacific: that Beijing now has the military and nuclear means to assert its dominance in the region.

"If you look at where Hawaii and Guam are, where US subs are based, and how they would operate across the Western Pacific, you can see why waters around Palau are important," she said.

In 2024, an investigation by the Center for Strategic and International Studies into 64 Chinese research vessels found 80 per cent demonstrated suspicious behaviour or had organisational links suggesting involvement in advancing Beijing's geopolitical agenda.

The study said China had developed the largest fleet of civilian research vessels in the world, heavily concentrating its surveys in the South China Sea and western Pacific Ocean.

Science or spying?

The dual-use nature of research vessels can make their true purpose difficult to discern, because mapping the sea floor can serve both scientific and military objectives.

A 2025 study published in the journal Frontiers in Political Science noted that "unlike other countries, China doesn't distinguish between ships operating for naval survey, scientific research, or commercial purposes".

But director of the Pacific Centre for Island Security, Leland Bettis, said there were clues in the vessels' patterns.

Leland Bettis says the patterns created by Chinese research vessels provide clues to their purpose. (ABC News: Kent Velesrubio)

Mr Bettis said the Ji Di was tracked in May following a pattern that suggested it was mapping the ocean floor near Guam along a corridor likely to be used by US submarines.

"It's doing a lawnmower pattern, which is typical of oceanographic survey work," he said.

"The fact it's doing the lawn-mowing positioning directly off of Guam where US submarines are based underscores the potential for some of the dual use capabilities."

Leland Bettis said the Ji Di's "lawnmower" movement pattern is typical of oceanographic survey work. (Micronesia Security Monitor)

A recent Lowy Institute report into China's military said two of the main priorities of the People's Liberation Army was developing the forces needed to invade Taiwan and deterring or defeating a US intervention.

As a hub for military operations in the Pacific, Guam is home to multiple US nuclear submarines and would likely be used as a staging area if the US intervened in a Taiwan conflict.

Mr Bettis said Chinese research vessels could be trying to track the "signatures" of US submarines or even planting listening devices.

"Increasingly we've seen the use of drones and other submersibles that float around or [are] managed by an operator to collect information," he said.

Guam is home to multiple nuclear submarines which operate in the Western Pacific. (Reuters)

Ms Parker, who is also a former Australian anti-submarine warfare officer, said understanding the sea floor was critical for operating and hunting submarines.

She said detailed mapping helped submarines navigate terrain like underwater mountains and trenches.

The shape and depth of the seabed, along with ocean temperature, also affects how sound travels through the water column.

Jennifer Parker says China aims to expand its submarine operations into the second island chain — a strategic line of Pacific islands stretching from Japan through Guam to Micronesia. (Reuters)

"The primary way you detect subs is through sound — passive by listening or active by putting sound in the water and getting it to bounce back," she said.

Playing by its own rules

Marine scientific research in another country's EEZ without permission is a breach of international law, said Ms Parker.

But Palau's options to stop China entering its territorial waters are limited.

In a diplomatic complaint to China, Palau said the incursion showed a disregard for its sovereignty and the "rules-based order" nations are supposed to follow.

Ms Parker said China had been operating under its own rules in its efforts to map vast expanses of the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

Jennifer Parker said China frequently breaches international law while mapping the ocean floor. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"It is uncommon to see countries conducting survey operations in another country's EEZ without permission, and the only country I can think of that does this at scale is China," she said.

China meanwhile has defended the activities of its vessels in the Pacific, saying in July an alleged incursion near the Japanese island Okinawa was "legitimate, lawful and beyond reproach".

The ABC reached out to the Chinese embassy for comment.

Ms Parker said as China continued to project power across the Indo-Pacific, research vessels would likely become a more common sight.

"China has been doing this more across the Pacific and Indian Ocean, including in places just north of Papua New Guinea, so I think we'll see more of this," she said.

World.title: US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS election US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions Michael Koziol August 13, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was always a bit unfair that US Democrats were put through the wringer over some of their more radical candidates for this year’s midterm elections, while Republicans escaped relatively unscathed. By and large, Republicans were not asked what it meant for their party that pillow mogul and famed election result denier Mike Lindell was seeking the Republican nomination to become governor of Minnesota – with President Donald Trump’s endorsement. My Pillow founder Mike Lindell failed to win the Republican primary in Minnesota as voters shied away from both parties’ extremes. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt In part, that’s because election denial, conspiracy theories and the far-right are by now so entwined with the GOP that it has become a moot point. There is no question about a Trumpist takeover of the Republican Party – it has already happened. But there was a reality check on Tuesday night when Lindell, despite the president’s backing, lost the primary to Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives.



It was a good night for moderates in both parties – and a wake-up call, potentially, for their more extreme factions. In Wisconsin, state politician and declared democratic socialist Francesca Hong lost her bid to become the Democrats’ nominee for governor of Wisconsin, losing to establishment-backed candidate David Crowley in a tight contest that the polls got wrong. Francesca Hong narrowly lost to her establishment rival in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh Hong, 37, came to national attention – and not in a good way – for some of her past statements, including a 2020 tweet arguing that Thanksgiving should be permanently cancelled because it celebrated colonialism. Asked on CNN whether she stood by that view, she told an anecdote about being a chef, in a widely circulated clip that some analysts believe cost her the win.



Hong tried and failed to win endorsements from progressive kingmakers Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who said they weren’t getting involved in gubernatorial races. View post on X But AOC was also critical of Hong’s excesses. “Woke 1 was crazy,” she said, laughing, on America’s ABC News on Sunday, attributing the phrase to one of her local councillors. She basically went on to say – in nicer language – that most people had moved on from some of the opinions they articulated during the COVID-19vpandemic, which more or less aligned with a time people now describe as “peak woke”. “Woke 1 was crazy”: Progressive hero Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said people had evolved from their COVID-era views. Bloomberg



“Especially during COVID, there was a huge opening of the Overton Window,” AOC said. “The doors were really opened in trying to entertain every and any policy that was going to get us to a better place.” She maintained that “the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful”. Abdul El-Sayed, the populist progressive Democrat who won a US Senate primary in Michigan last week – beating an establishment candidate backed by the party elite and $US60 million ($85 million) in outside funding – was a much different proposition to Hong. Related Article US politics Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment Articulate and seasoned, he had already recanted some of his earlier positions such as defunding the police – though he maintained a tough line on ending US military aid to Israel. In the end, voters were savvy enough to reward the reasonable candidate, and take a pass on the outlandish one who wasn’t sure about Thanksgiving and didn’t seem quite ready for prime time.



And in Minnesota, voters were smart enough to give Lindell a wide berth – not that he’ll admit it. The My Pillow founder refused to concede defeat on Tuesday night, insisting his team had found “anomalies” with the vote. My Pillow chief executive Mike Lindell and President Donald Trump at the White House in 2020. AP “I’m not going to sit by until these numbers are explained,” he said, to applause. “We will get a full report on this … I’ve been on the phone with a lot of people. As you know, I’m very good at looking at elections.” It was true to form. Lindell was one of the most vocal proponents of the false claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from Trump. He pushed false conspiracy theories about voting machines by the company then known as Dominion.

World.title: Punched, strangled, spat on with blood: The reality for mental health workers who say system is more broken than ever
World.content:
The crumbling state of Victoria’s mental health system has been exposed by workers who say they are being subjected to violence weekly and the sector is more broken now than it was before the royal commission.
