Their verdict comes as the government is asked to explain where $40 million to deliver 2000 homes for people with mental illness has gone and the fly-in, fly-out boss of the state’s flagship youth service quits. Professor Patrick McGorry is concerned about the lack of progress on mental health reform. Aaron Francis The Community Housing Industry Association [CHIA] Victoria has called on the Carroll government to come clean about its housing commitment, claiming it’s been quietly abandoned, and the funding has disappeared. The 2000 supported living places were a recommendation of the Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System and received $40.4 million in the 2021-22 budget, with pledges to provide the homes as part of the state’s Big Housing Build.



But progress on these spots has stalled, and the funding commitment has disappeared from future budget papers. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence CHIA chief executive Sarah Toohey said the government had so far broken its promise to deliver and fund the supported homes. “The government is quietly walking away from this royal commission recommendation to deliver mental health supported homes for Victorians,” she said. When asked about the project, the Carroll government pointed to 368 purpose-built mental-health supported dwellings constructed through the Social Housing Growth Fund, a program set-up in 2018.



Homes Victoria is also building 505 homes for people living with mental illness, but the CHIA says these are not yet “supported housing”, which requires funding for specialised staff and care. A government spokesperson did not detail what had happened to the money, but said they were delivering more homes for people with mental health challenges. “This is an important and complex reform, and we are taking a careful approach to ensure people living with mental health challenges get the long-term housing and specialist support they need.” More than five years after the royal commission handed down a final report, that then-premier Daniel Andrews promised to implement in full, an investigation by The Age has exposed serious failings in the sector and how it is being managed by government. This included that an independent watchdog’s report being reworked before its release so it was less critical of the government’s progress; a damning assessment on reform by advocate Patrick McGorry and accusations of violence, drug use and an exodus of senior staff from the state’s flagship youth mental health service.



Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service (PYMHWS) chief executive Dr Leanne Geppert on Wednesday resigned a day after The Age revealed she had been leading the organisation under a fly-in, fly-out arrangement. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force The service’s board chair, Cath Bowtell, announced Geppert was stepping down, thanking the Brisbane-based boss for her “extraordinary contribution”. “This has been a difficult and deeply considered decision for Leanne,” Bowtell said. “Having led PYMHWS through its establishment and first year of operations, she has been considering for some time when the right point would be to step away. Importantly to her, she wanted to see the organisation through a number of significant milestones.”



Frontline mental health workers across the state have also voiced their concerns at failed reforms promised by the royal commission. A survey of more than 500 workers across 11 Victorian health services reported a deterioration in conditions for patients and staff as well as escalating violence and drug usage in secure psychiatric wards. Two-thirds of mental health workers reported to the Health and Community Services Workers Union (HACSU) that they had been assaulted in the past year, with patients who are more acutely unwell on presentation contributing to the rise in aggression. “I have witnessed colleagues be punched so hard they are concussed, strangled, scratched, have blood-borne virus infected blood spat at them, facial bones fractured,” one worker said. Another reported clients at their hospital were not being treated in appropriate timeframes, which meant their health deteriorated and the risk to staff increased.



“The consumers are not being actively treated and are being discharged too soon, often very unwell,” the mental health worker said. “Most recently a client [who] had an admission was discharged to [the] community and remained unwell. She was readmitted one week later and remains in the intensive care unit. She was not actively treated and now her in-admission is much longer than it should have been.” More than 48 per cent of survey respondents said they disagreed or strongly disagreed that their health services were better placed now than they were before the royal commission. Less than 15 per cent of the workforce said they believed the mental health system had improved, while the remaining workers were neutral in their opinions about the impact of the reforms.



“In so many ways we have gone backward since the royal commission and nothing has actually changed,” a worker wrote. “In fact, access to mental health care has been worse.” HACSU Victorian branch secretary Paul Healey said the survey responses painted a concerning picture of the reality facing mental health workers, consumers, carers and families across Victoria. ”We need to be clear that this is not about blaming people experiencing mental illness,” he said. “Mental health workers understand the complexity of mental health care and are committed to providing compassionate support. “But a system that is under-resourced, overstretched and unable to provide the right care at the right time, built on the broken promises of a royal commission, increases risks.



Related Article Opinion

Mental health I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate “These workers have carried the system through enormous challenges. They deserve more than being told change is coming, change needs to happen now.” In parliament on Wednesday, Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said her government was proud of the support they’d provided the mental health workforce. “We have increased the workforce by over 30 per cent in the mental health sector. We have increased the number of acute beds available across the system,” she said. “We have delivered modern fit-for-purpose services across the state, including at the Thomas Embling Hospital and including at youth recovery and prevention centres in every region in the state.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Family first, integrity, no drugs’: The billionaire will dispute that exposed a secret family succession plan
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two months before his death in Greece, billionaire Nick Andrianakos met his youngest son for lunch at upmarket Glen Iris restaurant Grazia, where he anointed him successor to the family’s petrol and property empire. The ailing founder of Milemaker Group told Theo Andrianakos he would have full control of the family’s multibillion-dollar businesses, and that his vast portfolio of assets in Australia and Greece would also be passed on to Theo and his two sons. Nick Andrianakos, pictured in Greece in 2022, aged 78. Athina Souli Theo also learned at the meeting in January 2025 that his father intended to bequeath €5 million ($8.17 million) to his substantially younger partner Hatouna Sakvarelintze, an architect the ailing businessman had met a couple of years earlier on a hotel redevelopment project. However, there was a sticking point in the patriarch’s grand succession plan – Andrianakos’ three other children, who would later claim in the Supreme Court of Victoria that the revised “family agreement” had not been relayed to them, nor formalised in a signed will. The death of the 81-year-old patriarch on March 17 last year – just days before he was due to sign the will and the family agreement – sparked a toxic legal battle between the siblings over control of their late father’s assets and extensive business interests. The case was set to proceed to trial last month, with siblings Kristina and Paul Andrianakos and Vicky Papamarkou relying on the original documents, signed by their father in 2018 and 2019, which gave the sisters a greater slice of their father’s $183 million estate, and the siblings shared control over Milemaker Group.



Under the signed will, Andrianakos wanted to give his sons the bulk of his inheritance – allocating them $83 million each, and his daughters $24 million respectively. However, the siblings reached an eleventh-hour agreement that avoided a trial and ultimately allowed Justice Peter Gray to grant probate of the unsigned will. Two city penthouses, listed as being worth more than $4 million, are among the division of assets. Domain The settlement, on July 17, handed Theo and his sons all of Andrianakos’ estate, which included CBD penthouses, beachfront homes on the Mornington Peninsula, and properties in Greece, along with a $200,000 black Bentley and a tractor. Theo received the lion’s share of the estate, reducing his brother’s inheritance and seeing his sisters receive substantially less than the $24 million they were originally entitled. The court dispute also laid bare the tensions between the family and Andrianakos senior’s partner, Sakvarelintze. The daughters claimed in respective affidavits that during the months that the drastic changes to their father’s estate were drafted, he had been frail and could no longer understand English.



Papamarkou warned her father that his Greek girlfriend was “probably only after his money” a year before he made changes to bequeath her millions, she claimed in her sworn statement. “I warned him that it was strange to see a woman so young be romantically interested in someone around 80 years of age,” she said in an affidavit. “I told my father to be careful because she was probably only after his money. My father responded by saying words to the following effect: ‘There is no way Hatouna is getting any of my money or property. I am leaving all my property to my children’.” The late billionaire’s wealth planner Peter Pagonis claimed the revised, unsigned will represented the lawful and legitimate plan for his inheritance. Pagonis, who consults to more than 450 ultra-high-net-worth families, said in an affidavit that the family patriarch first ordered him to draft the changes in November 2024 after expressing concerns the three siblings would seize control of Milemaker Group. Nick Andrianakos and son Theo. “The deceased said word to the effect that he was concerned that Vicky, Paul and Kristina would ‘gang up’ on Theo, who was CEO of Milemaker Group, and who was instrumental in operating and growing the Milemaker Group business with [Andrianakos],” he said.



“He was concerned his children Vicky, Paul and Kristina will disrupt the family legacy and seek to break up the family assets and the business that he had grown over time.” Pagonis said that Andrianakos told him in November 2024: “I want to make sure that Theo has full control of the business going forward.” The order came only a few months after the tense exchange between Papamarkou and her father over his romance, which had strained their relationship. She said after that confrontation in July 2023, the pair did not speak for some time until finally reconciling in August 2024. One of the family’s city penthouses. Domain Andrianakos’ instructions in November 2024 led to significant changes to the family agreement, the formal succession document which includes clauses of the family values (among them: family is first, business for future generations, integrity, and no drugs). The succession plans were later thrashed out over a series of meetings – including several lunches at Grazia and secret meetings at Andrianakos’ CBD penthouse – during what would be his last visit to Melbourne.



A $20,000 tractor was part of the estate. Kubpower.com.au The businessman jetted into town on Christmas Eve 2024 with Sakvarelintze, in time for the family’s Christmas lunch, held at Nobu in Crown Casino. Paul, Vicky and Kristina did not attend any of the estate discussions, with Papamarkou noting she didn’t discuss it with her father over Christmas lunch. “When the family met on Christmas day, my father appeared frail and unwell. Because the Christmas lunch was very busy, I did not get to spend any one-on-one time with my father that day,” she said. Papamarkou said when she did later catch up with her father, he was unwell and had difficulty getting up off the couch. Before returning to Greece in January 2025, Andrianakos visited Kristina’s home, where she claims he reassured her about his estate: “My father brought up his will again and told me that Vicky and I would be included and get a share of everything.” The Andrianakos family mansion sits on acreage in Greenvale. Justin McManus

World.title: The email many authors dream of getting – and why it’s a trap
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Less than two weeks after her debut novel Touch Grass was published in June, Mary Colussi received a dream email for many young Australian authors: a message from the head of prestigious UK publishing house Granta, Bella Lacey, raving about her novel’s “originality, intelligence, and distinctive narrative voice” and asking to discuss future projects. The email was detailed and effusive – the kind of praise that “as a writer, you want to believe”, Colussi says. Except it wasn’t from Bella Lacey or anyone from Granta – and the person who sent it almost certainly had not read Colussi’s novel. One of the red flags, Colussi says, was that “everything that they were praising is something that you can find in the synopsis, and in one paragraph they actually quoted directly from the synopsis”. The definitive giveaway was the email address, which ended with @aol.com. A quick check of the Granta website confirmed her suspicions: a warning note from the publisher about fraudulent emails being sent from scammers impersonating staff and offering publishing deals in exchange for money. Novelist Mary Colussi. Colussi’s experience is increasingly common, thanks to a new wave of AI-generated scam emails targeting authors internationally, offering publishing or promotional opportunities in exchange for money. In the past year, the Australian Society of Authors (ASA) has been inundated with messages from writers seeking advice and sharing their experiences, some of them receiving multiple scam emails a day. Email scams targeting authors have existed almost as long as email itself, but they have been turbocharged by AI. The latest wave of scams is “far more sophisticated”, says ASA chief executive Lucy Hayward. “It’s not just that they might be impersonating people from the book industry, it’s that they’re able to provide detail and give the impression that they have read an author’s work, which makes the email convincing. And they can do that because the author’s work has either already been ingested [by AI companies], or it can be ingested by these AI tools and then summarised.” Kelly Gardiner, an established author and member of the ASA board who receives these kinds of AI-generated emails daily, says “authors have been getting unsolicited approaches from PR ‘experts’ for a while, but the sudden expansion of AI has turned it into a flood”. An example of one of the scam emails increasingly being sent to authors.



Most authors have a story – or several. Veteran author and academic Dennis Altman has written about receiving effusive, detailed emails about his books from individuals purporting to be acclaimed authors Annie Ernaux and Patrick Süskind; Walter Marsh described being “flooded” by emails offering paid reviews and promotion after the publication of his second novel (ironically, a novel about theft and fraud) late last year; and Jane Sullivan detailed a “highly convincing” email ostensibly from the (real) Melbourne-based Classic Book Club, offering to promote her 2024 crime novel. While authors are the primary targets, respected editors, literary agents and media figures are caught on the other side of the sting. Scammers steal their names and professional authority to trick writers into fake pitch offers, promotional junkets or film deals. Such was the case with a recent scam email purporting to be from ABC Radio National presenter Sally Sara, offering an author a guest appearance on her show. By leveraging the cachet of a major public broadcaster, the scammers created an offer that felt almost too prestigious for a writer to turn down (the ABC was contacted for comment). Some of the initial emails mention money, but most don’t. Instead, they lead with flattery and promises, waiting to hook the author before they raise the issue of fees. These kinds of scams are sometimes referred to as “pig butchering” operations, a term that originated with romance scams and graphically evokes the process of fattening up a prospective victim with flattery before draining them financially. Most of the emails don’t mention money, instead they lead with flattery. Like romance scams, author scams target vulnerability and play on emotions. “They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted,” Hayward says. The tactic has proved remarkably lucrative for its perpetrators. In a recent case, the US government determined that just one of these publishing scam operations, based in the Philippines, defrauded nearly 800 writers of more than $48 million over six years. US author Victoria Strauss, who has covered author scams since 1998 via the website Writer Beware, says they have proliferated over the past decade, fuelled by outfits based in the Philippines, Pakistan and India. The more recent AI-driven scams come from a different location, however.



“I’ve gotten hundreds of reports of these AI scams, and I traced a lot of them back to the payment information, and everything that I can collect and deduce indicates that they primarily come from Nigeria,” says Strauss. “I see them as kind of a descendant of the ‘Nigerian prince’ scams of old.” Authors who have been inundated with these kinds of emails have become far more adept at identifying them. “The AI-generated copy is its own genre now and you can spot it once you’ve seen a few,” says Gardiner. The emails also have telling similarities: “same terms, same logic, same sentence structures”. Lucy Hayward, the chief executive of the Australian Society of Authors. They’re also often about older books. Gardiner says most of the scam emails she receives “are about two young adult books I published years ago. Perhaps it’s something to do with how often they were ingested in a pirate database used to train AI. No real publicist would want to talk to me about them, although sometimes local schools or readers do, so I always have to check.” Hayward says sifting the real emails from the fake has become a problem in itself. “[At this point] it’s not so much that authors are falling for these scams and handing out money, it’s the volume of the emails that they are receiving. It becomes very difficult to determine what might be a legitimate offer and what is a scam.” One of the key ways to check is looking at the email address, she says, “but for Australia, we have a smaller market, and where book clubs and podcasts are concerned, you might not have someone with a professional email address”. They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted. “You waste time trying to sift the real from the fake,” Gardiner says. “No doubt some genuine approaches have not got through, too, which means writers and readers miss out on real opportunities to engage.”



How are scammers continuing to thrive, if authors are getting wise? Strauss says the dozen or so emails she receives each week about people who have lost money to these scams involve non-professional and first-time authors. “There are a lot of people who just want to write one book; they want to write a memoir, or they want to write about their cancer journey or something they feel is meaningful and will help people. There are a lot of older people who retire and write children’s stories, or a memoir,” she says. Related Article Literature The Australian author who went from rejection letters to global bestseller These people are vulnerable to scammers in more than one way: not only are they unaware of how the publishing industry works and outside professional support networks and communities, but the personal nature of their material can make them particularly susceptible to emotional manipulation. “I sometimes hear from the relatives of older people, often on fixed incomes, who’ve lost enormous amounts of money – tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars – and cannot be convinced that they’re being scammed because the scammers are using psychological manipulation to establish personal relationships,” Strauss says. As she embarks on her career, Colussi can well understand how people are taken in. “Writing a book is such a dream for so many people. They are waiting for that one ‘yes’, and pretending that you are that one ‘yes’ is unfortunately an easy way to take advantage of someone.” What else is happening in the book world?

World.title: Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script
World.content:
★★ CultureTV & radioReview Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script Kylie Northover August 13, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Falling ★★ A new series from British screenwriter Jack Thorne is usually exciting for a TV buff – as well as the gritty trilogy This Is England, the stage adaptation of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, and dozens of other acclaimed works, Thorne was the co-writer of the groundbreaking series Adolescence. Keeley Hawes and Sister Anna and Paapa Essiedu as Father Hicks in Jack Thorne’s Falling. Channel 4/The Forge/Robert Viglasky And on paper, his new series sounds brilliant – Falling is Thorne’s first love story, and he’s gone for the “hot for preacher” trope, with a nun falling for a priest. The cast is amazing – TV veteran Keeley Hawes (who’s been in everything from Spooks to The Assassin) is the nun who, after almost 30 years, gives it all up to be with Father Hicks, played by Paapa Essiedu (I May Destroy You, The Lazarus Project and star of HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter TV series), and it’s mostly directed by Peter Hoar, the Emmy Award-winning director of the feted The Last Of Us episode Long, Long Time. The forbidden love angle has long been a popular romance novel archetype but surely, I thought, Thorne would tackle it in a novel way. The answer is a hard no. (Said the Bishop to the actress.)



Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks Hawes is Anna, a nun in a cloistered Catholic order in rural England, where she spends her days in the convent’s garden, leaving the grounds only to deliver vegetables to the local food bank. She’s a devoted member, primed to take over from the convent’s abbess Francesca (Niamh Cusack). That is, until a visit from Father Hicks. We’re first introduced to Hicks, dressed in full cassock, having a ciggie on the side of a motorway where his car has broken down; that, and his obvious youth, are how we know he’s a “Cool Priest”. He serves a gritty Bristol parish, where he’s considered “radical”; rather than spending money on church heating, as his bishop (Jason Watkins) wants, Hicks is more concerned with setting up a needle exchange. He’s en route to the convent to meet with the abbess about bringing congregation members to experience a “life of conviction”. When he arrives, he meets Anna, and much coy eye-flirting takes place. Then, when she’s making eggs, she burns herself and Hicks rushes to help soothe her wound – and accidentally touches her hand! This seals the Mills & Boon-esque deal. Yes, that’s all it takes to overturn their lives. Even in civilian clothes, there’s zero chemistry between Father Hicks and Sister Anna. Channel 4/The Forge/Robert Viglasky There’s a second visit with more sustained eye contact, and the series’ best, if utterly implausible, line, when Hicks asks if he can see Anna’s cabbages, to which she replies, “Only if you get me really drunk first”. Trust me, that’s as saucy as things get. Shortly afterwards, Anna walks out of the convent and heads to Hicks’ church to declare her feelings. But this series is achingly slow, and Hicks spends the next three episodes looking bewildered; don’t expect any habit-ripping.



Mercifully, only the first four episodes were available to preview, during which there’s no actual romance, and a phenomenal lack of chemistry between the leads. At no point does this “love” feel plausible, despite the brilliant actors. Related Article ★★★

Review Ted Lasso goes beyond extra time with its fourth season, and we pay the penalty The story widens out to take in Hicks’ dealings with his parishioners (teens in trouble; abusive fathers; giving Last Rites), and Anna trying to reintegrate into modern life (she hasn’t seen a mirror for more than 20 years, despite clearly adhering to an incredible skincare routine), but even those scenes, which are more in Thorne’s wheelhouse, are weighed down by an unimaginative earnestness. Even the crises of faith our two leads must endure (very slowly), fail to go deep; Hicks, predictably, has a secret former life to grapple with, while Anna’s issue is very little knowledge of life outside the convent. Forbidden love has never looked so unappealing; you might find yourself praying for either something to actually happen, or for it to end. Falling is not even a curate’s egg – it’s just plain dull. But the biggest sin here is the script: the writing is stolid, earnest and preachy. If Thorne goes to confession over this series, he deserves some serious penance.

World.title: This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s
World.content:
Legendary producer John Edwards, the man behind The Secret Life of Us, Offspring, Rush, The F Ward and more.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A



Related Article Review Aussie drama Tangle is ripe for rediscovery (and now free to watch) Amid the host of productions that bear Edwards’ name as a producer or executive producer, there’s a particularly consequential string of loosely connected series – almost a spine through the body of work. It’s a choice selection of shows that resists neat generic categorisation and that portrays the challenges of life over generations. It begins with the spirited twenty-somethings of The Secret Life of Us (2001-04), moves on to the troubled thirty-somethings of Love My Way (2004-07), and then to the fraught forty-somethings of Tangle (2009-12). This trio will soon become a quartet with the arrival of Dalliance on Paramount+, which turns its attention to life, love, regret and death among sixtysomethings and features a cast including Heather Mitchell, Hugo Weaving, Georgie Parker and David Wenham. These are original drama series created for TV, but if the impressive adaptation of Kathy Lette’s Puberty Blues (2012-14), dealing with teenagers and their troubled parents, is added to the list, Edwards’ shows span an even broader spectrum of life, from tentative adolescent romances and early sexual experiences, through pregnancy and parenthood, to grandparenting and memorial services. Georgie Parker, Hugo Weaving and Heather Mitchell Dalliance. Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+ All of these series showcase vibrant ensembles, memorable collections of artfully drawn and cleverly cast characters. They’re also notable for displaying Edwards’ “old head, young head” philosophy, on-screen and behind the scenes. He’s long believed that pairing experienced writers and actors with gifted newcomers creates the ideal combination, and the rewards of that approach have been abundant. The pairing of Edwards’ longtime collaborator, actor, writer and producer Claudia Karvan with novice screenwriter Kelsey Munro to create and develop Bump (2012-24) delivered one of the country’s best local productions (if you skip the regrettable telemovie tacked on at end). The series also gave us newcomers Nathalie Morris, Carlos Sanson Jr and Ioane Sa’ula in key roles, convincingly moving from high-school kids to adult parents negotiating family life and careers. They’re cast alongside proven players including Karvan, Angus Sampson and Anita Hegh, creating an ensemble alive with zesty energy. Claudia Karvan and Nathalie Morris in Bump.



But the practice reaches further back, reaping rewards on a host of series and revealing Edwards’ keen eye for emerging talent. Asher Keddie, Joel Edgerton, Samuel Johnson and Michael Dorman in Secret Life; Ashley Zukerman and Nicole Da Silva in Rush. Celia Pacquola displaying her range beyond comedy in Offspring and Beautiful Lie. Lincoln Younes perfectly cast as Ben Mendelsohn and Justine Clarke’s son in Tangle. These then-rising stars have shared the screen with some of the most accomplished actors in the country, Edwards’ frequent flyers including Susie Porter, Catherine McClements, Dan Wyllie and Rodger Corser. Related Article Australian TV Will there ever be an Australian show like Love My Way again? The credit roll behind the scenes presents a similar picture. Fledgling writers Judi McCrossin and Jacquelin Perske on Secret Life and Love My Way respectively; emerging producer Imogen Banks on Tangle and Offspring; rookie director Emma Freeman on Rush. And Dalliance features writer Christopher Lee, whose association with Edwards stretches back to Police Rescue. So as fresh talent is tapped, trusted colleagues continue their collaborations. Erudite, energetic and not one to hold back on his opinions, Edwards is not the kind of producer who restricts his role to simply that of a money man: he’s intimately involved in the creation and development of his shows. And with more than 40 TV productions to his credit, he’s had an indelible impact on the local industry. Now, his screen work comes through Roadshow Rough Diamond, the company he set up in 2016 with his son, Dan, co-creator of The F Ward. It’s an additional manifestation of the “old head, young head” strategy, as well, perhaps, as an indication of a generational passing-of-the-baton. Yet the indications are that Edwards Sr’s output, thoughtfully and compassionately exploring people struggling, stumbling, surviving and sometimes succeeding, is happily showing no signs of slowing down. The F Ward is streaming on Stan now. Dalliance premieres on Paramount+ August 27.

World.title: How a lost bag in an Uber spawned one of the best shows of the year
World.content:
Had Jude Troy taken her bag with her when she got out at Tullamarine, The Airport Chaplain might never have existed.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Inspiration comes from the strangest of places. In the case of the brilliant new SBS series The Airport Chaplain, it arrived in the back seat of an Uber. Or, to be precise, it departed, taking Jude Troy’s most vital belongings with it. It was August 2023 and Troy – the Irish-born producer whose company Wooden Horse (co-founded with Richard Finlayson, former head of television at the ABC) has made The Other Guy, Stuff the British Stole and The Clearing – was heading back to Sydney after the first public screening of her show Mother and Son at Melbourne’s ACMI. Editor's pick Streaming It may offend the book’s rusted-on fans, but this series should be approached with an open mind “I was really desperate to get home, distracted, running late as always for a plane,” she says. “I jumped out of the Uber, turned around, and the car disappeared into the late afternoon sun, taking my bag, my laptop, my phone, everything.” She stood on the footpath for a couple of minutes waiting for it to turn around “but it never came back”. Growing increasingly frantic, she tried to get assistance from Uber’s offshore “help” line using phones borrowed from strangers, and realised how few phone numbers we commit to memory these days. Finally, a federal police officer, about to race off to collect her kids after school, came to the rescue. “She said, ‘I’m going to introduce you to a gentleman called Martin, and he’ll look after you.’” Martyn Scrimshaw, the chaplain at Melbourne Airport, did exactly that. But first, he led Troy on what she calls a “two-hour, 25,000-step adventure deep into the bowels of the airport, through security, into the upper echelons of what is a class system in the airport”.



He told her stories “of people dying on aeroplanes, which happens every week; of the woman who comes to the airport every day and thinks she’s being watched by MI5; the young girl who’s camping on the roof of the airport because she’s been abused; the Russian who arrived with an empty suitcase and has literally no idea where to go. Story after story – the absurd, the ridiculous the emotional – and this man, Martyn Scrimshaw, is there to support those people and the workers in the canteens, in security, in the taxi ranks, the terminal manager and the check-in staff. So many people seek his counsel, it’s quite extraordinary.” That’s a wrap: Jude Troy and Hugo Weaving on the set of the show. SBS By 9pm, Troy was on a flight home, her retrieved bag beside her, in the business class seat for which Scrimshaw contrived an upgrade. “And next morning, I rang my co-pilot [writer Elise McCredie] and told her this story, and she was like, ‘We’re making a TV show.’” Troy tells me all this in an excited jumble – I suspect frantic is, in fact, her default mode – while we sit at a plastic table beneath a temporary marquee in a carpark at Flemington Racecourse. Related Article Exit Interview

Australian TV ‘Hate on my colleagues’: The brutal feedback Race Around the World contestants faced We’re not here for the horses. We’re here for the hustle and bustle of Melbourne International Airport, re-created with cunning sleight-of-hand in the Members Stand. (For obvious reasons, filming the series at the airport was impractical.) Watching Hugo Weaving as the fictional Tobias Wallace, it’s easy to see why McCredie was as inspired by the promise as Troy. It’s fast-paced, dynamic, full of drama and comedy and generosity and tension, and all neatly resolved (more or less) within a half-hour (SBS has commissioned eight episodes in this first season; the show’s creators hope there will be many more to come).



McCredie met the real-life airport chaplain, too, spending several days following him around the airport, also wearing a hi-vis vest emblazoned with the words “Airport chaplain”. This functions – at least when accompanied by the man himself – as a kind of access-all-areas pass. The Airport Chaplain is the first big Australian role for Shabana Azeez since The Pitt made her a star. Ben King/SBS “He told me it’s the best job in the world because every day he doesn’t know what’s going to happen,” she says. “He meets different people. He’s a problem solver, he gets to laugh and be joyful, but then he also helps people in really dark places. And so for a series, it just had everything for me as a writer.” The rollcall of characters and micro-dramas provides endless short-term storylines, but a series needs a continuing narrative to make it more than just a collection of vignettes. This is where Shabana Azeez lands. Related Article Logies ‘I think you can do it all’: Can Robert Irwin make the Logies relevant again? The 28-year-old from Adelaide, who had plugged away in indie fare for seven years before The Pitt catapulted her to fame last year, plays new terminal manager Mira Ansari-Cole, an MBA-toting corporate drone whose only loyalty is to the bottom line. Virtually her first interaction with Tobias is to offer him a redundancy. Things only get worse from there. Mira – a single mother, an outsider (she’s come to Australia via the UK and Hong Kong), and not especially gifted with interpersonal skills – is at first glance the polar opposite of Tobias. Not just a formidable foe, she’s also someone fighting her own battle for acceptance in a corporate structure that regards people as headcounts on a spreadsheet.



“This show starts with Tobias’ perspective and it slowly shifts to a more holistic view of the airport,” says Azeez. The challenge is to make Mira, a “complicated” character, relatable despite the lack of obvious likeability. Hugo Weaving and Claudia Karvan in The Airport Chaplain. “There’s something about how women in positions of power gain power, how they keep power, and how hard it is for women to be likeable when they have power,” says Azeez, adding “we’re really happy to build women up to tear them down”. Mira has been brought into “an impossible position”, she says. “Her predecessor has made some choices that have left the airport compromised, and she’s coming into a shitshow, frankly, tasked with fixing it. “And nobody likes her because she’s not trading on likeability or beauty or any of these things that historically have been the ways women get power. She’s trading on competence, and a lot of people are getting in the way of her doing her job. So that raises a lot of tension and drama in the workplace.” Related Article City life Deaths on planes and romance scammers: Life as an airport chaplain Azeez is “very, very excited by the idea of playing young women who are complicated. I really want my career to be me going into bat for young women – until I’m not a young woman any more; you know, there’s a real timeline on that – so I’m grateful to have this opportunity now. I think it’s a really political show, a socially aware show, and it’s very complex and layered.”



Azeez’s sister, two years older, works in management, and she tapped her for insights. “She’s also a psychologist, so she’s very useful for every role, ever.” She also tapped friends with kids for insights into juggling work and parenting. And she drew on her own experience of being a child of migrants – her parents were born and raised in Fiji – for that aspect of Mira’s backstory. “For me, acting is the perfect job in terms of the work of it,” Azeez says. “I love to research, I love to interview people, I love to read. I’m quite obsessive, and I can get hyper-fixated on things. The research is my favourite, and then flow state – performance is flow state when it’s going well.” Azeez never studied drama, not at school – “I did maths” – or university. “My parents were like, ‘Absolutely over our dead bodies.’ Lawyer, doctor, accountant: those were the options.” Shabana Azeez (left) with Noah Wylie in the hit medical drama The Pitt. They consented to her trying for one drama school, though, on the basis that if she didn’t get in they would never have to hear about this ridiculous acting thing again. “And I crashed my car on the way to the audition – it was horrible – and I just fumbled the whole thing.” She did an arts degree, with the aim of doing something acting-adjacent, and landed a job in arts administration. Her boss could tell her heart wasn’t in it though, and when Azeez confessed all she really wanted to do was act, the boss took action. “Within an hour, she got me an audition, and I booked it, and that tape got sent around to a bunch of directors, because it’s Adelaide,” she says. Soon, she was cast in indie shorts, and eventually features. “Adelaide being Adelaide is why I have a career,” she says. “Just, like, seven people being really nice to me.”

World.title: The 12-year sacrifice behind Socceroo’s life-changing decision
World.content:
SportSoccerA-League Men The 12-year sacrifice behind Socceroo’s life-changing decision Roy Ward August 13, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For 12 years, Socceroos attacker Awer Mabil made his dreams come true in Europe but paid a price with his beloved family back home. Mabil has gone to two World Cups, played in the UEFA Champions League and taken the pitch for clubs in Spain, Denmark, Turkey, Portugal, Switzerland and Czech Republic. Socceroo and new Melbourne City signing Awer Mabil poses at AAMI Park on Wednesday. Getty Images The 30-year-old South Australian is at “the peak of his powers” and has chosen to come home to the A-Leagues and sign a three-year deal with Melbourne City, in part to make up for lost time with those he loves. “I’ve done 12 years, I reckon that might be enough,” Mabil said.



“I want to be close to family, close to my friends. It’s very important now because I’ve sacrificed 12 years and I’ve seen my little brothers grow. “When I left one was three, one was five and now one is 16 and other is 13 – so there are certain things that are bigger than just football. New Melbourne City signing Awer Mabil. Getty Images “I’ve come to the point of my life where I know my friends and family have sacrificed a lot, so it is only right to give back.” Legacy is a word Mabil used multiple times on Wednesday, as one of Australia’s first South Sudanese players to star in the A-Leagues and move onto the Socceroos and Europe, he laid a path that others of African descent have followed led by Socceroos teammates Nestory Irankunda, Mohamed Toure and Tete Yengi.



By returning now, he can cement a legacy with achievements in the A-Leagues and the Socceroos who he still plans to play a big role for starting at the AFC Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January. Editor's pick FIFA World Cup One club, seven Socceroos: Melbourne team’s $1.2 million World Cup windfall “I’m 30, I’m the perfect age,” Mabil said. “You can see now, people are playing until 40 and I’m mentally, physically, at the peak. “I want to pass on my experience to the younger players and for my [South Sudanese] community, right now, it could have been easy to go [elsewhere] for money, but, for me, the most important thing is leaving a legacy, a blueprint for the young ones to follow.



“Now I’m playing in Australia. For sure, there will be a lot of South Sudanese at every stadium. I want to inspire the next generation.” Mabil sidestepped questions about whether his home club, Adelaide United, were in the running for his services. The Reds currently field a young side, led by another Socceroos attacker in Craig Goodwin, and they aren’t believed to have had the buying power to compete with City. But by coming home, his loved ones can still watch him play on TV during waking hours. Socceroo Awer Mabil, left, is kissed by teammate Bruce Djite after scoring for Adelaide United in 2014. Getty Images



“Adelaide is my home, my family is there,” Mabil said. “But I also have to look for what gives the best possibility to also win stuff. I think I’ve made the right choice for this moment in my career.” He joins fellow Socceroos Aziz Behich and Mathew Leckie at City although starting goalkeeper Patrick Beach has left the club to join Ligue 1 club Troyes. The A-League has become a young man’s competition recently and many of those players have looked up to Mabil, but will be out to beat him once play starts in October. “If you have beaten me, then I’ve done my job,” Mabil beamed.



“For me, the most important thing is showing an example and I’ve worked hard to try and do that. I’m happy when I see everybody, not just young African players but young Australian players, making that next step. “That’s what I’m here for.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions
World.content:
Analysis WorldNorth AmericaUS election US voters give both parties a reality check on their radical factions Michael Koziol August 13, 2026 — 5:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It was always a bit unfair that US Democrats were put through the wringer over some of their more radical candidates for this year’s midterm elections, while Republicans escaped relatively unscathed. By and large, Republicans were not asked what it meant for their party that pillow mogul and famed election result denier Mike Lindell was seeking the Republican nomination to become governor of Minnesota – with President Donald Trump’s endorsement. My Pillow founder Mike Lindell failed to win the Republican primary in Minnesota as voters shied away from both parties’ extremes. AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt In part, that’s because election denial, conspiracy theories and the far-right are by now so entwined with the GOP that it has become a moot point. There is no question about a Trumpist takeover of the Republican Party – it has already happened. But there was a reality check on Tuesday night when Lindell, despite the president’s backing, lost the primary to Lisa Demuth, the speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives.



It was a good night for moderates in both parties – and a wake-up call, potentially, for their more extreme factions. In Wisconsin, state politician and declared democratic socialist Francesca Hong lost her bid to become the Democrats’ nominee for governor of Wisconsin, losing to establishment-backed candidate David Crowley in a tight contest that the polls got wrong. Francesca Hong narrowly lost to her establishment rival in the Democratic primary for governor of Wisconsin. AP Photo/Nam Y. Huh Hong, 37, came to national attention – and not in a good way – for some of her past statements, including a 2020 tweet arguing that Thanksgiving should be permanently cancelled because it celebrated colonialism. Asked on CNN whether she stood by that view, she told an anecdote about being a chef, in a widely circulated clip that some analysts believe cost her the win.



Hong tried and failed to win endorsements from progressive kingmakers Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who said they weren’t getting involved in gubernatorial races. View post on X But AOC was also critical of Hong’s excesses. “Woke 1 was crazy,” she said, laughing, on America’s ABC News on Sunday, attributing the phrase to one of her local councillors. She basically went on to say – in nicer language – that most people had moved on from some of the opinions they articulated during the COVID-19vpandemic, which more or less aligned with a time people now describe as “peak woke”. “Woke 1 was crazy”: Progressive hero Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said people had evolved from their COVID-era views. Bloomberg



“Especially during COVID, there was a huge opening of the Overton Window,” AOC said. “The doors were really opened in trying to entertain every and any policy that was going to get us to a better place.” She maintained that “the discussions that were had in that time were quite fruitful”. Abdul El-Sayed, the populist progressive Democrat who won a US Senate primary in Michigan last week – beating an establishment candidate backed by the party elite and $US60 million ($85 million) in outside funding – was a much different proposition to Hong. Related Article US politics Left-wing populist wins in Michigan as Democrats reject party establishment Articulate and seasoned, he had already recanted some of his earlier positions such as defunding the police – though he maintained a tough line on ending US military aid to Israel. In the end, voters were savvy enough to reward the reasonable candidate, and take a pass on the outlandish one who wasn’t sure about Thanksgiving and didn’t seem quite ready for prime time.



And in Minnesota, voters were smart enough to give Lindell a wide berth – not that he’ll admit it. The My Pillow founder refused to concede defeat on Tuesday night, insisting his team had found “anomalies” with the vote. My Pillow chief executive Mike Lindell and President Donald Trump at the White House in 2020. AP “I’m not going to sit by until these numbers are explained,” he said, to applause. “We will get a full report on this … I’ve been on the phone with a lot of people. As you know, I’m very good at looking at elections.” It was true to form. Lindell was one of the most vocal proponents of the false claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen from Trump. He pushed false conspiracy theories about voting machines by the company then known as Dominion.

World.title: Punched, strangled, spat on with blood: The reality for mental health workers who say system is more broken than ever
World.content:
The crumbling state of Victoria’s mental health system has been exposed by workers who say they are being subjected to violence weekly and the sector is more broken now than it was before the royal commission. Their verdict comes as the government is asked to explain where $40 million to deliver 2000 homes for people with mental illness has gone and the fly-in, fly-out boss of the state’s flagship youth service quits. Professor Patrick McGorry is concerned about the lack of progress on mental health reform. Aaron Francis The Community Housing Industry Association [CHIA] Victoria has called on the Carroll government to come clean about its housing commitment, claiming it’s been quietly abandoned, and the funding has disappeared. The 2000 supported living places were a recommendation of the Royal Commission into Victoria’s Mental Health System and received $40.4 million in the 2021-22 budget, with pledges to provide the homes as part of the state’s Big Housing Build.



But progress on these spots has stalled, and the funding commitment has disappeared from future budget papers. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence CHIA chief executive Sarah Toohey said the government had so far broken its promise to deliver and fund the supported homes. “The government is quietly walking away from this royal commission recommendation to deliver mental health supported homes for Victorians,” she said. When asked about the project, the Carroll government pointed to 368 purpose-built mental-health supported dwellings constructed through the Social Housing Growth Fund, a program set-up in 2018.



Homes Victoria is also building 505 homes for people living with mental illness, but the CHIA says these are not yet “supported housing”, which requires funding for specialised staff and care. A government spokesperson did not detail what had happened to the money, but said they were delivering more homes for people with mental health challenges. “This is an important and complex reform, and we are taking a careful approach to ensure people living with mental health challenges get the long-term housing and specialist support they need.” More than five years after the royal commission handed down a final report, that then-premier Daniel Andrews promised to implement in full, an investigation by The Age has exposed serious failings in the sector and how it is being managed by government. This included that an independent watchdog’s report being reworked before its release so it was less critical of the government’s progress; a damning assessment on reform by advocate Patrick McGorry and accusations of violence, drug use and an exodus of senior staff from the state’s flagship youth mental health service.



Parkville Youth Mental Health and Wellbeing Service (PYMHWS) chief executive Dr Leanne Geppert on Wednesday resigned a day after The Age revealed she had been leading the organisation under a fly-in, fly-out arrangement. Related Article Exclusive

Mental health Kids’ mental health unit shut as staff investigated for use of force The service’s board chair, Cath Bowtell, announced Geppert was stepping down, thanking the Brisbane-based boss for her “extraordinary contribution”. “This has been a difficult and deeply considered decision for Leanne,” Bowtell said. “Having led PYMHWS through its establishment and first year of operations, she has been considering for some time when the right point would be to step away. Importantly to her, she wanted to see the organisation through a number of significant milestones.”



Frontline mental health workers across the state have also voiced their concerns at failed reforms promised by the royal commission. A survey of more than 500 workers across 11 Victorian health services reported a deterioration in conditions for patients and staff as well as escalating violence and drug usage in secure psychiatric wards. Two-thirds of mental health workers reported to the Health and Community Services Workers Union (HACSU) that they had been assaulted in the past year, with patients who are more acutely unwell on presentation contributing to the rise in aggression. “I have witnessed colleagues be punched so hard they are concussed, strangled, scratched, have blood-borne virus infected blood spat at them, facial bones fractured,” one worker said. Another reported clients at their hospital were not being treated in appropriate timeframes, which meant their health deteriorated and the risk to staff increased.



“The consumers are not being actively treated and are being discharged too soon, often very unwell,” the mental health worker said. “Most recently a client [who] had an admission was discharged to [the] community and remained unwell. She was readmitted one week later and remains in the intensive care unit. She was not actively treated and now her in-admission is much longer than it should have been.” More than 48 per cent of survey respondents said they disagreed or strongly disagreed that their health services were better placed now than they were before the royal commission. Less than 15 per cent of the workforce said they believed the mental health system had improved, while the remaining workers were neutral in their opinions about the impact of the reforms.



“In so many ways we have gone backward since the royal commission and nothing has actually changed,” a worker wrote. “In fact, access to mental health care has been worse.” HACSU Victorian branch secretary Paul Healey said the survey responses painted a concerning picture of the reality facing mental health workers, consumers, carers and families across Victoria. ”We need to be clear that this is not about blaming people experiencing mental illness,” he said. “Mental health workers understand the complexity of mental health care and are committed to providing compassionate support. “But a system that is under-resourced, overstretched and unable to provide the right care at the right time, built on the broken promises of a royal commission, increases risks.



Related Article Opinion

Mental health I’m a psychiatrist of 40 years. It’s mass gaslighting to claim we’ve made progress Patrick McGorry Psychiatrist and mental health advocate “These workers have carried the system through enormous challenges. They deserve more than being told change is coming, change needs to happen now.” In parliament on Wednesday, Mental Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said her government was proud of the support they’d provided the mental health workforce. “We have increased the workforce by over 30 per cent in the mental health sector. We have increased the number of acute beds available across the system,” she said. “We have delivered modern fit-for-purpose services across the state, including at the Thomas Embling Hospital and including at youth recovery and prevention centres in every region in the state.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘Family first, integrity, no drugs’: The billionaire will dispute that exposed a secret family succession plan
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two months before his death in Greece, billionaire Nick Andrianakos met his youngest son for lunch at upmarket Glen Iris restaurant Grazia, where he anointed him successor to the family’s petrol and property empire. The ailing founder of Milemaker Group told Theo Andrianakos he would have full control of the family’s multibillion-dollar businesses, and that his vast portfolio of assets in Australia and Greece would also be passed on to Theo and his two sons. Nick Andrianakos, pictured in Greece in 2022, aged 78. Athina Souli Theo also learned at the meeting in January 2025 that his father intended to bequeath €5 million ($8.17 million) to his substantially younger partner Hatouna Sakvarelintze, an architect the ailing businessman had met a couple of years earlier on a hotel redevelopment project. However, there was a sticking point in the patriarch’s grand succession plan – Andrianakos’ three other children, who would later claim in the Supreme Court of Victoria that the revised “family agreement” had not been relayed to them, nor formalised in a signed will. The death of the 81-year-old patriarch on March 17 last year – just days before he was due to sign the will and the family agreement – sparked a toxic legal battle between the siblings over control of their late father’s assets and extensive business interests. The case was set to proceed to trial last month, with siblings Kristina and Paul Andrianakos and Vicky Papamarkou relying on the original documents, signed by their father in 2018 and 2019, which gave the sisters a greater slice of their father’s $183 million estate, and the siblings shared control over Milemaker Group.



Under the signed will, Andrianakos wanted to give his sons the bulk of his inheritance – allocating them $83 million each, and his daughters $24 million respectively. However, the siblings reached an eleventh-hour agreement that avoided a trial and ultimately allowed Justice Peter Gray to grant probate of the unsigned will. Two city penthouses, listed as being worth more than $4 million, are among the division of assets. Domain The settlement, on July 17, handed Theo and his sons all of Andrianakos’ estate, which included CBD penthouses, beachfront homes on the Mornington Peninsula, and properties in Greece, along with a $200,000 black Bentley and a tractor. Theo received the lion’s share of the estate, reducing his brother’s inheritance and seeing his sisters receive substantially less than the $24 million they were originally entitled. The court dispute also laid bare the tensions between the family and Andrianakos senior’s partner, Sakvarelintze. The daughters claimed in respective affidavits that during the months that the drastic changes to their father’s estate were drafted, he had been frail and could no longer understand English.



Papamarkou warned her father that his Greek girlfriend was “probably only after his money” a year before he made changes to bequeath her millions, she claimed in her sworn statement. “I warned him that it was strange to see a woman so young be romantically interested in someone around 80 years of age,” she said in an affidavit. “I told my father to be careful because she was probably only after his money. My father responded by saying words to the following effect: ‘There is no way Hatouna is getting any of my money or property. I am leaving all my property to my children’.” The late billionaire’s wealth planner Peter Pagonis claimed the revised, unsigned will represented the lawful and legitimate plan for his inheritance. Pagonis, who consults to more than 450 ultra-high-net-worth families, said in an affidavit that the family patriarch first ordered him to draft the changes in November 2024 after expressing concerns the three siblings would seize control of Milemaker Group. Nick Andrianakos and son Theo. “The deceased said word to the effect that he was concerned that Vicky, Paul and Kristina would ‘gang up’ on Theo, who was CEO of Milemaker Group, and who was instrumental in operating and growing the Milemaker Group business with [Andrianakos],” he said.



“He was concerned his children Vicky, Paul and Kristina will disrupt the family legacy and seek to break up the family assets and the business that he had grown over time.” Pagonis said that Andrianakos told him in November 2024: “I want to make sure that Theo has full control of the business going forward.” The order came only a few months after the tense exchange between Papamarkou and her father over his romance, which had strained their relationship. She said after that confrontation in July 2023, the pair did not speak for some time until finally reconciling in August 2024. One of the family’s city penthouses. Domain Andrianakos’ instructions in November 2024 led to significant changes to the family agreement, the formal succession document which includes clauses of the family values (among them: family is first, business for future generations, integrity, and no drugs). The succession plans were later thrashed out over a series of meetings – including several lunches at Grazia and secret meetings at Andrianakos’ CBD penthouse – during what would be his last visit to Melbourne.



A $20,000 tractor was part of the estate. Kubpower.com.au The businessman jetted into town on Christmas Eve 2024 with Sakvarelintze, in time for the family’s Christmas lunch, held at Nobu in Crown Casino. Paul, Vicky and Kristina did not attend any of the estate discussions, with Papamarkou noting she didn’t discuss it with her father over Christmas lunch. “When the family met on Christmas day, my father appeared frail and unwell. Because the Christmas lunch was very busy, I did not get to spend any one-on-one time with my father that day,” she said. Papamarkou said when she did later catch up with her father, he was unwell and had difficulty getting up off the couch. Before returning to Greece in January 2025, Andrianakos visited Kristina’s home, where she claims he reassured her about his estate: “My father brought up his will again and told me that Vicky and I would be included and get a share of everything.” The Andrianakos family mansion sits on acreage in Greenvale. Justin McManus

World.title: The email many authors dream of getting – and why it’s a trap
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Less than two weeks after her debut novel Touch Grass was published in June, Mary Colussi received a dream email for many young Australian authors: a message from the head of prestigious UK publishing house Granta, Bella Lacey, raving about her novel’s “originality, intelligence, and distinctive narrative voice” and asking to discuss future projects. The email was detailed and effusive – the kind of praise that “as a writer, you want to believe”, Colussi says. Except it wasn’t from Bella Lacey or anyone from Granta – and the person who sent it almost certainly had not read Colussi’s novel. One of the red flags, Colussi says, was that “everything that they were praising is something that you can find in the synopsis, and in one paragraph they actually quoted directly from the synopsis”. The definitive giveaway was the email address, which ended with @aol.com. A quick check of the Granta website confirmed her suspicions: a warning note from the publisher about fraudulent emails being sent from scammers impersonating staff and offering publishing deals in exchange for money. Novelist Mary Colussi. Colussi’s experience is increasingly common, thanks to a new wave of AI-generated scam emails targeting authors internationally, offering publishing or promotional opportunities in exchange for money. In the past year, the Australian Society of Authors (ASA) has been inundated with messages from writers seeking advice and sharing their experiences, some of them receiving multiple scam emails a day. Email scams targeting authors have existed almost as long as email itself, but they have been turbocharged by AI. The latest wave of scams is “far more sophisticated”, says ASA chief executive Lucy Hayward. “It’s not just that they might be impersonating people from the book industry, it’s that they’re able to provide detail and give the impression that they have read an author’s work, which makes the email convincing. And they can do that because the author’s work has either already been ingested [by AI companies], or it can be ingested by these AI tools and then summarised.” Kelly Gardiner, an established author and member of the ASA board who receives these kinds of AI-generated emails daily, says “authors have been getting unsolicited approaches from PR ‘experts’ for a while, but the sudden expansion of AI has turned it into a flood”. An example of one of the scam emails increasingly being sent to authors.



Most authors have a story – or several. Veteran author and academic Dennis Altman has written about receiving effusive, detailed emails about his books from individuals purporting to be acclaimed authors Annie Ernaux and Patrick Süskind; Walter Marsh described being “flooded” by emails offering paid reviews and promotion after the publication of his second novel (ironically, a novel about theft and fraud) late last year; and Jane Sullivan detailed a “highly convincing” email ostensibly from the (real) Melbourne-based Classic Book Club, offering to promote her 2024 crime novel. While authors are the primary targets, respected editors, literary agents and media figures are caught on the other side of the sting. Scammers steal their names and professional authority to trick writers into fake pitch offers, promotional junkets or film deals. Such was the case with a recent scam email purporting to be from ABC Radio National presenter Sally Sara, offering an author a guest appearance on her show. By leveraging the cachet of a major public broadcaster, the scammers created an offer that felt almost too prestigious for a writer to turn down (the ABC was contacted for comment). Some of the initial emails mention money, but most don’t. Instead, they lead with flattery and promises, waiting to hook the author before they raise the issue of fees. These kinds of scams are sometimes referred to as “pig butchering” operations, a term that originated with romance scams and graphically evokes the process of fattening up a prospective victim with flattery before draining them financially. Most of the emails don’t mention money, instead they lead with flattery. Like romance scams, author scams target vulnerability and play on emotions. “They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted,” Hayward says. The tactic has proved remarkably lucrative for its perpetrators. In a recent case, the US government determined that just one of these publishing scam operations, based in the Philippines, defrauded nearly 800 writers of more than $48 million over six years. US author Victoria Strauss, who has covered author scams since 1998 via the website Writer Beware, says they have proliferated over the past decade, fuelled by outfits based in the Philippines, Pakistan and India. The more recent AI-driven scams come from a different location, however.



“I’ve gotten hundreds of reports of these AI scams, and I traced a lot of them back to the payment information, and everything that I can collect and deduce indicates that they primarily come from Nigeria,” says Strauss. “I see them as kind of a descendant of the ‘Nigerian prince’ scams of old.” Authors who have been inundated with these kinds of emails have become far more adept at identifying them. “The AI-generated copy is its own genre now and you can spot it once you’ve seen a few,” says Gardiner. The emails also have telling similarities: “same terms, same logic, same sentence structures”. Lucy Hayward, the chief executive of the Australian Society of Authors. They’re also often about older books. Gardiner says most of the scam emails she receives “are about two young adult books I published years ago. Perhaps it’s something to do with how often they were ingested in a pirate database used to train AI. No real publicist would want to talk to me about them, although sometimes local schools or readers do, so I always have to check.” Hayward says sifting the real emails from the fake has become a problem in itself. “[At this point] it’s not so much that authors are falling for these scams and handing out money, it’s the volume of the emails that they are receiving. It becomes very difficult to determine what might be a legitimate offer and what is a scam.” One of the key ways to check is looking at the email address, she says, “but for Australia, we have a smaller market, and where book clubs and podcasts are concerned, you might not have someone with a professional email address”. They’re trying to capitalise on an author’s genuine desire to have their work published, to have their work promoted, to have their work adapted. “You waste time trying to sift the real from the fake,” Gardiner says. “No doubt some genuine approaches have not got through, too, which means writers and readers miss out on real opportunities to engage.”



How are scammers continuing to thrive, if authors are getting wise? Strauss says the dozen or so emails she receives each week about people who have lost money to these scams involve non-professional and first-time authors. “There are a lot of people who just want to write one book; they want to write a memoir, or they want to write about their cancer journey or something they feel is meaningful and will help people. There are a lot of older people who retire and write children’s stories, or a memoir,” she says. Related Article Literature The Australian author who went from rejection letters to global bestseller These people are vulnerable to scammers in more than one way: not only are they unaware of how the publishing industry works and outside professional support networks and communities, but the personal nature of their material can make them particularly susceptible to emotional manipulation. “I sometimes hear from the relatives of older people, often on fixed incomes, who’ve lost enormous amounts of money – tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars – and cannot be convinced that they’re being scammed because the scammers are using psychological manipulation to establish personal relationships,” Strauss says. As she embarks on her career, Colussi can well understand how people are taken in. “Writing a book is such a dream for so many people. They are waiting for that one ‘yes’, and pretending that you are that one ‘yes’ is unfortunately an easy way to take advantage of someone.” What else is happening in the book world?

World.title: Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script
World.content:
★★ CultureTV & radioReview Hot priest? I wish! This holy love story will instead have you praying for a better script Kylie Northover August 13, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Falling ★★ A new series from British screenwriter Jack Thorne is usually exciting for a TV buff – as well as the gritty trilogy This Is England, the stage adaptation of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, and dozens of other acclaimed works, Thorne was the co-writer of the groundbreaking series Adolescence. Keeley Hawes and Sister Anna and Paapa Essiedu as Father Hicks in Jack Thorne’s Falling. Channel 4/The Forge/Robert Viglasky And on paper, his new series sounds brilliant – Falling is Thorne’s first love story, and he’s gone for the “hot for preacher” trope, with a nun falling for a priest. The cast is amazing – TV veteran Keeley Hawes (who’s been in everything from Spooks to The Assassin) is the nun who, after almost 30 years, gives it all up to be with Father Hicks, played by Paapa Essiedu (I May Destroy You, The Lazarus Project and star of HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter TV series), and it’s mostly directed by Peter Hoar, the Emmy Award-winning director of the feted The Last Of Us episode Long, Long Time. The forbidden love angle has long been a popular romance novel archetype but surely, I thought, Thorne would tackle it in a novel way. The answer is a hard no. (Said the Bishop to the actress.)



Editor's pick Review What to stream this week: Netflix’s new take on an Australian classic, plus five more picks Hawes is Anna, a nun in a cloistered Catholic order in rural England, where she spends her days in the convent’s garden, leaving the grounds only to deliver vegetables to the local food bank. She’s a devoted member, primed to take over from the convent’s abbess Francesca (Niamh Cusack). That is, until a visit from Father Hicks. We’re first introduced to Hicks, dressed in full cassock, having a ciggie on the side of a motorway where his car has broken down; that, and his obvious youth, are how we know he’s a “Cool Priest”. He serves a gritty Bristol parish, where he’s considered “radical”; rather than spending money on church heating, as his bishop (Jason Watkins) wants, Hicks is more concerned with setting up a needle exchange. He’s en route to the convent to meet with the abbess about bringing congregation members to experience a “life of conviction”. When he arrives, he meets Anna, and much coy eye-flirting takes place. Then, when she’s making eggs, she burns herself and Hicks rushes to help soothe her wound – and accidentally touches her hand! This seals the Mills & Boon-esque deal. Yes, that’s all it takes to overturn their lives. Even in civilian clothes, there’s zero chemistry between Father Hicks and Sister Anna. Channel 4/The Forge/Robert Viglasky There’s a second visit with more sustained eye contact, and the series’ best, if utterly implausible, line, when Hicks asks if he can see Anna’s cabbages, to which she replies, “Only if you get me really drunk first”. Trust me, that’s as saucy as things get. Shortly afterwards, Anna walks out of the convent and heads to Hicks’ church to declare her feelings. But this series is achingly slow, and Hicks spends the next three episodes looking bewildered; don’t expect any habit-ripping.



Mercifully, only the first four episodes were available to preview, during which there’s no actual romance, and a phenomenal lack of chemistry between the leads. At no point does this “love” feel plausible, despite the brilliant actors. Related Article ★★★

Review Ted Lasso goes beyond extra time with its fourth season, and we pay the penalty The story widens out to take in Hicks’ dealings with his parishioners (teens in trouble; abusive fathers; giving Last Rites), and Anna trying to reintegrate into modern life (she hasn’t seen a mirror for more than 20 years, despite clearly adhering to an incredible skincare routine), but even those scenes, which are more in Thorne’s wheelhouse, are weighed down by an unimaginative earnestness. Even the crises of faith our two leads must endure (very slowly), fail to go deep; Hicks, predictably, has a secret former life to grapple with, while Anna’s issue is very little knowledge of life outside the convent. Forbidden love has never looked so unappealing; you might find yourself praying for either something to actually happen, or for it to end. Falling is not even a curate’s egg – it’s just plain dull. But the biggest sin here is the script: the writing is stolid, earnest and preachy. If Thorne goes to confession over this series, he deserves some serious penance.

World.title: This TV legend has guided us through every decade of life. Next up? Our 60s
World.content:
Legendary producer John Edwards, the man behind The Secret Life of Us, Offspring, Rush, The F Ward and more.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A



Related Article Review Aussie drama Tangle is ripe for rediscovery (and now free to watch) Amid the host of productions that bear Edwards’ name as a producer or executive producer, there’s a particularly consequential string of loosely connected series – almost a spine through the body of work. It’s a choice selection of shows that resists neat generic categorisation and that portrays the challenges of life over generations. It begins with the spirited twenty-somethings of The Secret Life of Us (2001-04), moves on to the troubled thirty-somethings of Love My Way (2004-07), and then to the fraught forty-somethings of Tangle (2009-12). This trio will soon become a quartet with the arrival of Dalliance on Paramount+, which turns its attention to life, love, regret and death among sixtysomethings and features a cast including Heather Mitchell, Hugo Weaving, Georgie Parker and David Wenham. These are original drama series created for TV, but if the impressive adaptation of Kathy Lette’s Puberty Blues (2012-14), dealing with teenagers and their troubled parents, is added to the list, Edwards’ shows span an even broader spectrum of life, from tentative adolescent romances and early sexual experiences, through pregnancy and parenthood, to grandparenting and memorial services. Georgie Parker, Hugo Weaving and Heather Mitchell Dalliance. Lisa Tomasetti/Paramount+ All of these series showcase vibrant ensembles, memorable collections of artfully drawn and cleverly cast characters. They’re also notable for displaying Edwards’ “old head, young head” philosophy, on-screen and behind the scenes. He’s long believed that pairing experienced writers and actors with gifted newcomers creates the ideal combination, and the rewards of that approach have been abundant. The pairing of Edwards’ longtime collaborator, actor, writer and producer Claudia Karvan with novice screenwriter Kelsey Munro to create and develop Bump (2012-24) delivered one of the country’s best local productions (if you skip the regrettable telemovie tacked on at end). The series also gave us newcomers Nathalie Morris, Carlos Sanson Jr and Ioane Sa’ula in key roles, convincingly moving from high-school kids to adult parents negotiating family life and careers. They’re cast alongside proven players including Karvan, Angus Sampson and Anita Hegh, creating an ensemble alive with zesty energy. Claudia Karvan and Nathalie Morris in Bump.



But the practice reaches further back, reaping rewards on a host of series and revealing Edwards’ keen eye for emerging talent. Asher Keddie, Joel Edgerton, Samuel Johnson and Michael Dorman in Secret Life; Ashley Zukerman and Nicole Da Silva in Rush. Celia Pacquola displaying her range beyond comedy in Offspring and Beautiful Lie. Lincoln Younes perfectly cast as Ben Mendelsohn and Justine Clarke’s son in Tangle. These then-rising stars have shared the screen with some of the most accomplished actors in the country, Edwards’ frequent flyers including Susie Porter, Catherine McClements, Dan Wyllie and Rodger Corser.
