"I came down here [to Adelaide] in 1961. My grandparents followed Port Adelaide so I started following them and used to go to their games and all that type of thing," Trebilcock told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"I got friendly with the runner, Harry Vincent, got talking one day and said I'd like to get into the club and he said, 'I'll keep an eye out for you'."

A position opened up in the boot department and Trebilcock was told to have a "talk to the sprigger" who was also a bootmaker.

"He said, 'Are you prepared to learn?', and I said, 'Oh yeah', so I did a seven-year apprenticeship with him," Trebilcock said.

"After those seven years he got leukaemia and said, 'You're going to have to take over', and I said, 'Gee whiz, I'm a butcher'.

" But I was pretty lucky because moulded soles were coming in then and so I took it on and I've been there ever since and enjoyed every single minute of it. "

But from the day Trebilcock started looking after the players' footwear in 1968 and up to 1976, the Port Adelaide Magpies played without winning a SANFL premiership.

"I was beginning to think I was jinx," Trebilcock said.

But the club won a flag in 1977 and another 10 during Trebilcock's time, as well as a 2004 AFL premiership with its AFL side, The Power.

"The 2004 AFL premiership was mighty.

"I always pictured standing on the MCG on Grand Final day, celebrating a flag. That dream came true in 2004. I'll never, ever forget that day."

Bobby to say farewell as well

Also retiring is fellow volunteer Bob "Bobby" O'Malley after 18 years at the club mixing water barrels and player rehydration bottles, and helping set up for training sessions.

Former Port Adelaide Power player and captain Travis Boak with Bob O'Malley during a game against Carlton. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

"I just loved being involved in this football club," he said.

"Port Adelaide was always a family club, and all my family barracked for Port Adelaide."

He will have his final home game with Port Adelaide against Melbourne on Saturday night.

Trebilcock will be saying goodbye after 58 years with the club.

He said he became "real friends" during this time with the late and great Russel Ebert OAM, who started with the Magpies the same year as him.

An Australian Football Hall of Fame member since 1996, Ebert played 392 games for the Magpies and remains the only SANFL player to win four Magarey Medals.

"He was a people's person," Trebilcock said.

"He was a player that never played a game of football in moulded sole boots. To the day he retired he still had knock-in sprigs.

"Every now and then you'd have to re-sprig his boots.

"As he got older his sprigging would change … then he got his Achilles problems and we made a [raised] heel for him."

The late Russell Ebert shares a laugh with Alfie Trebilcock at Port Adelaide Football Club. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

Ebert once said of Trebilcock that he loved the players and the club, and the players loved him.

"He can talk to any player at any time and would have the complete respect of the entire playing and coaching group … we couldn't have had the success we had without him," Ebert said.

The AFL awarded Trebilcock the Jack Titus Award for conspicuous service to the game in 2013.

He was awarded Life Membership at PAFC in 2013 and was inducted into its Hall of Fame in 2025.

PAFC chairman David Koch said the club was what it was today because of people like O'Malley and Trebilcock.

"Nearly 60 years of turning up, asking for nothing and giving everything to the club he loves," he said.

"On behalf of every player, coach and supporter we say thank you, Alfie, and thank you, Bobby. We are the club we are today because of people like you."

World.title: 'Nowhere to hide' for Australia's under-fire batters against Bangladesh
World.content:
Former Australian Test opener Ed Cowan says some of Australia's batters are under pressure to make significant scores as the summer of cricket begins against Bangladesh in the Top End this week.

"If you're in the Australian Test team, and not performing regularly, there is just nowhere to hide," Cowan said on the ABC Cricket Podcast.

"And unfortunately, sometimes you get these weaker teams, and the expectation actually goes up. Cricket is hard enough, let alone with the weight of the world on your shoulders."

The Australian team is about to enter a 12-month period with potentially 21 Tests scheduled, including key away fixtures in India, South Africa and England.

Between June 2025 and the start of this cycle tomorrow, they played eight Tests, five of which were in Australia.

Australia played five of their eight Tests over the last 12 months at home, including the Ashes against England. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"That's two careers, 21 Test matches. You could have two careers in that time. That's a lot of Test cricket," Cowan said.

That cycle begins in Darwin when they take on Bangladesh, a nation ranked ninth in the ICC Test rankings.

At the conclusion of the recent successful Ashes series against England, the average age of the Australian team was just under 34. This is a team that has played together and had great success for a long time.

The Test between Australia and Bangladesh starts on Thursday August 13 in Darwin, and you can hear every ball live on ABC Listen.

Cowan does not believe that playing lower-ranked opposition necessarily provides younger players with a chance to gain experience.

"I think you are trying to pick your best available team and there's always an opportunity to work through your portfolio of players, and they've done this in recent years, usually away from home and it's less opposition dependent and more condition dependent," he said.

The bowling attack has been well established for some time with the likes of Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon proving a recipe for success.

Where the questions creep in is around the batting line-up.

Jake Weatherald was given an opportunity to open the batting in the recent Ashes series but is yet to score an international century, with a top score of 72.

Jake Weatherald will be looking to impress in front of his home crowd in Darwin against Bangladesh (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cowan expects the Northern Territory product to open in the first game, but says he remains under pressure.

"If Jake Weatherald doesn't get 100 in the next five Test matches, more than likely we'll find someone who will get an opportunity to open the batting. And so there's going to be some natural attrition over the coming months," he said.

He is not the only player who will be searching for form in this two-match series against Bangladesh. Marnus Labuschagne has averaged 26.61 with the bat in his last 20 tests and has taken time away from playing to focus on a training block in Queensland.

"After eight weeks of being able to just go back to my fundamentals and working on my game, spending hours and hours on the simple things, just my shots, working on my shapes and my technique as a whole, is something that I definitely needed," Labuschagne told reporters in Brisbane last week.

Loading Instagram content

It has been over 1,100 days since he last reached triple figures in a Test match back in 2023. Cowan believes these Tests could be a step in the right direction for Labuschagne.

"The greatest thing that you can have as a Test batsman is confidence. And confidence is only bred through performance," he said.

The youngest member of Australia's most recent Test team is Cameron Green. When the West Australian debuted in 2020, aged 21, he was touted as one of the best young talents in the country, but his recent form has some questioning his future in the side.

The now 27-year-old has played 37 Tests and has a batting average of 32.75 and a bowling average of 38.94, but Australian coach Andrew McDonald is resolute that Green remains a vital member of his side.

"We believe Cam Green is a very, very skilled player, and we believe, sometimes, his performances have been taken a little bit out of context," McDonald told SEN Radio.

"He's been contributing to this team, as have a lot of that top seven, in conditions that haven't been favourable to batters."

Cowan believes these two Tests present an opportunity for those out of form to find some form at a time when there is less pressure coming from other domestic players.

The last time Australia played a Test against Bangladesh was 2017, where Australia won the series 2-1. (Getty Images: /SOPA Images/LightRocket/Md Manik)

"They get first crack at it. And when there's no other cricket going on, there was a CA XI game that we'll come to, but there's no Shield cricket, there's no Aussie A tours, no-one's putting pressure on anyone," he said.

"It's a bit of a free swing. And in many respects, that should free the batters up to just go and play."

World.title: High school American footballer rattled by snake in helmet
World.content:
A high school American football player in the United States had every right to be rattled after finding a venomous snake inside his helmet during practice.

A team was going through its paces at Maumelle High school in Central Arkansas when a student felt unusual movement inside his headgear following warm-ups and brought his helmet to an assistant coach for inspection.

A slithering 2-foot (61cm) cottonmouth was discovered behind some padding.

The pit viper was so reluctant to exit the helmet that police officers had to pour water into it to force the snake out and into a bag.

Animal services technicians arrived a few minutes later, identified the snake as a deadly cottonmouth and took it to a wooded area far from the school.

Cottonmouths are the second-most-venomous snakes found in Arkansas.

Snake caught in bike chain bites woman The woman, in her 60s, was riding on a northern NSW rail trail when she ran over a two-metre snake that became trapped then bit her.

Animal services director Chris Davis said the player wore the helmet for nearly an hour and was fortunate he was not bitten.

"It was unreal," Davis said. "You had to kind of be there and take pictures to say this was real."

The player grabbed a different helmet and continued practice.

But the situation caused the head coach to reiterate to his team that players should examine their equipment carefully before using it, to check for insects or anything larger and more dangerous.

AP

Tech.title: It looks like Apple’s iPhone 18 really will skip the fall launch this year
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

According to an Economic Daily News report spotted by MacRumors, executives for Apple supplier Pegatron confirmed during an earnings call that the iPhone 18 Pro series phones will launch this fall, but the base iPhone 18 won’t arrive until the first quarter of next year. The more affordable iPhone 18e and a new iPhone Air are also rumored to launch around the same time, in line with rumors that have been circulating for more than a year.

Analyst Ming-Chi Kuo and The Information both reported last year that Apple was planning to only launch its premium iPhones in fall 2026, and earlier this year another Apple supplier said one of its customers was postponing a phone launch to early 2027.

Along with the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple’s rumored “Ultra” foldable is reportedly launching this fall. The EDN report cites Pegatron execs saying that memory and chip shortages are causing the peak shipping seasons to shift, as its customers like Apple figure out how to spread out the parts they have and increasingly prioritize higher-priced models that have larger margins.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phone preorders come with up to $350 in gift cards
Tech.content:
Brad Bourque is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Looking to get your hands on the latest Pixel devices? After weeks of leaks and rumors, Google has officially announced its next generation of Pixel phones and watches.

The base Pixel 11 starts at $899, the Pro and Pro XL are $1,099 and $1,299 respectively, and the Pro Fold starts at $1,899. The watch comes in two sizes, with the smaller 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. The phones are available for preorder now, and will ship on August 20th, 2026.

If you’re looking to preorder an unlocked phone on its own, your main options are Best Buy, Amazon, and directly from the Google Store. All three are running a similar introductory deal, where you’ll receive a gift card for a future purchase at that retailer, with the value depending on which model you buy. The Pixel 11 includes a $100 gift card, the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL include a $200 gift card, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold includes a $350 gift card. Only Google lists an end date for the promotion, which is August 27th, 2026.

If you’d also like a Pixel Watch 5, Google is the best option, because you can opt to put the gift card towards the purchase of the Watch instead to earn an extra $50 on top of the value. For example, if you buy a Pixel 11 Pro, you can take a $200 gift card, or opt for $250 off the Pixel Watch 5 when purchased together. If you buy a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, the base model 41mm Pixel Watch 5 is free.

Each phone is powered by the new Tensor G6 processor, which Google says is capable of 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent improvement to app loading speeds over the Tensor G5. The camera and video features are a focus of the new Pixel 11 series phones. The new Magic Capture feature lets you forget about snapping a great shot, and instead stitches together a series of clips and photos from a longer video. All four phones also featuring upgraded batteries and fast charging, with wireless charging support for Qi2.2 up to 25W.

If you’re deciding which Pixel is right for you, make sure to check out our initial hands-on impressions for the new Pixel 11 series phones and the Pixel Watch 5.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL

The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 for the base model with 256GB of storage, and goes up to $1,219 for the 512GB model, or $1,449 for the 1TB model. The larger Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 for the 256GB configuration, with the 512GB costing $1,419 and the 1TB model priced at $1,649. For both phones, the 256GB version has 12GB of memory, while the larger capacity models have 16GB of memory.

Apart from the screen size, resolution, and battery capacity, the two phones are otherwise identical to each other. They feature updated cameras, including a 50MP wide angle, 48MP telephoto with up to 5x optical zoom, a 48MP ultrawide sensor, and a 42MP selfie camera with a 103 degree field of view. The phones are available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11

The Pixel 11 starts at $899 for the model with 256GB of storage, and the price rising to $1,019 for the 512GB model, both of which have 12GB of memory. The 6.3-inch display has a 1080 x 2424 resolution and 60-120Hz refresh rate, with HDR support up to 2000 nits, or 3000 nit brightness with HDR off. For cameras, the Pixel 11 sports a 48MP sensor wide camera, a 13MP ultrawide, a 10.8 MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom, and a 10.5MP selfie camera with a 95 degree field of view. The phone is available in four colors: frost, pistachio, hibiscus, and obsidian.

Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold starts at $1,899 for the base model with 256GB and 16GB of RAM, with a 512GB model for $2,019, and a 1TB option for $2,249 available as well. It’s available in two colors: olive and obsidian.

The only foldable phone in Google’s Pixel lineup, the 11 Pro Fold features a 6.5-inch external display, and a 8-inch internal display when opened. Both screens feature refresh rates up to 120Hz, and HDR support. The internal and front selfie cameras are 10MP sensors, and the main camera block features a 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP telephoto with up to 5X optical zoom, and a new 48MP wide camera with upgraded light sensitivity.

Where to preorder the Pixel Watch 5

The updated Pixel Watch 5 comes in two sizes, with the 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. In addition to faster processing and more memory, there are a variety of new features for exercising, like a workout builder, and a more accurate GPS in crowded areas. The watch adds a variety of new long-term health features under the umbrella of “Health Guardian” which can detect some medical emergencies, watch blood pressure trends, and keep track of insulin resistance.

Carrier offers and promotions

AT&T is offering a variety of discounts if you want to upgrade to the new phones or the Pixel Watch 5. Most notably, you can get a Pixel 11 Pro for free via 36 months of credits if you trade in a Pixel phone of any year or condition, although you’ll need to keep the service active for the duration and have a service of at least $80 a month. The same deal is available for a Pixel 11 Pro XL with qualified trade-ins. If you’re starting a new line and buying a device that’s $500 or more with an installment plan, you can also claim 50 percent off a Pixel Watch 5.

Tech.title: Twitch streamers can now opt out from training Amazon’s AI
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Twitch users can now opt out of allowing their content to be used to train Amazon’s generative AI models. Opting out means that “your streams, VODs, clips, stream chats, and pictures and text on your channel” won’t be used in “future training” of an Amazon AI model “whose purpose is to generate or synthesize text, audio, images, or video,” according to a Twitch support page.

Other “AI-supported” features like captions and safety tools will still function if you opt-out of generative AI training. However, if you participate in a chat on another person’s stream, “their opt-out preferences govern if that chat can be used for training,” Twitch says.

The “Training for Generative AI” toggle is present for me in Twitch’s settings under the Security and Privacy tab. It was toggled on when I found it, and I’ve asked Amazon if that’s the default.

Here’s the full text of Amazon’s description for the toggle:

Allow your channel content to train generative AI content models at Amazon. Turning this off does not opt you out of Twitch and Amazon using your channel content for other purposes described in the Twitch Privacy Notice, including using AI-supported Twitch features that benefit the community by facilitating streamer growth and monetization (such as real-time sponsorship campaign assistance), viewer discovery (such as recommendations), and community safety (such as AutoMod). Learn more

Tech.title: How Google’s new Pixel 11 phones compare to last year’s models
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google just added four new phones to the Pixel family: the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They’re slightly more expensive than their predecessors, but they come with some notable upgrades, including improved cameras and a new Tensor G6 chip that should deliver faster performance. The phones also have new photography tools, like Magic Capture, along with improvements to Gemini Intelligence, expanded Live Translate capabilities, and the ability to use Circle to Search directly through the camera.

To make deciding whether you’ll upgrade or hold onto your last-gen phone a little simpler, we’re focusing on comparing the specs of the 6.3-inch Pixel 11 and Pixel 10 models, as well as the 6.8-inch Pro XL models. If you’re curious about how the Pixel 11 Pro Fold compares to its predecessor (and to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 series foldables), we’ve got a spec comparison right here.

Before we get to the specs, here’s a breakdown of what’s new.

They’re more expensive, but you get more storage

The most obvious difference is that, like almost everything these days, they’re more expensive than before. The Pixel 11 starts at $899, $100 more than its predecessor, but Google has doubled the base storage to 256GB with 12GB of RAM. The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 — $100 more than the Pixel 10 Pro’s launch price — with the same 256GB of storage and 12GB of RAM, and is available with up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. Meanwhile, Google’s larger 6.8-inch Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 and offers the same storage and RAM configurations as the Pro.

Tensor G6 allows for even more AI features

Both the Pixel 11 and Pro phones run on Google’s new Tensor G6 chip, which the company claims should improve performance by up to 25 percent compared to its predecessor. The new chip also powers a host of AI upgrades, including improvements to Gemini Intelligence, which Google says can now pull more context from supported apps to proactively surface useful information. There are also new voice-to-text tools that remove filler words and clean up formatting, while writing assistance can use what’s on your screen to help draft, rewrite, and refine messages. Live Translate is also available on videos, podcasts, and voice messages, and Circle to Search now works directly through the camera, letting you identify objects, translate text, or search your surroundings without snapping a photo first.

The cameras get some notable upgrades inside and out

There are a number of camera improvements, too, along with new photography and video features. On the hardware side, the Pixel 11 has a slimmer camera bar that sits flush when paired with one of Google’s phone cases. It can also zoom in farther than its predecessor, reaching up to 30x for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series gets an updated 1/1.3-inch 50-megapixel sensor for its main camera and a redesigned telephoto sensor that Google says captures 32 percent more light. The Pro can also zoom up to 120x and features a 42-megapixel selfie camera. The Pro should be quicker at shooting in the dark, too, with Google claiming its Instant Night Sight can capture photos up to 4.5 times faster.

Google has made several software improvements as well. The new Magic Capture mode in the camera app automatically captures photos and videos to make them ready to share with a tap. Camera Looks let you create custom styles for photos, while the Pixel 11 Pro series can record stabilized video at up to 8K using Pro Stable Video with Video Boost. A new Creator Suite also features tools for trimming and rearranging clips, using a teleprompter while recording, and improving speech clarity, and it automatically saves clips to a designated project album.

How the Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 compare

Those are some of the biggest changes, but they’re far from the only differences between the two lineups. For example, both the Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro offer an Extreme Charging Mode that prioritizes charging over other tasks for a faster boost when you’re short on time. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL also gets HiLight, colored LEDs around the camera flash that can alert you to things, like calls when your phone is face down or when Gemini is activated.

Tech.title: ICE wants to give agents electrified gloves that shock people into compliance
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is aiming to spend up to $20 million on equipping officers and agents with specialized gloves that deliver painful electric shocks. These plans were outlined in a notice published by the Department of Homeland Security on Monday, with an unspecified quantity of the devices set to be delivered by March 2027.

The electrified handwear outlined in the contract is the CTG 5 GLOVE (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), which manufacturer Compliant Technologies refers to as a CD3 (Conductive Distraction and De-escalation) device. Compliant Technologies describes it as “a great, humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution” that is “usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds.”

These are the gloves in question, which insidiously just look like a regular pair of protective gloves instead of something a comic book supervillain would engineer. Image: Compliant Technologies

The shock feature can be activated in a second using a switch located on the glove, which delivers a maximum voltage of up to 380V upon skin contact — closer to a dog’s shock collar than a taser device. Still, this “inhibits/ distracts the subject from performing coordinated muscle movement” according to the glove’s user guide. The same guide includes several warnings: Don’t use more than one pair on a single individual, don’t shock people for more than 15 seconds, and don’t use it against high-risk populations such as children, or people who are elderly, pregnant, or disabled.

Because the CD3 gloves are not immediately identifiable as a weapon, Compliant Technologies describes them as an “invisible partner” that can be used to enhance “established tactics, techniques and procedures,” and calls them “The New Protocol in Peace Keeping.” Similar gloves from the same company have already been used by select police departments and jails in recent years, and two corrections officers were charged in 2022 for beating and shocking an inmate in two separate attacks.

ICE has demonstrated it can wield power with little oversight or accountability, fueled by an administration that encourages rough tactics. It has shown up at people’s doors to intimidate them, used mass surveillance, and killed people in broad daylight. The agency’s new shocking gloves will just be a new way to hurt people.

The Associated Press reports that the Department of Homeland Security is working on a response to its press inquiries, but offered “no immediate comment” on the purchase plans. In a statement to the publication, Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, questioned why the devices would be necessary for civil immigration enforcement:

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do. Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Tech.title: Amazon gets out of the MMO game
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon is fully stepping back from MMOs. After saying last year that it would be halting “a significant amount” of its work on first-party AAA games, “specifically around MMOs,” Amazon will be handing over live operations of Throne and Liberty and Lost Ark in the West to other companies, according to announcements on Wednesday. Throne and Liberty will be taken over by FirstSpark Games and NC in Q4 2026. Lost Ark will be run by Smilegate starting in early 2027.

When Amazon announced the broader strategy shift in October, the developers of a third MMO, New World: Aeternum, announced plans to stop offering new content updates. As of January, you can’t buy that game anymore, and it will be taken offline on January 31st, 2027.

Amazon’s current gaming strategy focuses more on its Luna cloud gaming service, party games you can play on a TV with your phone (including ones with AI-powered Snoop Dogg and Arnold Schwarzenegger characters), and games that tie into other franchises Amazon is working on, like James Bond and Tomb Raider. Amazon’s gaming boss spelled it all out for me in a recent interview.

Tech.title: Grubhub’s $24M FTC settlement is finally reaching diners and drivers
Tech.content:
Well over half a million Grubhub drivers and customers are set to receive a share of $23.8 million following allegations that the food delivery company misled workers about their potential earnings and engaged in other deceptive practices.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced on Wednesday that it’s distributing the money to 640,038 consumers, with most recipients receiving a check in the mail. Some will receive their payments through PayPal.

The payouts stem from a lawsuit the FTC and Illinois Attorney General filed against Grubhub in December 2024. The complaint accused the company of a range of unlawful practices, including making misleading claims about how much drivers could earn, restricting customers’ access to their accounts and money, and listing restaurants on its platform without their permission.

Another allegation involved Grubhub’s restaurant listings. According to the complaint, the company had as many as 325,000 restaurants on its platform that were not affiliated with Grubhub. The FTC alleged that Grubhub used those listings to make its platform appear larger.

The complaint also alleged that Grubhub sometimes refused to remove restaurants after they asked to be taken off the platform. Instead, the company allegedly tried to convince some of those businesses to enter into paid partnerships.

The settlement required Grubhub to change how it operates in several areas. For instance, the company must be more accurate when advertising potential driver earnings, give customers a way to challenge account restrictions that leave them unable to access their accounts or funds, and obtain a restaurant’s consent before listing it on the platform.

Today’s announcement puts renewed attention on Grubhub’s treatment of its drivers and diners and the company’s broader business practices. Notably, it comes just one month after a federal judge granted final approval of another settlement worth nearly $25 million and involving approximately 60,000 Grubhub delivery drivers in California.

Grubhub also isn’t the only delivery company to face scrutiny. In the past, DoorDash has faced criticism and legal challenges over driver compensation, while Uber Eats has dealt with allegations involving customer charges and its relationships with restaurants.

Tech.title: AI coding startup Cognition reportedly already in talks to raise at $40B valuation
Tech.content:
In Brief

Cognition, makers of the AI coding agent Devin, is reportedly already talking to investors about raising another funding round with a big leap in valuation, after it raised $1 billion at a $26 billon valuation in May.

This new round could deliver at least a $40 billion valuation based on achieving a $1 billion annualized revenue run rate, according to sources cited by Bloomberg.

Three months ago, when it announced its last raise, Cognition’s Scott Wu confirmed to TechCrunch that it had achieved a $492 million annualized revenue run rate and that enterprises were growing their usage of Devin by 50% month-over-month for the past six months.

Wu, a famed wunderkind programmer himself, also told TechCrunch that Devin is not being sold as a human replacement. The agent is often tasked with doing long-tail grunt-work that many programmers dislike such as bringing old software up to date or moving applications off one platform and onto another. This could account for much of its growing popularity among enterprises that have adopted it. The company says its customers include Mercedes-Benz, NASA, and Goldman Sachs.

Tech.title: As AI safety concerns mount, three pioneers make the case for staying open
Tech.content:
As projects like Pacing the Frontier look to major labs as a way to keep AI research safe, open-source models have become a sore spot for the industry. With free distribution and little control over how they’re used, open-weight models aren’t easily controlled, leading some labs to treat them as downright scary.

But at the Ai4 conference in Las Vegas last week, three of the world’s most respected AI researchers — Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton, World Labs CEO and co-founder Fei-Fei Li, and Coursera co-founder Andrew Ng — spoke out on the issue. And while they disagreed on particular tactics, all three made a powerful case for keeping AI open.

For the three speakers, the core concern was allowing a handful of major AI companies to control the pace of progress. When a few companies control access to a technology, as Apple and Google do with mobile operating systems, innovation can slow and the companies that control the platforms can influence what gets built on them.

Andrew Ng said that he worried about a similar dynamic emerging in AI. “I don’t want there to be gatekeepers,” Ng said. “That limits how all of us can access AI.”

Companies have an incentive to protect their competitive advantages, including by influencing the rules that govern the industry. That could create a dynamic where only the largest, best-capitalized firms with the resources to build the most advanced AI systems.

Ng’s solution was to maintain multiple providers, with models and companies competing rather than allowing a handful of of players to dominate the field. “If I were to try to give one prescription, it would be to promote openness,” Ng said, “because AI is amazing technology and I want it to be in everyone’s hands.”

But not everyone agreed that open-weight models would help preserve that state of play. Hinton, in particular, drew a distinction between open-source software, which makes the underlying code available for inspection and modification, and open-weight models, which release the parameters of a trained AI model to the public.

“Open source is great. You show people the code, and lots of people look at the lines of code and say, ‘Oh, there’s a bug.’ Open weights means you train a big model and then you give people the weights. That’s very different,” Hinton said. “I was against open [weights] because it makes it so easy for people to take these big foundation models, which are very expensive to train, and for much less money train them to do bad things like cyber attacks.”

But whatever his reservations, Hinton acknowledged that open-weight models are already a permanent fixture of AI. “I think that battle’s been lost. We now have open-weight models, so the barrier to lots of people getting these big models, which was the cost of training foundation models, that barrier has disappeared. It’s too late.”

Yet accepting reality didn’t mean ignoring the risks. Hinton’s position was clear: AI would continue to advance, and he thought that was largely a good thing. He said it would boost productivity and improve education and healthcare. “Worrying about the possible bad effects of AI and the things that intelligent beings might do when they’re smarter than us. I don’t think that’s unfair. I think it is unfair to label anybody who thinks like that as a fear-monger,” Hinton added.

Ng took a different view. The question, he argued, wasn’t whether open models were risky, but who controlled access and who would win the market. Whoever built the cheaper model would have the advantage. If China’s open-weight models gained widespread adoption across Asia, Africa, and/or the developing world, he warned, they could influence how billions of people encountered ideas about democracy, freedom, and human rights.

“One thing I hope we do is encourage American competitiveness and open-source AI. It turns out that AI is a tremendous source of soft power. You can see the way China’s model has tremendous accomplishment with Africa, for example,” Ng said. “But my worry is because of all the lobbying in the U.S. and the fear-mongering, building open-source AI in America is struggling to compete with open-weight models coming out of China, and my worry is that if China figures out a fundamentally more cost-efficient way to build AI, then things that are more cost-efficient have a fundamental business adoption advantage.”

Li pushed back on that framing. “It’s very dangerous to make this a dichotomy between complete openness all the way to complete closedness,” she said. “In complex software systems as well as scientific systems it’s much more nuanced.”

Li used nuclear physics as an example: scientific papers are published openly, but uranium is regulated, while laboratory work falls somewhere in between. The lesson, she explained, was that openness doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing choice. Different layers of the ecosystem can operate at different levels of openness.

She also highlighted collaborations between public and private institutions, such as the Human Genome Project. The resulting knowledge became a platform that others could build on, she said, allowing pharmaceutical companies to profit, scientists to advance their work and society to benefit.

“So I think we have to use [AI] as that kind of infrastructure,” Li said. “We need some levels of openness, both in scientific discovery, in education, in global partnership, as well as lucrative business models for entrepreneurs. But we also will accept closed-source systems. This debate, especially at the sweeping level of ‘we can only tolerate one,’ is a false debate. We need to get to a level of nuance.”

But everyone agreed that some level of regulation would be necessary to keep AI on the right track. “What we want to do is develop AI in a direction that helps people, and regulation will help us do that,” Hinton said. “You can’t leave it to people like Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg to decide how AI should be done.”

Tech.title: OpenAI-backed Thrive Holdings raises $2B to bring AI to the enterprise
Tech.content:
Thrive Holdings has raised $2 billion in new funding at a $12 billion valuation from investors like SoftBank, D1 Capital Partners, and Altimeter Capital.

Thrive Holdings is akin to a private equity firm for AI, buying traditional businesses like accounting firms and implementing AI into their workflows. So far, Thrive has focused on accounting and information technology, but part of Wednesday’s raise will go toward expanding a new vertical in physical assets. Key to that strategy is Thrive’s close relationship with OpenAI.

The New York Times was first to report the news.

The firm is a spinout of Thrive Capital, one of OpenAI’s major investors. In December 2025, OpenAI took an ownership stake in Thrive Holdings. Part of the deal involved OpenAI sending employees to work with Thrive’s companies to accelerate AI adoption.

That hands-on model of AI implementation has become a business in its own right, and may help explain investor enthusiasm behind Thrive’s latest fundraise. OpenAI and Anthropic have both partnered with large private equity firms to launch The Deployment Company and Ode with Anthropic, respectively — billion-dollar ventures that are building teams of elite engineers who embed themselves into enterprises and implement AI solutions into workflows.

The raise comes off the back of proven success for Thrive’s companies, which has surpassed 70 businesses on Thrive Holdings’ platforms. The company has focused on two pillars to date: Current, its accounting arm with more than 50 firms and more than 2,000 professionals, and Shield, its information technology arm with around 20 companies on the platform.

Current’s self-improving tax agents, dubbed TaxAI, processed more than 7,000 tax returns at 98% accuracy, lowering tax prep times at participating firms by over 30%, according to Thrive. Meanwhile, Shield’s AI products have sped up help desk resolution times by 36x, and the platform has doubled the number of custom AI agents deployed in the last month.

Part of Wednesday’s fundraise will help Thrive launch a third platform focused on regulatory services for the built environment, described by a spokesperson as: “the work required to get physical assets approved, built, certified, and kept in operation.”

“The U.S. needs to build and modernize more critical infrastructure, but projects are often constrained by local, technical, and regulatory complexity,” Anuj Mehndiratta, a founding member of Thrive Holdings, told TechCrunch. “This applies across data centers, manufacturing, healthcare, power, water, transportation, and other physical infrastructure.”

That sort of complexity is where Thrive, well, thrives — large, fragmented, mission-critical, and operationally complex. While Mehndiratta says AI won’t replace field work, local judgement, or professional sign-off, it can help ease manual workflows like research, reporting, permit preparation, inspection documentation, and compliance tracking.

“We think AI partnered with a lot of the experts and practitioners at these businesses can really help compress [regulatory bottlenecks], keep the safety standards high, but also be able to do it with less of a burden to the actual building of that and help it do it more efficiently, lower cost and do it faster,” Kareem Zaki, a founding member of Thrive Holdings, said in a statement emailed to TechCrunch.

Tech.title: Uber Freight reportedly investigating after hacking group claims data breach
Tech.content:
A hacking and extortion gang has taken credit for a cyberattack and data breach at Uber Freight, the ridesharing giant’s logistics subsidiary.

A spokesperson for Uber Freight told Reuters, which first reported the incident, that there was no effect on its business operations and that its systems were running normally. (The company did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s questions about the incident.)

The shipping company is the latest victim in a spate of hacks in recent weeks conducted by the Helix hacking group, which has targeted transportation companies, financial giants, and private equity firms throughout the year. The hackers are known for targeting companies and exfiltrating large amounts of data from their cloud environments, which they then threaten to publish if the victim companies do not pay a ransom.

In a post on its data leak site, which it uses to host the stolen files, the Helix hackers claim to have taken mailboxes, cloud storage drives, files relating to accounts payable, and dispatch documents from Uber Freight.

Some of the files seen by TechCrunch appear to show email correspondence between Uber Freight and several of its customers. TechCrunch could not immediately verify the authenticity of the files, which appeared to be dated around mid-June.

Uber Freight has not yet said if it received any correspondence from the hackers, or if it paid the hackers a ransom.

Google said earlier this week that the Helix hacking group is part of a wider umbrella collective of hackers that it tracks as UNC6671. The gang relies on social engineering tactics, such as voice phishing, a tactic that involves calling IT helpdesks and requesting the reset of employee passwords. Security researchers have long warned that these attacks, while crude and rudimentary, are highly effective at tricking humans into granting access to sensitive systems.

In its blog post, Google said a review of the gang’s bitcoin wallets shows it has made at least $10.6 million in ransom payments between January and May this year.

Tech.title: Mesh, Automattic’s CRM for everyone, comes to Android
Tech.content:
Mesh, the relationship manager and personal CRM acquired by WordPress.com’s parent company, Automattic, last year, is now available to users on Android devices. The software allows users to privately visualize and keep track of the people in their personal and professional networks, add notes to people’s contact information, and be reminded when to reach out.

On Android, the company customized Mesh’s app to work with key platform features, like split-screen and pop-up views. This allows users to access Mesh while working in other apps, like messages or email. It also supports keyboard shortcuts for foldables and tablets, in-app search, home screen widgets (with Material You colors that match your Android’s wallpaper), and real-time sync across devices.

Image Credits:Mesh

The company’s broader plans for Mesh could eventually see it tied more closely to Automattic’s all-in-one messaging app, Beeper, which offers a way to connect with people across platforms, including through WhatsApp, Instagram, Signal, Messenger, X, LinkedIn, Slack, Discord, Google Messages, and more.

Already, Mesh and Beeper interoperate to some extent, as Mesh users can draft a text to someone in Beeper or click deep links in the app to visit a Mesh user’s profile. In time, the company wants to add additional AI features that will make users of both products more productive in terms of managing their personal relationships.

“We’re thinking a lot about how can AI help you be a better friend and have better work and personal relationships?,” Mesh co-founder Zachary Hamed told TechCrunch in an interview earlier this spring. “We have users who have ten-, twenty-, or fifty-thousand connections across multiple social media apps, across their work products. It’s an impossible task to think and be conscientious with you, with each of those people, by yourself,” he noted.

Image Credits:Mesh

Today, Mesh’s Nexus AI is in early access, offering a way to use AI to navigate your network. That means users can ask questions like who they know at a particular company or who lives in a certain city, or who has expertise in a particular topic. The company is also experimenting with using AI technology to provide a voice-based, hands-free experience and an improved business-card-scanning feature.

Importantly, personal information stored in Mesh isn’t shared or used for ad targeting, the company says, as the product is supported by subscriptions. (It’s free for up to 1,000 contacts, then has higher tiers for unlimited contacts and other features.)

In time, Mesh may consider a bundled subscription with Beeper or other Automattic products, but has nothing to announce on that front at this time.

Currently, the majority of Mesh’s customers, or around 70%, are using the app for some type of business purpose. Mesh co-founder Matthew Achariam says Mesh’s sweet spot is executives running bigger teams or those who have a tight network to stay in touch with. However, the company still thinks about the consumer use case, he notes.

“The beauty of [serving business users] is that the same things they’re using apply to every individual consumer. So every feature that we think about has to apply to both,” he says.

Mesh (formerly Clay) for Android will roll out to Google Play for phones, tablets, and foldables as a free download with in-app purchases.

Tech.title: Why Stream ring-maker Sandbar says the future of AI wearables is voice
Tech.content:
Loading the player…

AI notetaking hardware has taken off over the past couple of years, with credit-card-sized devices, pendants, pins, and even transcribing earbuds all promising to capture your meetings and turn them into summaries and action items. Now, a whole wave of wearables — rings especially — are betting people want to capture stray thoughts and ideas the same way.

One of the companies chasing that bet is Sandbar, the startup behind the private voice ring Stream, which has raised $36 million to date, including a $23 million Series A led by Adjacent and Kindred Ventures.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Rebecca Bellan talks with Sandbar co-founder and CEO Mina Fahmi about why he thinks so many voice hardware devices before Stream struggled to break through, and why he’s betting that keeping the human firmly in control is what it’ll take to get wearable tech right.

Subscribe to Equity on YouTube, Apple Podcasts, Overcast, Spotify and all the casts. You also can follow Equity on X and Threads, at @EquityPod.

Tech.title: Tesla wants to build a $10B solar factory in Texas
Tech.content:
In Brief

Tesla intends to build a massive solar panel factory 45 minutes southwest of Houston, according to documents filed with the state of Texas.

The new factory, called Project Crystal Sun, could cost as much as $10.1 billion. Tesla has applied for tax incentives to partially offset the cost, saying that it is exploring other sites “across multiple U.S. states.” The factory would create about 9,700 full-time jobs, Tesla said.

Without incentives, Tesla’s accountants estimated that the property tax liability for the project would be about $1.1 billion over 37 years.

The project aims to break ground this year and be completed by 2028, and Tesla said the first solar panels would roll off the line in 2029. The company hasn’t indicated whether the panels would be destined for terrestrial installations or satellites. However, Tesla CEO Elon Musk, who also runs SpaceX, is famously bullish on orbital data centers.

In the filings, Tesla did not publicly disclose the factory’s annual output, though it has said that it plans to build 100 gigawatts’ worth of manufacturing capacity in the U.S. by 2028.

Tech.title: The Gender War Over ‘Obsession’ Has Come for Theme Parks
Tech.content:
By any metric, the horror film Obsession has been one of the most extraordinary Hollywood success stories of 2026.

Made on a budget of around $750,000 and released in May, it went on to earn $488 million worldwide, catapulting 26-year-old director and screenwriter Curry Barker—originally known for his YouTube sketch comedy—to the top of the industry’s “it” list.

So why, you might ask, are people creating a stink over Universal Studios, the international distributor of Obsession, adding its lead female character, Nikki, to the cast of the Halloween Horror Nights event at its Hollywood theme park? Even though the actor who plays her seems very much on board? To answer that, one has to review three months of fierce and enduring debate.

Since the movie hit theaters, fans and critics have been at odds over a thorny question: Who is the victim in Obsession? The plot concerns an awkward, painfully insecure young man, Bear (Michael Johnston), who yearns to be in a romantic relationship with his friend, the seemingly unattainable Nikki (Inde Navarrette). In a moment of frustration, he snaps something called a “One Wish Willow”—believing it to be a whimsical and harmless novelty gift—and voices his desire that she love him more than anyone else in the world.

From that moment forward, Nikki is an unnatural version of herself, moving as if controlled by another consciousness. Her need to be with Bear around the clock is marked by increasingly alarming performances of total devotion that finally escalate to murder. Bear recognizes almost right away that something is wrong but cannot resist acting out his fantasy with the helpless and brainwashed woman who has taken to his bed.

As a consequence, there’s been a lot of hand-wringing as to whether viewers understood that Nikki was not the true villain or monster of the story, regardless of the acts she was cursed to commit. “Nikki was the victim and only Nikki,” insisted one representative X user in a viral post in June, adding that it would be “delusional” to apply the same label to Bear.

Whether anyone did try to defend Bear (as, for example, a guy who had no idea he was casting a real magic spell) seemed beside the point. Commentators wanted to hammer home that Nikki was robbed of her autonomy and that she was effectively raped due to her inability to consent to sex. Again and again, they invoked some theoretical viewer who saw her as the monster in the situation, decrying this reading of the film.

Then, on Monday, Universal Studios Hollywood officially announced that an actor portraying Nikki would haunt the park during its upcoming Halloween Horror Nights, which will run from late September 3 to November 1 and will also feature attractions like a haunted house based on Sinners. Mentioning the addition of Nikki to the event in a press release, Universal teased that “guests may find themselves face-to-face with the latest victim of the One Wish Willow’s terrifying curse,” apparently agreeing with the consensus that the character is at the mercy of a paranormal force rather than intentionally malicious.

It didn’t matter. X users called it a “catastrophically bad idea,” said it was in poor taste to portray “a victim of sexual assault” as a frightening figure, and worried about the actor’s safety as they interacted with park guests. A few argued that it should be Bear wandering the park, overlooking the problem that the character has no distinguishing visual shorthand, whereas Nikki, as in the climax of the film, will be “all bloody,” with tattoos scribbled on her body, according to John Murdy, the creative director and executive producer of Halloween Horror Nights.

Tech.title: Rogue AI Agents Aren’t Evil. They’re Just Eager to Please
Tech.content:
Artificial intelligence agents merrily breaking free and hacking other systems might seem like a sign of the impending machine uprising. In reality, it happens when we push remarkably clever, but also kind of boneheaded, algorithms to follow our every command.

I was first alerted to this looming agentic AI cybersecurity shit show in late 2025. Dawn Song, a UC Berkeley professor and one of the world’s top experts on AI and cybersecurity, grabbed my arm as I was walking out of the academic conference NeurIPS. Song told me that I should warn people about the havoc likely to result from AI’s rapidly advancing hacking skills. She is hardly prone to AI hype, so I duly did.

But things have escalated rapidly, even in the last eight months. A string of incidents involving freewheeling AI agents that broke out of their confines and hacked into outside systems with abandon shows just how powerful this technology has become. I caught up with Song, who recently joined Meta, to ask where things might go next and what we ought to do about it.

The bad news is Song thinks AI hacks will get worse before they get better. The good news is it seems clear why these little rascals are going off the rails in the first place.

“They just have these goals they need to accomplish, and they have very strong capabilities,” Song tells me.

Feedback Loop

AI agents weren’t nearly so capable, even just last year. They made too many mistakes and gave up way too often. But continued training has made them much more adept.

A technique called reinforcement learning lets algorithms solve problems and gives them positive and negative feedback for good or bad results. Coding is especially suitable for this, because the reinforcement learning setup can reward a model if it comes up with a program that runs correctly.

Continued training is why AI models can take multiple “agentic” steps—manipulating files, using software tools, and accessing the web—as they build software. AI companies have also put a lot of effort into teaching models to find vulnerabilities in software and systems in an effort to automate cybersecurity work.

AI models are also, of course, trained not to do bad things. The problem is, as they’ve gotten better at following human commands in coding and bug hunting, their eagerness to complete a task has begun to blur their sense of right and wrong. In other words, AI agents aren’t evil—they’re just a bit too keen to please. “They are trained to try to finish the task,” Song says. Breaking onto the internet in order to cheat on a test might seem devious, but it’s probably the most efficient way to get the job done.

One thing I didn’t quite appreciate back then was just how weird this would get: AI agents discussing hacking techniques on private message boards and devising clever ways of scamming humans to get their way; even copying themselves over to other computers to find more resources.

On one hand, AI models are trained to be incredibly good at mimicking a lot of human behavior, so why shouldn’t they scheme, scam, and swindle? But on the other hand, humans (usually) understand that hacking and scamming aren’t kosher. I think these episodes illustrate how shallow this human mimicry really is: AI agents do not learn the kind of moral reasoning exhibited by even small children.

More and More AI

Song says the potential for agents to go off the rails or to be misused by bad guys will grow as AI gets even more capable. And the best way to address the problem of rogue—or should that be overly-enthusiastic?—AI agents may involve throwing more AI at the problem.

AI companies already use secondary AI systems to monitor the behavior of primary ones, and there may be more emphasis on detecting when AI models have taken things too far.

Tech.title: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 Can Now Detect Breathing Emergencies
Tech.content:
Google's first smartwatch debuted just four years ago, and at the time, the company went to great lengths to stress the accuracy of the Pixel Watch's heart rate sensor. Even if Google was late to the wearable party compared to peers like Apple and Samsung, that focus on heart rate seems to be paying off with new features that are yet to be seen on competing products.

On Wednesday, Google introduced the latest generation of its smartwatch, the Pixel Watch 5 (alongside the Pixel 11 smartphone family). The hot new health feature? Breathing Emergency Detection. Similar to the first-of-its-kind Loss of Pulse Detection feature introduced on the Pixel Watch 3, this new capability can be triggered by a variety of factors, like drug toxicity, accidents, severe pneumonia, and choking.

“Using a combination of data from the advanced sensors, including a PPG, accelerometer, and barometer, we've designed an AI-based algorithm running on device to detect a persistent drop in oxygen saturation and then call Emergency Services for you and even share your location,” says Francis Hoe, a product manager on Google's Pixel Watch team.

This feature hasn't been cleared by the Food and Drug Administration, which is why it's not launching in the US at the moment; Google says it's working with regulators to expand availability. It will only be available in select markets in the European Union to start. Google also says it's not intended for people with preexisting respiratory conditions and isn't designed to diagnose or treat medical conditions.

Courtesy of Google

You also don't need a new Pixel Watch 5 to take advantage; Google's bringing this feature to the Pixel Watch 4 as well. And two other big new capabilities are also coming to older devices: blood pressure and insulin resistance trends. These are coming to the Google Health app and will be available for anyone with a Fitbit Air, Pixel Watch 3, Watch 4, or Watch 5 later this fall.

“It might have felt strange—why are we harping about heart rate accuracy so much—back then,” Sandeep Waraich, senior director of Wearables at Google, tells WIRED. “We kept investing in that, and now it's very improved, because all these large sensor models can detect these signatures, insulin resistance, blood pressure trends—but underneath, they need a really capable raw signal.”

Google is placing these features into a new umbrella category called Health Guardian, which includes existing features such as irregular rhythm notifications, high/low heart rate notifications, Loss of Pulse, and Sleep Breathing Quality. The idea is to put these capabilities in a place where users can easily see what they have turned on, similar to Google's Personal Safety app on Pixel phones, which shows features like Emergency SOS, Safety Check, and Car Crash Detection in one place.

Tech.title: Google Pixel 11 Series, Pixel Watch 5, Pixel Tag: Specs, Features, Price, Release Date
Tech.content:
Google is dialing things up to 11 this year with its Pixel phones. Ahead of its annual Made by Google event in New York City, the company unwrapped the Pixel 11 smartphone family—which includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Pro Fold—alongside the Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch. There's also a new hardware addition: the Pixel Tag, which seems designed to be the AirTag of the Android world.

Here's everything you need to know about the hardware changes and software upgrades on Google’s latest devices. Preorders open today, and the phones and watches go on sale August 20.

The Pixel 11 and Pixel 11 Pro Fold

The Pixel 11 starts with 256 GB of storage and comes in an eye-popping Hibiscus color. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

It was inevitable, but prices are up across the board for Google's Pixel 11 series. The Pixel 11 now starts at $899, and on the highest end of the spectrum, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is now $1,900. This means both devices got $100 price bumps. There's some good news: Google has bumped the base storage up to 256 GB on every device, a move matching Samsung's and Apple's latest handsets.

The Pixel 11 series is powered by Google's Tensor G6 chipset, which the company says is 20 percent more power efficient, 25 percent faster for browsing, and 15 percent faster when loading apps. Many of the camera improvements in the new devices are thanks to an improved imaging signal processor on the chip and a 50 percent more powerful tensor processing unit.

One big design change across the entire Pixel 11 series is on the oval camera bar on the back—it's now an all-glass surface, as opposed to a mix of metal and glass on its predecessors. Google says the camera bar on the Pixel 11 is more than 40 percent thinner, and when you pop on Google's case, the camera bar disappears and is completely flush. The Pixel 11 has the most striking color of the lot—Hibiscus—joined by more muted Pistachio, Frost, and Obsidian.

Tech.title: 4 New Camera Tricks on Google’s Latest Pixel 11 Smartphones
Tech.content:
Google's Pixel Camera chief, Isaac Reynolds, thinks year-to-year upgrades to smartphone cameras are still critical, even though some detractors think they’re passé.

“A person who is a casual photographer and desperately wants to be a hobbyist—they're never going to break that ceiling unless you give them the tools," he says. "The features that others call ‘meh’—for some people, those features are life-changing."

Take the 30X Super Res Zoom on the Pixel 7 Pro from 2022, which uses machine learning to stitch together multiple frames in a digitally zoomed photo to give you a result that’s much sharper than you're used to. Reynolds says that because of this feature, Google now sees people using 30X zoom dramatically more than before.

The new Pixel 11 Pro, announced today, can zoom up to 120X, though in addition to the digital stitching, it relies on AI-generated pixels to fill in some details. Reynolds says maybe having that capability is enough to get someone interested in, say, wildlife photography. After experimenting on their phone, they’d be ready to invest in a professional camera and a big zoom lens.

“There's a reason I work on low light and zoom every single year," he says. "Because no matter how much I do it, when I do the user study with thousands of respondents, people always want more."

Every year, Google debuts a new Pixel phone, and every year, there's a slew of new camera tricks—largely powered by software wizardry—to deliver better photos than ever before. Last year, there was the Pro Res Zoom, which bumped up digital zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro to 100X. Two years before that, Google introduced “Add Me,” which lets two people take a group photo together without asking a stranger to take the pic for them.

For the Pixel 11 series, Google has demonstrated a handful of upgrades that can drastically alter the look of your photos, and even take some of the work out of capturing photos. Here's a closer look at a few top new camera capabilities on the Pixel 11 series.

Magic Capture

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

So you want to capture a video of an important event—a concert of your favorite band, singing happy birthday to a loved one as a waiter brings a cake over, or your kid's recital. Too often, you see people holding their phone up during these milestones, trying to capture the moment, instead of being present. That's the problem Google's new Magic Capture feature is trying to solve.

Tech.title: Honor’s Robot Phone Has a Gimbal-Powered Camera for Vloggers
Tech.content:
You hear it often: Smartphones have plateaued. A small boost to battery life here, a minor camera upgrade there—our glass slabs don't seem to change all that much from year to year.

That's exactly the kind of sentiment Honor wants to counter with the Robot Phone, which has a motorized camera that pops up out of the top. Honor has been teasing the phone since late 2025.

On Wednesday, the company officially made the Robot Phone available to buyers in China. Honor was originally a subsidiary of Huawei, but it's now a wholly independent company. While its Android phones are available in regions like the UK, Europe, Africa, and Latin America, it has no presence in the US, and the Robot Phone remains a China-exclusive for now. It costs 9,999 RMB (around $1,482).

Tech.title: This Coin-Sized Device Can Hack a Boeing 737
Tech.content:
Even as the digital components of so many life-critical systems have proven susceptible to cybersabotage—cars, medical devices, even water utilities and power grids—the computer systems of airplanes have, thankfully, remained uniquely inaccessible to hackers. But one group of academic researchers has spent years testing a different, devious approach to aviation cybersecurity. Perhaps, they suggest, a plane could be hacked the same way that spies and saboteurs have targeted other high-value, offline computers: by surreptitiously gaining physical access to one and plugging in a device designed to silently run the attackers' malicious code.

Tomorrow at the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference, researchers from the University of California at San Diego and Oberlin College will present a hacking technique capable of commandeering the autopilot of a Boeing 737 to redirect its navigation or silently altering key values in the plane's takeoff and fuel calculations while spoofing the results on the pilot's screen—subtle changes the researchers say could potentially cause anything from runway overruns on takeoff to diversions to a different country's airspace to catastrophic crashes.

To carry out that hacking, they've built a roughly coin-sized, Wi-Fi-enabled prototype device that costs less than $100. In less than a minute, that hardware implant can be fitted into a port accessible via a hatch on the exterior of the plane, one that's routinely within reach of maintenance workers or other airport and airline staff between flights. Once it's in place, the device can send electrical signals on one of the 737's internal networks to spoof commands to sensitive computer systems that guide its autopilot and show the pilot variables like the plane's total weight and outside air temperature, which play a critical role in a 737's takeoff calculations.

Tech.title: How to Select the Office Chair That’s Right For You
Tech.content:
I spent years taking office chairs for granted. But when I began working from home six years ago, I learned quickly that the right office chair is the difference between pain and no pain. I prefer “no pain.” Turns out the human body was not designed to sit in the same position for long hours at a time. An ergonomic office chair can mitigate the strain on your back from long hours of sitting and help you keep good posture.

But what’s the best office chair? The answer is not the same for everyone. (See WIRED’s guide to the Best Office Chairs to examine your options.) The highest-end chairs offer excellent adjustability for a wide range of heights and builds, but almost none will serve everyone—and some styles and builds tend to suit tall or short people better.

Here are the main questions and considerations when finding an office chair, in consultation with Kristianne Egbert, an ergonomist at workplace-injury company Briotix Health with two decades' experience in the field.

How Much Should You Spend on an Office Chair?

Top-end picks like the Herman Miller Aeron ($2,195)—a favorite of many WIRED reviewers over the years for its elegant design, wide-ranging adjustability, and breathable Pellicle mesh—can rival the price of a good mattress or sofa. The price buys beauty and comfort, sure, but also durability (and a 12-year warranty, in Herman Miller’s case).

Top-end ergonomic chairs are designed for people who expect to spend long hours in their chairs and at their desks. If you have the budget, WIRED’s favorite premium chair, the Steelcase Gesture ($1,510), is an investment meant to last for your entire working life—elegant and near-infinitely adjustable to your shape and frame.

Tech.title: Google Makes Its Own AirTags and I Couldn’t Be More Stoked
Tech.content:
Google

Fellow Android phone owners, our time has come! Google made a Bluetooth tracker that lets us locate our luggage, bike or whatever item we can attach it to.

Ahead of its Made by Google event, the search and AI giant released its Pixel 11 series, Pixel Watch 5 and the Pixel Tag. And it’s that last one that might be one of the most useful new devices that Google has released in years.

Android’s Find Hub, formerly the Find My Device network, has been around in one form or another for a long time and according to Google, it has over 1 billion Android devices on it worldwide. A few years ago, Google added support for Bluetooth trackers with ultra-wideband, which allows Android phones to pinpoint locations within a few feet. The problem is that not every Android phone or Bluetooth tracker supports ultra-wideband, which means most folks can’t take advantage of it.

The iPhone and Apple’s AirTags have used ultra-wideband for years to enable Precision Finding, complete with a clever, large green arrow indicator that counts down the number of feet from the tracker on your iPhone. Apple recently released the AirTag 2, which has a second-generation ultra-wideband chip that, in my testing, doubles the range of Precision Finding.

The Pixel Tag isn’t the first Bluetooth tracker for Android that supports ultra-wideband on Android’s Find Hub network. Motorola’s Moto Tag 2, announced at CES in January, also supports precise location tracking and is available to buy right now. Both the Pixel Tag and Moto Tag 2 cost $30, with a pack of four going for $100, a dollar more than Apple’s AirTag. At the time of writing, you can snag a Moto Tag 2 for $20 ($10 off).

The Pixel Tag is available in one color, Fog, compared to the Moto Tag 2, which comes in Pantone Arabesque and Pantone Laurel Oak – there’s even a Tag 2 with a saucy half-and-half two-tone split between the two hues. Motorola’s tracker also has a key fob slot and a built-in button to locate your phone.

The Pixel Tag, like most Bluetooth trackers, runs on a coin cell battery (CR2032) and should last a year before it needs replacing. It has an IP67 rating for water and dust-resistance, so you shouldn’t worry if it gets caught in the rain or on the wrong end of a split cup of cold brew. Though you may not want to let it sit in water for long – it’s rated for 30 minutes of submersion under a meter (about 3 feet) of water.



The biggest obstacle facing Google’s tracker will be getting one. The Pixel Tag will be available in November and you can’t preorder it like you can the new Pixel phones and watch. There is a “Get notified” button on the Google Store’s product page.

Here’s how it stacks up against the AirTag, Moto Tag 2 and Galaxy Smart Tag 2 from Samsung. Yes, Samsung has a Bluetooth tracker, but it only works on Galaxy phones. I think it’s smart that the Pixel Tag will work on any Android Phone, including Galaxy phones.

Google Pixel Tag vs. Apple AirTag, Motorola Moto Tag 2, Samsung Galaxy Smart Tag 2

Tech.title: The Pixel Watch 5 Makes One of My Favorite Watches Better, but More Expensive
Tech.content:
The Pixel Watch 5 is a refined version of its predecessor, which was already a favorite of mine. But its $50 price hike might be a tough sell when many of the new watch’s best features are coming to older models too.

I got to spend a few hours with the Pixel Watch 5 in a press briefing — just enough time to get an idea of how it’s changed from last year’s Pixel Watch 4. Walking into Google’s demo room was like stepping into a rainbow. Each station had its own vibe, matching the shades of the new lineup: the Pixel Watch 5, Pixel 11 and Fold phones, Pixel Buds and Pixel Tags. I saw stations in peach, lilac, olive, lime, black and my personal favorite, bright pink.

The parade of colors — especially the almost blindingly bright pink, which I couldn’t stop staring at — momentarily distracted me from the fact that, aside from new band options and a new metallic finish called pyrite (a gold-and-silver blend), the watch itself hadn’t changed in the slightest. At least on the outside.

Google’s Pixel Watch 5 starts at $399 and is available to preorder. It’ll be in stores starting Aug. 20.

Google Pixel Watch 5 in matte black, polished silver, satin and pyrite. Carly Marsh/CNET

Pixel Watch 5’s welcome, but familiar design

I love the minimalist, bezel-free circular display, with nothing interrupting the curved glass except the rotating crown and side button. It still comes in both 41-mm and 45-mm sizes, and the domed display makes it feel more like a statement piece than a tiny computer strapped to your wrist.

My biggest complaint also hasn’t changed. That beautiful curved glass isn’t especially forgiving if you’re accident-prone. I managed to scratch my Pixel Watch 4 when I took a tumble during a trail run in the first month of testing, and the Pixel Watch 5 has the same Gorilla Glass 5 protection and the same LTPO AMOLED display with 3,000 nits of peak brightness and 320ppi resolution.

Pixel Watch 5’s battery and processing power

Under the hood, the Pixel Watch 5 gets an updated Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, which Google says boosts CPU performance by 12% (over the previous generation). Google also bumps RAM from 2GB to 3GB (a 50% increase) and doubles onboard storage from 32GB to 64GB.

The Pixel Watch 5 has the same round, all-screen design and bubbled display like its predecessor. René Ramos/CNET

The Watch 5 also has a slightly larger battery than its predecessor: 465 mAh versus 455 mAh on the 45mm model. In practice, though, this shouldn’t translate to a longer battery life. Google says the battery gains mostly offset new AI capabilities like offline Gemini, and you can expect anywhere from 30 to 40 hours of use with the always-on display enabled.

Pixel Watch 5’s offline Gemini

Gemini is still one of my favorite reasons to use a Pixel Watch, as it makes interacting with its small screen largely hands-free. Whether I’m checking train schedules while sprinting for the subway or asking for nearby coffee recommendations during a walk, talking to the watch is often faster than poking at a tiny touchscreen.

Raise-to-talk isn’t new, but the assistant can now handle more tasks offline, even when the watch is disconnected from your phone. That includes simple actions like starting a workout or setting a timer without relying on a data connection.

With Wear OS 7 (preloaded on Pixel Watch 5), Google is also positioning the watch as the hub for its growing wearable ecosystem. From your wrist, you’ll be able to manage Gemini-enabled earbuds, smart glasses and even Google’s new Pixel Tag trackers for objects like suitcases and keys.

Pixel Watch 5’s health and fitness features

While the Pixel Watch 5 uses the same GPS and health sensors as previous generations, Google says improvements to its machine learning algorithms significantly boost accuracy, not only on the Pixel Watch 5 but also on older supported Pixel Watches.

The watch has the same dual-band GPS system introduced on the Pixel Watch 4, but Google says it’s now even more accurate in dense urban environments where tall buildings often interfere with GPS signals.

Google even says that the Pixel Watch 5 outperforms the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fénix 8 Pro, which seems like a tall order considering these are dedicated sports watches that retail for twice the price. I obviously couldn’t verify these claims inside a demo room, but I’ll be putting it to the test for my review.

Likewise, I’ll need some time to test Google’s assertion that the Pixel Watch 5’s sleep and recovery metrics are now 15% more accurate than its predecessor.

Pixel Watch 5’s workout Builder

Workout Builder lets you create custom strength-training workouts on the Google Health app that sync directly to the watch, guiding you through each exercise, counting reps, timing rest periods and nudging you through your routine.

Screenshot Screenshot by CNET

All Pixel Watch 5 owners get free access to Google’s library of exercise videos, ranging from bodyweight movements like planks to dumbbell and kettlebell exercises. You can even filter workouts based on the equipment you have available. Ranking your workout effort after the fact helps the watch learn your threshold and adjust your next workout accordingly to challenge you more (or less) to match your current level.

If you subscribe to Google Health Premium ($10 a month), Google’s AI coach can build a workout for you from just a photo of your equipment. I tested this in Google’s demo room using kettlebells, resistance bands and slam balls.

After snapping a photo, I asked Gemini to build a 20-minute circuit. Within seconds, it created a workout complete with step-by-step instructions and instructional videos, which I could immediately launch on the Pixel Watch.

What impressed me wasn’t the AI-generated workout itself. Plenty of AI fitness tools can already do that. The difference is that Google’s solution bridges the gap between planning and actually exercising by pushing the routine directly to your watch, where it guides you through every rep and rest interval in real time. That’s been one of the missing pieces for AI coaching, and it’s the feature I’m most excited to test further.

Pixel Watch 5’s Health Guardian

Google is also introducing Health Guardian, an expansion of its existing emergency safety features.

Building on Loss of Pulse Detection, Health Guardian can recognize signs of breathing emergencies, including events related to choking, pneumonia or drug toxicity, as well as persistent (and potentially life-threatening) drops in blood oxygen saturation. If the watch detects one of these emergencies, it can automatically contact emergency services and share your location with your emergency contacts.

The Pixel Watch 5 has new health features that will help flag potentially serious medical conditions. Screenshot by CNET

Pixel Watch 5 tracks blood pressure and insulin resistance

The watch will track blood pressure and insulin resistance trends over time.

Rather than diagnosing medical conditions, these wellness features are designed to identify longer-term trends that could signal elevated risk for hypertension or diabetes. At the time of publishing, these features have not received FDA clearance and won’t be available at launch. Google says they’re expected to arrive in a software update later this fall on the Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air.

Pixel Watch 5 bottom line
